summary: Verify every historical claim the Pacific Galleon game asserts, against fetched primary sources
logs: Verifying 6 claim clusters against fetched primary sources

claims.claim: "Took the treasure ship Cacafuego off Peru."
claims.finding: All three source traditions place the capture at Cape San Francisco, about 1 degree NORTH latitude, roughly 150 leagues south of Panama. That is the Esmeraldas coast of modern Ecuador, not Peru, and it is north of the equator. Hakluyt's marginal note reads "Cape de San Francisco standing in 1. deg. of North lat." The World Encompassed locates it "in the entrance of the bay of Panama, in 1 deg. of North latitude." San Juan de Anton's own deposition: "Off the Cape of San Francisco, at noon, they saw a sail." What IS Peruvian is the ship and her cargo: Anton and his clerk Domingo de Lizarza both depose that the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion sailed from Callao, the port of the city of Los Reyes (Lima), on 22 January 1579, topping up with registered silver at Guaura, Barranca and Trujillo. So she was a Peru-to-Panama treasure runner, caught at the Panama end of the run, on the coast of the province of Quito (Audiencia of Quito, within the Viceroyalty of Peru). The judicial inquiry was held not in Lima but by the Royal Audiencia of PANAMA, 16 March 1579, because that is where Anton limped in. In loose 16th-century usage "the coast of Peru" could stretch that far, and Lizarza uses "the coast of Peru" for waters where Drake had taken prisoners. But as geography "off Peru" is wrong by roughly 900 km.
claims.quote: "The place where we tooke this prize, was called Cape de San Francisco, about 150. leagues from Panama."
claims.source: Hakluyt, 'The famous voyage of Sir Francis Drake', in The Principal Navigations (1600), MacLehose edn, vol. XI, p. 116 (original folio III. 736); corroborated by The World Encompassed (1628), Hakluyt Society edn 1854, pp. 110-111; and San Juan de Anton's deposition, Panama, 16 March 1579, in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (Hakluyt Society, 1914), pp. 164-165, and Lizarza's deposition, ibid. pp. 176-177
claims.retrieval_note: Downloaded the djvu text and proved identity before use: title page reads "The Principal / Navigations Voyages Traffiques and / Discoveries of the English Nation / In Twelve Volumes / Volume XI / GLASGOW ... MACLEHOSE ... MCMIV"; the text carries the original 1600 folio references in brackets ("[III. 736.]") and the printed shoulder-notes ("The rich ship called the Cacafuego taken", "Cape de San Francisco"). Page numbers 115 and 116 appear as standalone lines bracketing the passage. I also checked the index volume (vol. XII) which cross-references "the Cacafuego taken by (1579) 116, 264" and "Anton, Juan de, Captain of a Spanish treasure ship captured by Sir Francis Drake, xi. 264" - so the quoted page is the one the edition's own index points to.
claims.game_impact: Change. "Off Peru" should become "off Cape San Francisco, on the Panama run" or "off the Quito coast (Ecuador), bound Callao to Panama". If the blurb must stay short, "took the Lima treasure ship bound for Panama" is both shorter and accurate. Flag the current wording as loose, not invented.

claims.claim: The ship's real name, and whether "Cacafuego" is a nickname.
claims.finding: Her registered name was Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion; San Juan de Anton was her master, pilot and owner. Two independent Spanish documents in the Panama inquiry give the name: the oidor Alonso Criado de Castilla summons "San Juan de Anton, the master and owner of the ship named 'Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion'", and the ship's clerk Lizarza opens his own deposition the same way. "Cacafuego" appears only in the ENGLISH sources, and both of them treat it as a jest rather than a name: Hakluyt and The World Encompassed both record the pilot's boy telling Drake the ship should be renamed the Cacaplata and Drake's ship the Cacafuego. Literally cagafuego / cagaplata = shitfire / shitsilver; Nuttall renders them politely as Spitfire and Spitsilver. One caution against over-reading: Nuttall (p. 165 n.) actually DISSENTS from the usual story, arguing from the ship's true registered name and from Anton's statement that he "did not carry artillery or arms" that the Concepcion could hardly have been nicknamed Spitfire, and that the name properly belonged to the Golden Hind, with the Spaniard being called Spitsilver in repartee. So the direction of the joke is contested; the ship's real name is not.
claims.quote: "We found her to be indeed the Cacafuego, though before we left her, she were new named by a boy of her owne the Cacaplata." And the boy's own words: "Captaine, our ship shall be called no more the Cacafuego, but the Cacaplata, and your shippe shall bee called the Cacafuego."
claims.source: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (1628), Hakluyt Society edn, ed. W. S. W. Vaux, 1854, pp. 110-111; the boy's speech also at Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose edn vol. XI, p. 116 (= 1854 appendix p. 242); real name in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914), pp. 164 (Anton) and 176 (Lizarza), with Nuttall's dissenting note at p. 165 n. 1
claims.retrieval_note: Nuttall identity proved from the front matter, which prints the Hakluyt Society series block ("WORKS ISSUED BY The Hakluyt Society / NEW LIGHT ON DRAKE / SECOND SERIES No. XXXIV / ISSUED FOR 1914") and the 1914 Council list (Albert Gray, President). Each cited document is anchored by its own running head in the OCR - "DEPOSITION OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 165", "DEPOSITION OF DOMINGO DE LIZARZA 177" - and by the archival citation Nuttall prints as a footnote: "Archive General de Indias, Seville, E. i, C. i, L. 2-21". The 1854 World Encompassed was proved by its Hakluyt Society title page (Murchison as President, E. H. Major Hon. Sec.) and by its running heads "BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE" / "THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD" with page numbers.
claims.game_impact: Keep, but gain a free flavour item: the ship's real name was Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion and Cacafuego was a sailors' obscenity. The boy's jest is quotable primary-source dialogue. If the game wants to be scrupulous, note that Nuttall thinks the nickname was Drake's ship's, not hers.

claims.claim: Drake overhauled her over DAYS and disguised his own speed by trailing drags astern (mattresses, wine jars, cables) so she would not run.
claims.finding: The DRAGS are solidly in the sources, from two independent eyewitnesses on Drake's own ship, and the detail is better than the claim. John Drake (Drake's page, deposed at Lima 1587) says Drake pretended not to be following her and hung out cables and mattresses to slow the galleon; Nuttall notes his Spanish was "cabos y colchones". Nuno da Silva, Drake's captive Portuguese pilot, says they filled Spanish oil jars (botijas) with water and hung them by ropes at the stern. Crucially, Hakluyt's English version of da Silva MISTRANSLATES the purpose as "to make her sayle the better"; Nuttall's Simancas Spanish text reads "y porque su nao yva algo delantera y no navegase tanto hecho cables por popa con botijas llenas de agua" - because his ship was going somewhat ahead, and so that she should not make such headway. Nuttall cites Laughton and Corbett that drags were a common pirate device, and Corbett's point is that John Drake's testimony settles the direction: slow her down, not speed her up. Also confirmed: Drake was actively deceiving her. His own Spanish-speaking men hailed Anton claiming to be "the ship of Miguel Angel"; he lowered sail and hid his pinnace on the off side of the galleon. The "over DAYS" half is where the claim slips. The CHASE ran about a fortnight: Drake left Callao on 15/16 February on news of a rich ship, and took her on 1 March. But the drag-and-shadow ruse occupied a single afternoon and evening. John Drake first sighted her at three leagues (da Silva says four) "towards noone"; Hakluyt says John Drake descried her about three of the clock and they boarded about six; Anton says he saw the sail at noon, it altered towards him about eight, and came alongside at nine. So: hours, not days. Drake then kept the prize in company three to six days while transferring the silver.
claims.quote: John Drake: "In order to take her, Captain Francis pretended not to follow her and, to prevent his galleon from sailing too fast, he hung out many cables and mattresses which went dragging along." Nuno da Silva (Hakluyt's English): "they tooke a company of Botijas or Spanish pots for oyle, and filling them with water, hung them by ropes at the sterne of the ship".
claims.source: Second declaration of John Drake, Lima 1587, in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914), pp. 48-49 (with Nuttall's note on "cabos y colchones" and the botijas, p. 48 n. 3 and p. 267 n. 1); Nuno da Silva's second relation, ibid. pp. 266-267, Simancas Spanish text in Nuttall's footnote; chronology from Hakluyt, Principal Navigations XI, pp. 115-116, The World Encompassed (1854 edn) pp. 109-111, and Anton's deposition, Nuttall p. 165
claims.retrieval_note: Proved I was reading the right documents by their running heads in the OCR: "SECOND DECLARATION OF JOHN DRAKE 49" immediately after the mattress sentence, and "NUNO DA SILVA'S SECOND RELATION 267" immediately after the botijas sentence. The botijas footnote on p. 267 prints the Simancas Spanish verbatim and names Laughton and Corbett ("op. cit. i, p. 274"), which is the cross-reference that proves this is Nuttall's critical apparatus and not a stray page. I then checked the same episode independently in Hakluyt XI (pp. 115-116) and The World Encompassed (1854, pp. 109-111) for the timings.
claims.game_impact: Change the timescale, keep and upgrade the mechanic. The drags are real, triple-attested, and come with a free second deception layer (false hail: "we are the ship of Miguel Angel", sail lowered, pinnace hidden to leeward). But model it as a one-evening approach ruse at the end of a two-week pursuit, not a multi-day drag. If the game currently shows days of drag-trailing, that is an over-read.

claims.claim: She was taken "almost without a fight".
claims.finding: Nobody on either side was killed and the Spaniard never fired a shot, because she had nothing to fire: Anton deposes that he "did not carry artillery or arms" and "could not make any resistance", and Lizarza says they boarded "because she was powerless to resist". In that sense the claim is right, and it is a bigger finding than the game models: the richest ship on the Pacific treasure run sailed unarmed and unescorted. But she did not surrender tamely. Summoned to strike, Anton flatly refused. His own testimony to Sarmiento gives the exchange: told to strike or be sunk, "San Juan answered: 'What England is this [which gives me orders] for striking sail? Come on board to strike [the] sails yourselves!'" Lizarza's version is the blunt "San Juan de Anton replied that he would not." Only then did Drake open fire. Anton's account of what followed: a whistle and trumpet, a volley of about sixty arquebuses, many arrows into her side, chain-shot from a heavy gun that carried the mizzen overboard with its sail and lateen yard, a second great gun, then a pinnace alongside to port with about forty archers climbing the shrouds while the Golden Hind laid aboard on the other side. Hakluyt says three pieces of ordnance and the mizzen struck down; Lizarza says two heavy shots, one taking the mizzen, the other passing high near the main-mast; da Silva says one great piece shot her mast overboard and the master was wounded by an arrow. John Drake says an arrow wounded Anton and he then struck. Anton himself, notably, does not mention his own wound. He was alone on deck when they seized him and refused to answer their questions. Drake then embraced him with "ten paciencia que usanza es de guerra" (have patience, such is the usage of war), had his own table laid for him next morning, and later gave him a written safe-conduct.
claims.quote: "and chain-balls shot from a heavy piece of ordnance carried away the mizen and sent it into the sea with its sail and lateen yard... a pinnace laid aboard to port and about forty archers climbed up the channels of the shrouds and entered San Juan de Anton's ship, while, at the opposite side, the English ship laid aboard." And Anton's refusal: "San Juan de Anton respondio que no queria...."
claims.source: Testimony of San Juan de Anton, in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914), pp. 157-159; deposition of San Juan de Anton, ibid. p. 165; deposition of Domingo de Lizarza, ibid. pp. 176-177 (Spanish in n. 1); John Drake's second declaration, ibid. pp. 48-49; Nuno da Silva's second relation, ibid. p. 267; Hakluyt, Principal Navigations XI, p. 116
claims.retrieval_note: Each witness was located by running head and anchored on a printed Spanish phrase that Nuttall supplies in footnote, which is how I know I am on the deposition and not on Nuttall's commentary: p. 158-159 carries "TESTIMONY OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 159" with the footnote "'ten paciencia que usanza es de guerra'"; p. 177 carries "DEPOSITION OF DOMINGO DE LIZARZA 177" with footnote "'San Juan de Anton respondio que no queria....'"; p. 165 carries "DEPOSITION OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 165". I cross-read the same minutes in three other witnesses before accepting any of it.
claims.game_impact: Keep the outcome, change the texture. "Almost without a fight" is right as to casualties (zero) and Spanish resistance (none possible), but wrong if it implies she struck on demand. She refused the summons, took a sixty-arquebus volley, arrows, and chain-shot that took her mizzen over the side, and was boarded simultaneously from two sides by about forty archers. The real finding to model is that she was UNARMED: the treasure run had no guns and no escort.

claims.claim: What did she carry, and what did Drake take out of her?
claims.finding: The English and Spanish figures agree closely on the headline number and differ in the breakdown. ENGLISH (Hakluyt and The World Encompassed): jewels and precious stones; thirteen chests full of royals of plate; four score pound weight of gold; six and twenty tunne of silver; The World Encompassed adds fruit, conserves, sugars, meal and other victuals, two very fair gilt silver drinking bowls, and the valuation "about 360,000 pezoes", and says it was the weight of the treasure that made her "heauy and slow sayling". Hakluyt gives no valuation. Hakluyt separately records that Drake made the pilot give up one of his two silver cups and gave the other to the Golden Hind's steward. NUNO DA SILVA, aboard Drake's ship, gives a different and more granular tally: 1,300 bars or pieces of silver and fourteen chests of reals of eight and gold, of which the passengers said three hundred bars were the king's. SPANISH, sworn: Anton's deposition says about 360,000 pesos in gold, silver and reals, "registered or to be registered", including what belonged to sailors and passengers; Lizarza independently gives the same 360,000. Anton's fuller testimony to Sarmiento breaks it down: 362,000 pesos registered in bars, reals and gold, of which 106,000 belonged to His Majesty, "but, with what was on board beside this, the total amounts to more than 400,000 pesos". Drake also took victuals, two casks of water, tackle, sails, canvas and a cable. The Panama summary reckons Drake's whole South Sea haul from Valparaiso to Cape San Francisco at 447,000 pesos in coin, besides porcelain, jewels, precious stones, pearls, stuffs and victuals, plus another 100,000 in damage. An English state paper summarising the Seville merchants' 1580 depositions puts the Spanish global claim at "a million of pezos of golde, everye pezos worthe 450 maravedis", notes only 400,006 pesos could be proved registered, and records that "Sr Frances Drake dothe utterlye denye" it. He held the prize five or six days, killed no one, released her on 7 March with her crew and the remainder of her cargo, and gave Anton a safe-conduct.
claims.quote: "We found in her some fruite, conserues, sugars, meale, and other victuals, and (that which was the especiallest cause of her heauy and slow sayling) a certaine quantitie of iewels and precious stones, 13 chests of ryals of plate, 80 pound waight in gold, 26 tunne of vncoyned siluer, two very faire gilt siluer drinking boules, and the like trifles, valued in all at about 360,000 pezoes." And from the Spanish side: "The registered silver seized amounted to 362,000 pesos in bars, reals and gold. Of this 106,000 belonged to His Majesty and the rest to private individuals. This is what was registered but, with what was on board beside this, the total amounts to more than 400,000 pesos."
claims.source: The World Encompassed (1628), Hakluyt Society edn 1854, p. 111; Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose edn XI, p. 116; Nuno da Silva's second relation in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914), p. 267; Testimony of San Juan de Anton, ibid. p. 159; deposition of Anton, ibid. p. 165; deposition of Lizarza, ibid. p. 176; Panama summary, ibid. p. 162; English abstract of the Seville depositions, 1580, ibid. pp. 417-418
claims.retrieval_note: The World Encompassed figure is on a page whose running head the OCR preserves ("BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE. 111"), and the identical prize list minus the valuation appears independently in the Hakluyt vol. XI text at p. 116, which is a different scan of a different book - so the list is not an OCR artefact of one file. The Spanish figures were each located under their own running head, and the Seville abstract was confirmed by its own marginal notes, which the OCR reproduces ("At Chile", "Arica 34 barres of sylver", "Mr St Jo. de Anton ... Francisco 360.m registred") plus the signature line "D- 27" and page "4i8" (= 418).
claims.game_impact: Keep, with exact numbers available instead of round ones. Use 13 chests of reals, 80 lb of gold, 26 tons of silver, two gilt silver bowls, and a valuation of about 360,000 pesos registered (362,000 per Anton, of which 106,000 the Crown's, over 400,000 all told). Do NOT use the "million pesos" figure as fact: it is the Spanish claimants' estimate and Drake denied it. Note also that 26 tons of silver on a 100-ton ship means roughly a quarter of her burden in bullion.

claims.claim: Golden Hind particulars: tonnage, length, beam, guns, crew. The game models her at 72 ft long, 24.6 ft beam, 3 masts, the smallest and fastest and weakest-gunned of the four, best boarders.
claims.finding: TONNAGE: well attested and consistent - Hakluyt's fleet list: "The Pelican, admirall, burthen 100 tonnes, Captaine-generall Francis Drake" (the Pelican was renamed Golden Hind in the Strait). Spanish eyewitnesses who were put aboard reckoned her larger because they measured differently: Lizarza "about one hundred and eighty tons"; Nuno da Silva's sworn deposition, "The Capitana was the largest of all and was of about 220 tons", with Nuttall's note "which was of 100 tons English". GUNS: 18 is the best-supported figure, from three independent reckonings. Da Silva: "She has seven armed port-holes on each side, and inside she carries eighteen pieces of artillery, thirteen being of bronze and the rest of cast iron." Lizarza: twelve cast-iron heavy pieces, five a side and two at the poop, plus four more brought up from below (two bronze) and two more bronze in the ballast = 18. Corbett's fleet table, taking the guns from John Drake's deposition, also gives the Pelican 18 guns. Anton's figures as reported in the Panama summary are lower (fifteen heavy cast-iron pieces); Corbett quotes Anton elsewhere for a higher count. CREW: 164 at departure per Hakluyt and The World Encompassed ("These ships he mand with 164 able and sufficient men"), 150 and some boys per the Sloane MS, 140 per John Drake. In the Pacific the Golden Hind alone carried about 80: Lizarza "about eighty men, sixty of whom are good for fighting"; Benito Diaz Bravo "eighty men"; another witness "seventy or eighty men of which fifty appeared to be very good men for fighting". By the East Indies she was down to fifty-six. LENGTH AND BEAM: I could not find 72 ft or 24.6 ft, or any linear dimension at all, in any of the primary or early sources. No contemporary document in Hakluyt, The World Encompassed, Nuttall's Spanish depositions, or Corbett gives her length, beam or depth. Those figures are modern reconstruction values, and they do not sit comfortably with 100 tons burden: Elizabethan tonnage was keel x beam x depth / 100, and Corbett quotes Borough's own table giving the galleon Foresight at 290 tons for length 79, beam 27, depth 14 - i.e. a 24.6 ft beam belongs on a ship of two to three hundred tons, not one hundred. MASTS: no source states a number. Three is a safe inference, not a citation: Anton's testimony has Drake leaving the capture ground "under the mizen sail and foresails", and Hakluyt records the Pelican's main-mast being cut away at Falmouth, so main, fore and mizzen are all attested; whether she also carried a bonaventure mizzen is not recoverable. FASTEST: supported by the mechanism itself - Drake had to hang drags to stop overhauling her too fast - and by da Silva, "She is a good sailer and the rudder governs her well", though he also says she leaks badly in a high sea and is fit for two voyages Portugal-to-Brazil. BEST BOARDERS: well supported. 50 to 60 of about 80 aboard were rated fighting men; the Spaniards describe pikes, arquebuses, bows, firearms and concealable armour in the poop cabin; and the capture was made by about forty archers boarding from a pinnace while the ship laid aboard on the opposite side. WEAKEST-GUNNED: depends on the comparison set, which I cannot see. In absolute terms 18 light pieces is feeble beside any 18th-century warship. But 18 guns on 100 tons is a HIGH gun density for her type, so "weakest-gunned" is misleading if it is meant to say she was lightly armed for her size.
claims.quote: "1. The Pelican, admirall, burthen 100 tonnes, Captaine-generall Francis Drake." ... "These ships he mand with 164 able and sufficient men". And da Silva on the same ship: "She has seven armed port-holes on each side, and inside she carries eighteen pieces of artillery, thirteen being of bronze and the rest of cast iron, also an abundance of all sorts of ammunition of war, for none had been expended."
claims.source: The World Encompassed (1628), Hakluyt Society edn 1854, pp. 6-7 (fleet list and complement); Nuno da Silva's sworn deposition, Mexico 1579, in Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914), pp. 302-303 and Nuttall's n. 1 identifying the Capitana as the Pelican / Golden Hind "of 100 tons English"; Lizarza's deposition, ibid. pp. 177-178; Benito Diaz Bravo's deposition, ibid. p. 147; Panama summary, ibid. p. 162; Corbett, Drake and the Tudor Navy, 2nd edn, vol. I, pp. 217-218 and p. 359 n. 3 (Borough's dimensions for the Foresight) and p. 226 (fifty-six men)
claims.retrieval_note: Da Silva's ship description was confirmed to be about Drake's own flagship, not a prize, by Nuttall's footnote on the same page identifying "The Capitana" as "the 'Pelican,' afterwards rechristened 'The Golden Hind,' which was of 100 tons English" and by the next footnote identifying the two lost consorts as the Elizabeth (80 tons) and Marigold (30 tons) - the tonnages match Hakluyt's fleet list exactly, which is what proves the identification. Running head "NUNO DA SILVA'S SWORN DEPOSITION 303". For Corbett I verified the file is a Burt Franklin facsimile of Corbett's SECOND EDITION (its own "PREFACE TO THE SECOND EDITION" is present), i.e. the 1899 text, public domain, even though the IA metadata year is a reprint date; I kept Corbett quotations to a few words accordingly. The negative finding on dimensions was tested by grepping all five files for "feet", "keel", "beam", "length" - the only Elizabethan hull dimensions anywhere in them are for other ships (the 1576 row-barges, the Foresight, the Tiger).
claims.game_impact: Mixed. Tonnage (100 tons burden), guns (18), and crew (164 out of Plymouth, about 80 in the Pacific, 56 by the East Indies) are all citable and should be used as given. 3 masts is a reasonable reconstruction but has no source - mark it as modelled, not documented. FLAG 72 ft x 24.6 ft AS INVENTED: no source of any date in this cluster gives her dimensions, and 24.6 ft of beam is inconsistent with 100 tons by the period's own tonnage rule. If the game needs numbers, say so in the sources table as a modern reconstruction. "Fastest" and "best boarders" are defensible and evidenced; "weakest-gunned" needs a qualifier because her gun-to-tonnage ratio was high.

claims.claim: Drake's dates: "1577-80".
claims.finding: Correct. The fleet left Plymouth Sound about 5 in the afternoon of 15 November 1577, was forced by a southwester into Falmouth, lost the Pelican's main-mast in a gale there, returned to Plymouth, and sailed again finally on 13 December 1577. The Golden Hind came back into Plymouth on 26 September 1580, which the crew reckoned as Sunday because they had lost a day going west - The World Encompassed notices the discrepancy, one of the earliest date-line observations in English. Total: 2 years 10 months and some odd days. One trap: Hakluyt's 'Famous Voyage' text ends "We arriued in England the third of Nouember 1580. being the third yeere of our departure", which is wrong; the 26 September date from The World Encompassed is the one Corbett and the Hakluyt Society follow, and Nuttall's own title gives the span as 1577-1580. The engraved portrait reproduced as Nuttall's frontispiece carries the same dates in its Latin caption (returned "4. Cal. Octobris anno... 1580", set out "Decemb: anno 1577").
claims.quote: "Whence (hauing in few daies supplied all defects) with happier sayles, we once more put to sea, December 13, 1577." ... "And the 26 of Sept. (which was Monday in the iust and ordinary reckoning of those that had stayed at home in one place or countrie, but in our computation was the Lords day or Sonday) we safely with ioyfull minds and thankfull hearts to God, arrived at Plimoth, the place of our first setting forth, after we had spent 2 yeares 10 moneths and some few odde daies beside".
claims.source: The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake (1628), Hakluyt Society edn 1854, pp. 7-8 (departures) and pp. 162-163 (arrival); the erroneous 3 November date at Hakluyt, 'The famous voyage', 1854 appendix p. 241 (= Principal Navigations, MacLehose XI); title of Nuttall, New Light on Drake (1914): "a collection of documents relating to his voyage of circumnavigation, 1577-1580"
claims.retrieval_note: Both dates were read with their page numbers visible in the OCR: the 13 December sentence sits under the running head sequence that includes "O THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD," for p. 8, and the arrival passage is bracketed by "BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE. 161" and "162 THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD." I deliberately checked the Hakluyt 'Famous Voyage' ending as well, which is how I caught the conflicting 3 November 1580 date rather than assuming the sources agreed.
claims.game_impact: Keep "1577-80" as written. Optional precision if the game ever shows exact dates: 13 December 1577 (after a false start on 15 November) to 26 September 1580. Do not use 3 November 1580 - it is Hakluyt's error.

claims.claim: Was Drake "the first Englishman round the world"?
claims.finding: Defensible but loose as a singular. On the evidence I can reach, no Englishman had completed a circumnavigation before 1580. Only one circumnavigation had been completed at all - the Victoria's, 1519-22 - and Magellan's armada contained exactly one Englishman, who did not survive it. Guillemard, working from the fleet's pay books and muster rolls in the Seville archives, found "One Englishman there was, and one only, a certain Master Andrew of Bristol, master-gunner of the flag-ship", and records that on 9 March 1521 at the Ladrones "the sole Englishman in the fleet - 'Master Andrew of Bristol' - died, the succour having come too late to save his life". He was on the Trinidad, which never got home. So Drake's is the first English circumnavigation and only the second ever completed. Two honest qualifications. First, Drake did not do it alone: about fifty-six of his men were still aboard the Golden Hind in the East Indies, and they rounded the world at the same moment he did, so "the first Englishman" as a singular is imprecise - "led the first English circumnavigation" is the exact claim. Second, this is a negative claim about a 16th-century crew list, and a negative cannot be proved outright from the sources; what I can say is that the best archival enumeration of the only previous circumnavigating fleet finds one Englishman and records his death before the Pacific crossing ended. None of the contemporary narratives in Hakluyt, The World Encompassed or Nuttall actually makes the "first Englishman" boast in those words - I searched all four texts for it and found nothing.
claims.quote: "One Englishman there was, and one only, a certain Master Andrew of Bristol, master-gunner of the flag-ship." And: "On this day the sole Englishman in the fleet - 'Master Andrew of Bristol' - died, the succour having come too late to save his life."
claims.source: F. H. H. Guillemard, The Life of Ferdinand Magellan and the First Circumnavigation of the Globe, 1480-1521 (1890), pp. 137, 226, and p. 328 n. 1 (Andrew's pay, Seville archives, and the 4,014 maravedis paid after his decease); Drake's remaining complement of fifty-six from Corbett, Drake and the Tudor Navy, 2nd edn, I, p. 226, citing Vaux p. 184 and John Drake
claims.retrieval_note: Guillemard's identity was proved from the front matter (the Saturday Review puff, and his own preface noting that no life of the navigator had yet been written in English and pointing the English reader to "Lord Stanley of Alderley's 'First Voyage'"), and the Master Andrew finding appears three times in the book at consistent points - the crew-composition discussion (p. 137), the narrative of 9 March 1521 (p. 226), and the appendix analysis of the ships' books (p. 328) with a footnote citing a specific sum of maravedis from the Seville archives. Three mutually consistent appearances with an archival money figure is what persuaded me, not the single sentence. I also downloaded Lord Stanley's Hakluyt Society Magellan volume (1874) and grepped it for "English", "Ingles", "Bristol" - it contains no crew roster, which is a null result worth recording rather than a confirmation.
claims.game_impact: Change the wording, keep the substance. "The first Englishman round the world" should become "led the first English circumnavigation" or "first Englishman to command a voyage round the world" - about fifty-six of his crew did it alongside him. The stronger and still-true boast the game is not using: Drake was the first captain of ANY nation to command a circumnavigation and live to see it finished (Magellan died at Cebu; Elcano brought the Victoria home).

nulls: No linear dimensions for the Golden Hind / Pelican exist in any source I fetched. I grepped all of Hakluyt Principal Navigations vol. XI, The World Encompassed (1854 Hakluyt Society, which includes Fletcher's MS and the Famous Voyage appendix), Nuttall's New Light on Drake (the complete Spanish depositions), and both Corbett volumes for "feet", "keel", "beam", "length", "depth" and "burthen". The only Elizabethan hull dimensions anywhere in them belong to other vessels (1576 row-barges 45 x 18 x 11; the galleon Foresight 79 x 27 x 14 at 290 tons; the Tiger 50 x 24 x 13). The game's 72 ft and 24.6 ft therefore have no documentary basis I could find.

No source states how many masts the Golden Hind carried. Main, fore and mizzen are each separately attested in passing (Hakluyt on the main-mast cut away at Falmouth; Anton's testimony on Drake sailing "under the mizen sail and foresails"), but no text counts them and no text addresses a bonaventure mizzen.

No contemporary English narrative in the texts I fetched makes the "first Englishman round the world" claim in those words. I searched Hakluyt XI, The World Encompassed 1854, Nuttall and Corbett vol. I for "first Englishman", "first English", "first of our nation" and "first that ever": no hits in the relevant sense. The claim is a later formulation, not a contemporary boast I could source.

I could not obtain a crew roster of the Victoria's eighteen survivors to test the "no earlier Englishman" negative directly. Lord Stanley of Alderley's Hakluyt Society Magellan volume (1874, IA firstvoyageround00piga) was downloaded and grepped for "English", "Ingles", "Inglaterra" and "Bristol" - it has no roster at all, only the Trinidad narrative from Navarrete. I fell back on Guillemard 1890, who worked from the Seville pay books. The negative therefore rests on one archival enumeration, not two.

The sources disagree on when the Concepcion left Callao and I could not reconcile it. Anton and Lizarza both swear 22 January 1579; The World Encompassed says Drake heard at Lima of a rich ship "that had set forth of this hauen the second of Februarie" and was "gone from Lima 14 dayes before vs". Anton's stops at Guaura, Barranca and Trujillo to load registered silver may explain it, but no document in hand says so.

The sources disagree on which mast the shot took, and I did not resolve it. Anton's testimony, Anton's deposition, John Drake and Hakluyt all say the mizzen; Lizarza says one shot took the mizzen and the other passed near the main-mast; da Silva says simply "shotte her mast ouerboord"; Nuttall's OCR of Lizarza at one point reads "main-mast" where the sentence continues from the mizzen. Treat "mizzen" as the majority reading, not a settled one.

I did not establish the jurisdictional status of the Cape San Francisco coast in 1579 from a primary source. That it lay in the province of Quito within the Viceroyalty of Peru is my inference from the documents (Drake's prizes there come "from Quito" and "from Guayaquil"; Drake speaks of writing to "the Viceroy"; the Royal Audiencia of Peru and the Royal Audiencia of Panama both act in the papers). I did not find a document stating the boundary, and I am not presenting it as established.
