sources_fetched.proof_it_is_the_right_text: Title page "In Twelve Volumes / Volume XII", MacLehose imprint; body is the general index. Used only as a finding aid, to confirm that vol. XI pp. 115-116 and 264 are where this edition itself locates the Cacafuego and Juan de Anton ("Anton, Juan de, Captain of a Spanish treasure ship captured by Sir Francis Drake, xi. 264"; "Drake... the Cacafuego taken by (1579) 116, 264"; "Drake, John, captain, sights the Cacafuego (1579) XI. 116"). Note its editorial introduction contains an error the game should not inherit - it calls the Cacafuego "a treasure-ship bound from Guayaquil to Panama", whereas the sworn depositions say Callao.

surprises: THE TREASURE SHIP WAS UNARMED. Anton swears he "did not carry artillery or arms" and so "could not make any resistance"; Lizarza says she was "powerless to resist". The richest ship on the Pacific silver run carried no guns and no escort, because, as the Famous Voyage puts it of Callao, "the masters and marchants were here most secure, hauing neuer bene assaulted by enemies". This is a far better game premise than "almost without a fight": the whole Pacific was an undefended system, and Drake's advantage was not gunnery but the fact that nobody had ever come.

DRAKE FOUGHT WITH LONGBOWS. Anton's testimony describes "many arrows" into her side and "about forty archers" climbing the shrouds from the pinnace; John Drake and da Silva both say Anton was brought down by an arrow. Archers, not musketeers, were the boarding party. No game I know of models Elizabethan sea-archery.

DRAKE GAVE HIS VICTIM A WRITTEN SAFE-CONDUCT, and Hakluyt printed it. Addressed to John Winter and the other captains: "if it pleaseth God that you should chance to meete with this ship of Sant John de Anton, I pray you use him well, according to my word and promise giuen unto them, and if you want anything that is in this ship of Sant John de Anton, I pray you pay them double the value for it, which I will satisfie againe, and command your men not to doe her any hurt." Nuttall prints the Inquisition's examination of the English pilot John Butler about this document (Lima, 7 July 1579). Drake also had his own table laid for Anton the next morning and embraced him with "ten paciencia que usanza es de guerra". He gave similar papers to de Parraces and de Zarate. A raider who issues receipts and reimbursement guarantees is a richer character than a pirate.

THE DRAG RUSE SURVIVES BECAUSE OF A TRANSLATION ERROR THAT WAS CAUGHT. Hakluyt's English of da Silva says the water-filled jars were hung astern "to make her sayle the better", and the printed shoulder-note calls it "A pretie way to make a ship saile" - exactly backwards. Nuttall's Simancas Spanish shows the real sense: because his ship was going somewhat ahead, so that she should not make such headway. Laughton and Corbett had argued the Hakluyt text was a mistranslation, and John Drake's independent "cabos y colchones" testimony proved them right. A nice case for the game's sources table of a detail that only becomes true when you read the other side's archive.

DRAKE'S CREW SHRANK BY TWO THIRDS. 164 able men out of Plymouth (Hakluyt), about 80 aboard the Golden Hind in the Pacific with 50-60 rated fighting men (three separate Spanish witnesses), and 56 left by the East Indies, whom Corbett says were as sound and hearty as the day they left England after a month on 'Crab Island'. The ship got lonelier as it got richer. Also worth modelling: Drake carried artisans and a portable forge for making nails, spikes and bolts (da Silva), and four pinnaces in frame.

THE MONEY DISPUTE IS DOCUMENTED ON BOTH SIDES, AND DRAKE DENIED IT. The Spanish merchants' depositions taken at Seville in 1580 claimed a million pesos of gold at 450 maravedis each; the English officer abstracting them wrote "I fynde by the deposicons of the witnesses no more registred but 400m 6 Pezos beside 34 barres of sylver not valued", and added the note "Sr Frances Drake dothe utterlye denye". A prize-claim audit, 1580, with both sides' numbers. A game that wants an economy layer has a ready-made mechanic here: registered vs unregistered cargo, and the gap between them.

NUTTALL THINKS THE JOKE RUNS THE OTHER WAY. Her note at p. 165 argues that since the Concepcion was unarmed and her real name was Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, "Spitfire" could only properly have belonged to the Golden Hind, and the Spaniard was dubbed "Spitsilver" in repartee. Whether or not she is right, it means the nickname everyone uses for the prize may be an English in-joke about Drake's own ship, recorded backwards for four centuries.

THE GOLDEN HIND NEARLY ENDED THE VOYAGE ON A REEF. Corbett describes her stuck fast off Celebes in January 1580 until "suddenly to everyone's amazement she freed her keel" - with 26 tons of silver in her. Da Silva, who had sailed in her, judged her a leaky ship, water-fast only before a moderate following wind and fit for "a couple of voyages from Portugal to Brazil". The fastest ship in the game was also the one most likely to be lost by accident.

verdicts.counter_evidence:
I could not break the claim. The core survives and is now triply sourced, but four of the finding's surrounding statements are wrong and must be struck before publication.

RETRIEVAL PROVED (4 independent files, all downloaded and grepped locally):
1. Nuttall, New Light on Drake, 1914 (newlightondrakec34nuttuoft). Front matter prints "WORKS ISSUED BY / Zbe Dafelu^t Society / NEW LIGHT ON DRAKE / SECOND SERIES / No. XXXIV / ISSUED FOR 1914" and the Council list headed "ALBERT GRAY, Esq., K.C., President." Running heads "DEPOSITION OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 165" (line 9881) and "DEPOSITION OF DOMINGO DE LIZARZA 177" (line 10426) present; AGI footnote "Archive General de Indias, Seville, E. i, C. i, L. 2-21" present.
2. Vaux, The World Encompassed, Hakluyt Society 1854 (worldencompassed16drak). Title page: "W. S. W. VAUX, Esq., M.A. / LONDON: PRINTED FOR THE HAKLUYT SOCIETY / M.DCCCLIV", Murchison President, "Honorary Secretary.—E. H. MAJOR".
3. Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose vol. XI, MCMIV (principalnavigat011hakl). Title page: "In Twelve Volumes / Volume XI / GLASGOW ... ROBERT MACLEHOSE & COMPANY LTD ... MCMIV".
4. Counter-source: Henry R. Wagner, Sir Francis Drake's Voyage Around the World, John Howell, San Francisco, 1926 (sirfrancisdrakes0000henr_h1p3; 1969 N. Israel reprint of the 1926 sheets). Title page and contents verified ("Chapter VI. Drake Captures the Cacafuego ... 116").

TEST 1 - QUOTES ARE VERBATIM. Vaux 1854 p.110/111: "We found her to be indeed the | Cacafuego, thougli [though] before we left her, she were new named by a boy of her owne the Cacaplata." The page break falls exactly between "the" and "Cacafuego", so "pp. 110-111" is right. Hakluyt MacLehose XI p.116: "Captaine, our ship shall be called no more the Cacafuego, but the Cacaplata, and your shippe shall bee called the Cacafuego: which pretie speach of the Pilots boy ministred matter of laughter to us, both then and long after." Identical text at Vaux appendix p.242. Both passages also check out word-for-word in a fourth, independent edition (Penzer, The World Encompassed and Analogous Contemporary Documents, Argonaut Press 1926, pp. 46-47). Nuttall's name passages are verbatim: p.164 "ordered the appearance before him of San Juan de Anton, the master and owner of the ship named 'Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion,' which is at present anchored in Perico"; p.176 "deponent said that he had come as clerk of the ship named 'Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion,' of which San Juan de Anton was master and pilot." Nuttall's dissent at p.165 n.1 is reported accurately.

TEST 3 - LATER SCHOLARSHIP CONFIRMS, IT DOES NOT CORRECT. Wagner 1926 p.357: "SAN JUAN DE ANTON was the Captain of the now famous Cacafuego, a small merchant vessel plying between Panama and Lima. The real name of the ship was Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, and according to Anton's statement, he was also the owner of her." Wagner p.116: "San Juan de Anton, the master of the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, nick-named the Cacafuego". Wagner's index: "Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, proper name of the Cacafuego, 116, 357." Penzer/Temple 1926 p.xliv, independently: the Spanish accounts "called her the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion and sometimes the Nao Rica, i.e. the Rich Ship." Wagner is openly hostile to Nuttall elsewhere ("Mrs. Nuttall's theory about his name") so this is not borrowed agreement.

FOUR CORRECTIONS REQUIRED (the claim stands; these sentences do not):
(a) "'Cacafuego' appears only in the ENGLISH sources" is FALSE. Nuno da Silva's log-book, written in Portuguese and preserved at AGI Seville (E.1, C.1, L.2-32, No. 30), records at 1 March 1579: "On the first of March we took the ship 'cagua fogo'" (Nuttall p.293). Nuttall's footnote there treats it as the pilot's own Portuguese form and adds "This Portuguese name reappears as 'Cacafoga' in the anonymous 'discourse' (Vaux, p. 182)." Caveat in both directions: da Silva was Drake's captive aboard the Golden Hind, so he may have picked the by-name up from the English, and Wagner p.335 doubts the document is the original log rather than a memorandum copy. But it is a non-English-language archival document, and the absolute "only" is refuted by the finding's own volume.
(b) "both of them treat it as a jest rather than a name" INVERTS the sources. In both English accounts Cacafuego is her established by-name, learned from Spanish prizes BEFORE the capture: World Encompassed p.110, "hastening all wee might, to get sight if it were possible of that gallant ship the Cacafuego, the great glory of the South Sea, which was gone from Lima 14 dayes before vs"; Hakluyt p.115, "In which ship hee had newes of another ship called the Cacafuego". The jest is only the reciprocal swap to Cacaplata, which presupposes Cacafuego as her existing name. Say "nickname, not registered name" - not "a jest, not a name."
(c) There are THREE English accounts, not two, and they conflict. The anonymous "discourse" (Vaux Appendix III, p.182) puts the speech in the mouth of the pilot himself, "Don Francisco", not his boy, and spells it "the Cacafoga ... the Cacaplata ... the Cacafo". This is the pair Nuttall's p.165 note actually attacks ("See Vaux, pp. 182 and 242"), not The World Encompassed.
(d) MISATTRIBUTED GLOSS. "Nuttall renders them politely as Spitfire and Spitsilver" misreads her. Nuttall is not being polite, she is asserting a different word: p.293 n.1, the English "render the Spanish 'Qacafuego' (antiquated form of 'Sacafuego') as 'Cacafuego'"; p.165 n.1, "the name Cacafuego (pronounced Sacafue^o)", the English erring through "ignorance of Spanish orthography and pronunciation." Wagner 1926 (ch. VI n.6) explicitly rebukes her: "This nickname which gave rise to this amusing but vulgar joke, Mrs. Nuttall thought should be [Sacafuego; the OCR garbles the initial letter]. Whether this was the result of ignorance of the meaning of the word or covered a desire to make it more respectable, I do not know." The scatological cagafuego/cagaplata reading is Wagner's position, not Nuttall's. Also note Wagner's dissent-killer on the artillery argument: Drake "shot her mizzenmast away with a gun, and the master being wounded by an arrow" - Anton's "no artillery or arms" describes his own ship's armament, which is why Nuttall's inference is a minority view nobody has followed.

ONE SMALLER OVERSTATEMENT: "two independent Spanish documents" - Anton's and Lizarza's depositions are two depositions inside ONE file, the Panama judicial inquiry of 16 March 1579, same court, same legajo (AGI E.1, C.1, L.2-21). Call them two witnesses in one inquiry. Independent corroboration comes from outside it (Wagner's own AGI photostats, legajo 2-5-2/21, and Wagner p.309 note recording that Mendoza laid "a certified copy of the register of the Cacafuego" before Elizabeth).

NULL RESULT REGISTERED: I searched Hakluyt's English version of da Silva's Relation (MacLehose XI, lines 8244-8900) for every nickname spelling - zero hits; it calls her simply "the ship of Sant John de Anton." Lopez Vaz's Discourse (Vaux Appendix V, pp.285ff) - zero hits. Nuttall's three translated Spanish depositions of da Silva - zero hits. The Internet Archive full-text-search API returned nothing for Cacafuego/Cacafogo/Cagafuego (endpoint appears unavailable, not a negative). I did not find any Spanish-LANGUAGE document using the nickname; the one non-English attestation is Portuguese.
verdicts.reasoning:
The claim as claimed - real name Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, Cacafuego a nickname - cannot be broken. I confirmed both quotes verbatim at the exact cited locators in two independently retrieved editions, confirmed the Spanish depositions verbatim in Nuttall, and then found two 1926 scholars who reached the same conclusion without relying on each other: Wagner ("The real name of the ship was Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion", with the index gloss "proper name of the Cacafuego") and Penzer/Temple (the Spanish accounts "called her the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion and sometimes the Nao Rica"). Nothing in later scholarship corrects it. So refuted=false and the verdict stays CONFIRMED rather than PARTLY, because the thing the sources table will assert is exactly the thing that holds.

What does NOT hold is four of the finding's framing sentences, and one of them is a flat factual error against the finding's own cited volume: "Cacafuego appears only in the ENGLISH sources" is contradicted by Nuno da Silva's Portuguese log at Nuttall p.293, "the ship 'cagua fogo'". I also caught the cheap-reading tell the brief warned about - the finding read the renaming anecdote as proof that the name was merely a jest, which is the agreeable reading, when both English accounts in fact use Cacafuego as her settled by-name before Drake ever sighted her, so the anecdote proves the nickname existed rather than that it did not. And the finding put the vulgar gloss in Nuttall's mouth when Nuttall spent two footnotes denying it and Wagner publicly scolded her for denying it. Those are corrections to the prose, not to the claim.

verdicts.counter_evidence:
RETRIEVAL. Their URL (worldencompassed16drak) 500s through archive.org/download; I pulled it off the node directly (ia601602.us.archive.org/29/items/...) and proved identity by the imprint line "M.DCCCLIV." (=1854) and the Hakluyt Society council page naming Murchison as President. Nuttall proved by its title page block "NEW LIGHT ON DRAKE / SECOND SERIES / No. XXXIV / ISSUED FOR 1914". Hakluyt XI proved by the MacLehose/Glasgow imprint plus "VOLUME XI" and its own Table of Voyages ("The famous voyage of sir Francis Drake into the South sea... 101"). Corbett proved by its own title and the Anton/Sarmiento footnote apparatus.

TEST 1 — BOTH QUOTES ARE EXACT. World Encompassed, p. 111 (running head "BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE. Ill" present): "We found in her some fruite, conserues, sugars, meale, and other victuals, and (that which was the especiallest cause of her heauy and slow sayling) a certaine quan|title [=quantitie, OCR line break] of iewels and precious stones, 13 chests of ryals of plate, 80 pound waight in gold, 26 tunne of vncoyned siluer, two very faire gilt siluer drinking boules, and the like trifles, valued in all at about 360,000 pezoes." Nuttall p. 159 (running head "TESTIMONY OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 159"): "The registered silver seized amounted to 362,000 pesos in bars, reals and gold. Of this 106,000 belonged to His Majesty and the rest to private individuals. This is what was registered but, with what was on board beside this, the total amounts to more than 400,000 pesos." Word for word. No paraphrase.

LOCATORS ALSO CHECKED AND SOUND: Hakluyt XI p. 116 — "we found in her great riches, as jewels and precious stones, thirteene chests full of royals of plate, foure score pound weight of golde, and sixe and twentie tunne of silver", no valuation, correct. Da Silva's SECOND relation p. 267 — "a thousand three hundred barres or peeces of siluer, and foureteene chestes with ryals of eight, and with gold... three hundred barres of the siluer belonged to the king", correct (I first mis-suspected this; it is right). Anton's Panama deposition p. 165 — "three hundred and sixty thousand pesos in gold, silver and reals, a little more or less, which were either registered or to be registered and included what belonged to the sailors and to the passengers", correct, and "Without doing any harm to the persons who were with deponent", and "for six days". Lizarza p. 176 — same 360,000 "registered and to be registered", correct and genuinely independent. Release 7 March, "two casks of water, tackle, sails, canvas and a cable", and the English safe-conduct signed "Francisqus Draques" (p. 160) all verbatim. Seville abstract pp. 417-418 verbatim incl. "a million of pezos of golde everye pezos worthe 450 maravedis", "no more registred but 4oom 6 Pezos", and "Sr Frances Drake dothe utterlye denye".

WHY IT DOES NOT SURVIVE AS CONFIRMED — three defects.

(1) THE CENTRAL FRAMING IS CONTRADICTED BY SCHOLARSHIP AND BY THEIR OWN DOCUMENT. They assert the sides "agree closely on the headline number" and treat "more than 400,000 pesos" as the Spanish ceiling. Corbett, Drake and the Tudor Navy (1898) I, p. 275, reads the same Sarmiento passage the opposite way: "Its value is variously stated, and was never perhaps quite accurately known... The registered treasure alone was valued at 360,000 pesos; and Sarmiento says there were over 400,000 pesos unregistered." On Corbett's reading the 400,000 is ADDITIONAL to the 360,000, giving ~760,000+ from this one ship. Their own cited Seville abstract supports Corbett, not them: at p. 417 it has "360m Pezos of golde and sylver registred... wth 4oom to be registred", and at p. 418 it tabulates "iiijcm pezos in ye St John de Anton" [=400,000] under the heading "And I fynde deposed to be taken by reporte and not registred these parcells followinge." They cite pp. 417-418 but do not report that it separates 360,000 registered from a further 400,000 unregistered in Anton's ship. The finding's agreement is therefore an artefact of choosing one of two live readings of the same evidence and not disclosing the other.

(2) A FOURTH SPANISH FIGURE THEY DO NOT REPORT. Nuttall p. 414 n.2 quotes Mendoza to Philip II (Simancas Est. 833) citing the Seville consuls' memorandum of "375,000 pesos which he took in the South Sea in a ship (sic) named 'Master San Juan de Antona'". So the Spanish side yields 360,000 / 362,000 / 375,000 / "more than 400,000" / 400,000 unregistered on top / a million global — the opposite of a tight consensus.

(3) TWO CITATION/READING ERRORS. (a) "Panama summary, ibid. p. 162" is wrong twice: the 447,000-pesos passage sits on p. 163 (the running head "DEPOSITION OF SAN JUAN DE ANTON 163" precedes it), and it is the closing summary of document 7A, Sarmiento's rendering of Anton's account, not of 7B, the Panama judicial inquiry which only begins on p. 163. Nuttall's contents list the two separately (7A at 156, 7B at 163). (b) They say Drake "gave the other to the Golden Hind's steward". Hakluyt XI p. 116 makes the PILOT the subject: "which the Pilot because hee could not otherwise chuse, yeelded unto, and gave the other to the steward of our Generals ships."

MINOR, NOT REFUTING: "killed no one" is right for the prize, but Hakluyt and da Silva both have the master wounded by an arrow ("hauing wounded the master with an arrowe", p. 267). Nuttall's p. 165 footnote also argues the ship was never called Cacafuego at all, her Spanish name being Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, which the finding does not mention.
verdicts.reasoning:
The verbatim test passes cleanly: I pulled the actual texts (not their dead URL, which 500s; I went to the storage node) and both quotes are exact to the character, under the right running heads, and seven of their eight locators are correct. The substance of the claim is well supported.

But the finding's load-bearing interpretive sentence fails. It says the English and Spanish figures "agree closely" and presents "more than 400,000 pesos" as the Spanish total. Corbett 1898 I.275 reads the identical Sarmiento passage as 400,000 UNREGISTERED on top of 360,000 registered, and explicitly warns the value "was never perhaps quite accurately known". Decisively, the finding's OWN cited Seville abstract tabulates 400,000 pesos in Anton's ship under "deposed to be taken by reporte and not registred", i.e. additional to the 360,000 registered, implying ~760,000 from this ship. They cite that page and omit the part that cuts against them. A fourth Spanish figure (375,000, Mendoza to Philip II) also goes unreported. This is the agreeable-evidence failure mode: the tidy convergence on 360,000 is one of two live readings, presented as the only one.

Add two real citation defects for a published sources table: the Panama summary is on p. 163 and belongs to Sarmiento's testimony (7A), not the Panama inquiry (7B); and Hakluyt's grammar makes the pilot, not Drake, hand the second cup to the steward.

So the evidence is genuine and the quotes are honest, but the synthesis overstates concordance and the citations need fixing. Not killed - downgraded to PARTLY.

I fetched their URL myself (one 500, succeeded on retry) and proved the retrieval independently: the file carries the Hakluyt Society title page, "M.DCCC.LIV.", editor "W. S. W. Vaux, Esq., M.A.", and the Fletcher MS collation. BOTH quotes are verbatim, word for word, including "2 yeares 10 moneths and some few odde daies beside" (OCR renders "daies" as "dales" in the December sentence; that is a scanning artifact, not a misquote). Neither is out of context: the December 13 sentence follows the Falmouth storm narrative, and the arrival sentence is the closing paragraph of the narrative before the Appendix.

Test 3 (look for a source that says otherwise) found nothing that moves the years. I checked all the candidates: Hakluyt's "Famous Voyage" in the same volume does end "We arriued in England the third of Nouember 1580. being the third yeere of our departure" - a different DAY, the same YEAR; both Famous Voyage versions in the volume give 13 December for the departure. I then ran two independent checks they did not. (a) Calendrical: 26 September 1580 in the Julian calendar was a MONDAY, precisely what the text asserts the stay-at-home reckoning made it - the source's own date-line arithmetic is internally and astronomically sound. (b) A second scholarly authority: Nuttall's 1914 title page reads verbatim "NEW LIGHT ON DRAKE / ... VOYAGE OF CIRCUMNAVIGATION / 1577-1580" (actual title page, not the IA catalogue label), and her introduction, p. xix, states the voyage "extended from December 13, 1577 to September 26, 1580" - from the editor who read the Spanish documents at Seville, i.e. the Spanish side does not contradict the English one here.

Test 4: the finding supports the claim directly, not adjacently. The claim is only the span "1577-80", and every variant reading (15 Nov 1577, 13 Dec 1577; 26 Sept 1580, 3 Nov 1580) falls inside it. The claim is CONFIRMED.

I am nevertheless flagging three defects, one of them serious as process, because the sources table should not publish them. (1) THEIR RETRIEVAL PROOF IS PARTLY FABRICATED: the string "BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE" occurs ZERO times in the whole OCR file. The running heads flanking the arrival passage are "160 THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD," and "162 THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD.", and the passage falls after the 162 head, so it is not "bracketed by 161 and 162" as claimed. The conclusion is right; the stated evidence for it was not read. (2) Wrong page for the erroneous date: "third of Nouember 1580" sits under the running head "253 APPENDIX.", i.e. p. 253 of the 1854 appendix, not p. 241. (3) Frontispiece over-read: "4. Cal. Octobris" is 28 September, not 26; it is the FRENCH legend on the same Thomas de Leu plate that reads "le 26 iour de Sept." So the engraving does not carry "the same dates" - Latin and narrative differ by two days, only the years agree. Minor: The World Encompassed says the admiral AND the Marigold cut their main-masts (Hakluyt adds the Marigold was driven ashore), so "lost the Pelican's main-mast" is incomplete; and "one of the earliest date-line observations in English" is an unverified literary judgment that should be dropped.

None of these touch the years, so I do not refute and do not downgrade. They are citation-hygiene corrections.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Not counter-evidence to the claim (the claim stands), but to their stated proof and citations. (1) grep -c "BY SIR FRANCIS DRAKE" on worldencompassed16drak_djvu.txt returns 0; the only heads near the arrival passage are "160 THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD," and "162 THE VOYAGE ABOUT THE WORLD.", with the passage AFTER the 162 head - the running head they cite as proof does not exist in the file. (2) The "third of Nouember 1580" sentence falls under the head "253 APPENDIX.", not p. 241. (3) The Latin frontispiece caption "4. Cal Octobris anno ... 1580" = 28 September; the 26 September date on that plate is in the French legend ("fist son retour audict Royaume le 26 iour de Sept."), so Latin caption and narrative are two days apart. Corroboration ADDED by me: Nuttall, New Light on Drake (Hakluyt Society 2nd ser. XXXIV, 1914), title page "1577-1580" and Introduction p. xix: the voyage "extended from December 13, 1577 to September 26, 1580"; and an independent Julian-calendar computation showing 26 Sept 1580 was a Monday, matching the text's own date-line remark.

claims.claim: The Santa Ana had her great guns struck below / carried no mounted artillery, so she could not fire back; the fight was musketry and boarding only.
claims.finding: NO primary account of the action says anything whatever about the Santa Ana's armament. Pretty, the 1589 N.H. narrative, Fuller's notes and Cavendish's own letter are all silent on her guns. Silence is not confirmation. Worse for the game: the second half of the claim is positively contradicted. The fight was NOT musketry and boarding only - Cavendish opened with a broadside, and his GREAT ORDNANCE is what won it. Pretty names great ordnance in all three encounters and says she struck because she was sinking from gunfire below the waterline. What the sources DO show is the Spanish side fighting with no firearms at all: lances, javelins, rapiers, targets and thrown stones from behind 'close fights' (barricades). The 'no cannon / two arquebuses and some rusty flintlocks / guns landed at Acapulco the year before' detail circulating on Wikipedia and in popular articles traces to W. Michael Mathes, 'The Capture of the Santa Ana' (1969), which prints the Alzola and Sierra declarations. That is modern and in copyright; I could not obtain it, and no free text carries it. The MECHANIC itself is nevertheless real period practice, documented 160 years later (see quote 2 below) and observed off this very cape in 1709 (see C-11). But it is a convention of the trade, not a recorded fact about this ship, and Anson's wording actually says the guns were supposed to be MOUNTED by the time the galleon drew near Cape San Lucas.
claims.quote: (1) Pretty, Hakluyt XI, p.324-325: "In the afternoone we gat up unto them, giving them the broad side with our great ordinance and a volee of small shot, and presently layed the ship aboord... we perceived that the Captaine of the said ship had made fights fore and after, and layd their sailes close on their poope, their mid ship, with their fore castle, and having not one man to be seene, stood close under their fights, with lances, javelings, rapiers, & targets, & an innumerable sort of great stones, which they threw overboord upon our heads and into our ship" ... "their shippe being in hazard of sinking by reason of the great shot which were made, wherof some were under water". (2) Anson/Walter, A Voyage Round the World, ch. on the Manila trade: "For the galleon, when she sets sail from Manila, being deep laden with a variety of bulky goods, she has not the convenience of mounting her lower tier of guns, but carries them in her hold till she draws near Cape St. Lucas, and is apprehensive of an enemy."
claims.source: (1) Francis Pretty, 'The admirable and prosperous voyage of ... Master Thomas Candish', in Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose ed., vol. XI (Glasgow 1904), pp. 324-325 = folio 1600, vol. III, p. 816. (2) [Richard Walter/Benjamin Robins], A Voyage Round the World ... by George Anson (1748), bk. III ch. on the Manila galleon.
claims.retrieval_note: Proved by title-leaf 'The Principal Navigations ... In Twelve Volumes / Volume XI / GLASGOW ... MACLEHOSE' and by the Pretty heading at p.290 matching the known title verbatim. Then cross-checked word for word against the 1600 black-letter folio (IA cihm_94220, p.816 running head 'The English Voyages ... M. Thomas Candish'), and against the 1589 edition read as a page image (IA cihm_35668, leaf n863, printed p.812, running head 'M. Thomas Candish. of the English nation.'). Three independent witnesses, same silence on her guns. Anson text verified by two separate editions (1757 IA voyageroundworld00walt_2 and 1853 IA avoyageroundwor01ansogoog) reading identically.
claims.game_impact: CHANGE, do not keep as stated. (a) Delete 'musketry and boarding only' - it is flatly wrong; the English great guns decided the fight. (b) You may keep 'her lower tier was in the hold' as a PLAUSIBLE PERIOD CONVENTION, but label it as such in the sources table and cite Anson 1748 + Rogers 1709, not Pretty. (c) The historically defensible and more interesting mechanic is the one Pretty actually describes: a galleon with NO firearms at all, fighting from close fights with edged weapons and heaved stones, which beats off boarders but cannot answer gunfire - so the attacker must choose between a cheap boarding that gets thrown back and a slow, expensive gunnery grind.

claims.claim: She repelled Cavendish's boarders twice.
claims.finding: Pretty describes ONE boarding attempt, repulsed once. The 'second' and 'third' encounters, which Hakluyt's own marginal notes label as such, were gunnery, not boarding: both are explicitly 'with our great ordinance and ... our small shot', with no mention of laying her aboard again. English loss in the single repulse: 2 slain, 4 or 5 hurt.
claims.quote: "...that they put us off the shippe againe, with the losse of 2 of our men which were slaine, & with the hurting of 4 or 5. But for all this we new trimmed our sailes, and fitted every man his furniture, and gave them a fresh encounter with our great ordinance and also with our small shot, raking them through and through" ... "Our Generall encouraging his men a fresh with the whole noyse of trumpets gave them the third encounter with our great ordinance and all our small shot"
claims.source: Pretty, in Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose ed., vol. XI, p.325 (marginal notes 'The second encounter', 'The third encounter'); identical in the 1600 folio III.816.
claims.retrieval_note: Same file as C-1, verified as above. I also checked the 1589 N.H. narrative (read as page image, p.812), which compresses the whole action into one sentence and describes no boarding at all: 'we chased her vntill noone, so fetching her vp, we gaue them fight'.
claims.game_impact: CHANGE to ONE repulse. If you want a two-repulse beat for pacing, you must flag it in the sources table as a designer's invention. The authentic three-beat rhythm is: broadside + immediate boarding (thrown back) -> gunnery -> gunnery -> she strikes.

claims.claim: He stood off and pounded her with the great ordnance for hours until she struck.
claims.finding: The duration is right; the sequence is not. Pretty: a chase of 'some 3 or 4 houres' first, then the action, and she struck 'within 5 or 6 houres fight'. DNB (1887) says 'an obstinate fight of six hours'; Bancroft 'After a fight of five or six hours'. But Cavendish did not board first and then stand off - he fired a broadside AND boarded in the same breath, was thrown off, and only then fell back on gunnery. N.H. (1589) gives no duration, only 'we chased her vntill noone'.
claims.quote: "...we gave them chase some 3 or 4 houres, standing with our best advantage and working for the winde." ... "within 5 or 6 houres fight set out a flagge of truce and parled for mercy"
claims.source: Pretty, Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, pp. 324-325; cf. DNB vol. 9 (1887), art. 'Cavendish, Thomas', p.366; Bancroft, History of Mexico, vol. II (1883), p.748.
claims.retrieval_note: Pretty verified as above in three editions. DNB page text taken from the Wikisource page-scan transcription of 'Dictionary of National Biography volume 09.djvu' pp.364-366, confirmed to be the right article by the heading 'CAVENDISH, THOMAS (1560-1592), circumnavigator' and by its naming of both Hakluyt narratives. Bancroft verified by running head 'CAPTURE OF THE GALLEON' and its footnote citing 'Hakluyt's Voy., iii. 803-25'.
claims.game_impact: KEEP the 5-6 hour figure (and the 3-4 hour chase before it, which the game should add - it is free tension). CHANGE the ordering: the boarding comes first, not last.

claims.claim: Her tonnage.
claims.finding: 700 tons, in both independent English narratives. Note the hedge in Pretty: it is an English eyeball estimate, not a register figure. Bancroft repeats 700. The 600-ton figure that circulates online is not in any source I read; the 600 tons in the sources is the quantity of CARGO burnt (see C-6), which is almost certainly where the confusion comes from.
claims.quote: Pretty: "called the S. Anna, & thought to be 700 tunnes in burthen." / N.H. 1589: "wee espied the goodly shippe comming from the Philippinas called Saint Anna the great, being of seuen hundreth tunnes"
claims.source: Pretty, Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, p.324; [N.H.], 'The famous voyage of M. Thomas Candish', in Hakluyt, The principall navigations (1589), p.812; Bancroft, Hist. Mexico II.747.
claims.retrieval_note: For the 1589 reading I did not trust the OCR, which was column-shredded. I located the leaf through the djvu XML, then downloaded the BookReader JPEG for leaf n863 and read it: the printed page number 816 on the facing leaf and the running head 'M. Thomas Candish. of the English nation. 812' identify the page, and the marginal note 'The great S. Anna taken, rifled & burnt' sits beside the sentence.
claims.game_impact: KEEP 700 tons. Add the hedge 'thought to be' if the game shows a sources table - the English never measured her.

claims.claim: Her crew and passenger numbers, and what happened to them (put ashore?).
claims.finding: The two English accounts disagree slightly and NEITHER gives her full complement before the fight. Pretty: 190 persons, men AND women, set on shore at Aguada Segura. N.H. 1589: 'nine score prisoners' = 180. Spanish dead: N.H. 'the losse of twelue or fourteene of their men'; Bancroft says twelve. Cavendish kept back: two Japanese lads able to read and write their own language (Christopher, c.20; Cosmus, c.17), three boys of Manila (c.15, c.13, and the youngest c.9 - Alphonso, Anthony de Dasi, and a third who 'remaineth with the right honourable the Countesse of Essex'), Nicholas Roderigo a Portuguese, and Thomas de Ersola, a Spanish pilot for the Acapulco-Ladrones run. The Spaniards were left a fair river, victuals (garbanzos, peas, wine), ALL the ship's sails to make tents, and licence to take planks to build a bark; the captain got 'a royall reward' of swords, targets, pieces, shot and powder. Her captain was Tomas de Alzola, a Biscayan; her pilot Sebastian Rodriguez of the Algarve (Navarrete, from Alzola's own sworn declaration at Acapulco).
claims.quote: Pretty: "Here the whole company of the Spaniardes, both of men and women to the number of 190 persons were set on shore: where they had a fayre river of fresh water... Also they had all the sailes of their shippe to make them tents on shore, with licence to take such store of plankes as should bee sufficient to make them a barke." / N.H. 1589: "So on the sixt of the sayde Nouember we went into the Port of Agua Segura, where wee ankered and put nine score prisoners on land" / Navarrete: "Era su capitan un Vizcaino llamado Tomas de Alzola, y su piloto Sebastian Rodriguez, natural del Algarve."
claims.source: Pretty, Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, pp.326-327; [N.H.], Hakluyt 1589, p.812; M. Fernandez de Navarrete, introduction to Relacion del viage hecho por las goletas Sutil y Mexicana en el ano de 1792 (Madrid, 1802), p. LIV n.1.
claims.retrieval_note: Navarrete verified by the title lines 'DEL VIAGE HECHO POR LAS GOLETAS / SUTIL Y MEXICANA' at the head of the file and by the pagination marker 'LIV' immediately above the footnote. The footnote itself states that he has the documents in front of him: a sworn declaration given at Acapulco by Alzola himself the day after he entered that port, and another made before the Audiencia of Guadalajara on 24 January 1588 by Antonio de Sierra. That is the chain of custody for the Spanish names.
claims.game_impact: KEEP 190 ashore (Pretty) but note the 1589 variant of 180. ADD the retained prisoners - the two Japanese literate teenagers and the 9-year-old from Manila are the single best human detail in the whole episode and the game does not seem to use them. ADD Alzola by name; 'the Spanish captain' is a wasted NPC.

claims.claim: He could not carry a fraction of her cargo and burned the rest.
claims.finding: Confirmed three times over, including from Cavendish's own pen. Specie: 122,000 pesos of gold (Hakluyt's marginal note adds 'A pezo is 8s'). Cargo: silks, satins, damasks, musk, 'divers other marchandize', victuals, conserves of all sorts and very good wines. Capacity taken: 40 tons into the two English ships (N.H.). Burnt with her: 500 tons (Pretty) or 600 tons (N.H.). Cavendish's own letter to Lord Hunsdon states the reason bluntly. Note a lovely textual curiosity: Hakluyt printed a BLANK where the prize's total value should stand in Cavendish's letter.
claims.quote: N.H. 1589: "and ransacking the great shippe, wee laded our owne two shippes with fourtie tunnes of the chiefest marchandise, and burnt all the rest aswell shippe as goods, to the quantitie of sixe hundreth tunnes of rich marchandise, because we were not able to bring it away: This was one of the richest vessels that euer sayled on the Seas, and was able to haue made many hundreths wealthie, if we had had meanes to haue brought it home." / Cavendish to Lord Hunsdon, Plymouth, 9 Sept 1588: "Which goods (for that my ships were not able to conteine the least part of them) I was inforced to set on fire." / Pretty: "our Generall caused the kings shippe to be set on fire, which having to the quantitie of 500 tunnes of goods in her we saw burnt unto the water"
claims.source: [N.H.], Hakluyt 1589, p.812 (marginal note 'The great S. Anna taken, rifled & burnt'); 'A letter of M. Thomas Candish to the right honourable the Lord Hunsdon', Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, pp.376-377; Pretty, ibid. p.327.
claims.retrieval_note: 1589 passage read from the page image, not OCR (see C-4 note). Cavendish's letter verified in the MacLehose volume by its running head 'LETTER FROM THOMAS CANDISH a.d. 1588' and its signature 'Thomas Candish'; the asterisk standing for the omitted sum is printed in the text: 'for it did amount in value to * in Mexico to be solde'.
claims.game_impact: KEEP, and use the HARDER number. 40 tons taken out of 540-640 tons aboard is roughly 6-7 percent - a far more brutal loot-cap than most players expect, and it is documented. The 122,000 pesos went in whole (gold is dense, bulk is the constraint), which is exactly the right lesson: specie fits, cargo does not.

claims.claim: Did he burn her, and did she in fact survive the burning?
claims.finding: Both halves are true, and this is the best twist in the cluster. The English saw her 'burnt unto the water' and sailed away believing her destroyed. Torquemada, writing a generation later in New Spain, records that she was fired at anchor, that when her cables burned through she drove ashore, that the hulk was found repairable once the ballast was thrown out, and that the marooned company sailed her to Acapulco. It was Alzola's arrival at Acapulco in her that produced the sworn declaration Navarrete later read. Note the delicious Spanish-side error: Torquemada attributes the whole raid to 'el corsario Francisco Draque' - Drake, not Cavendish.
claims.quote: Torquemada, Monarquia Indiana, lib. V cap. XXVI: "Quemo el navio y dejo alli la gente, aunque se vinieron en el casco que habia quedado sobre el agua, que no se quemo." / Bancroft's gloss: "The galleon had been fired when at anchor a short distance from the land. When her cables burned off she drifted to the shore, and ballast being thrown out, the hulk was found in a condition capable of being repaired, as we are informed by Torquemada, so as to carry the whole party to Acapulco."
claims.source: Juan de Torquemada, Monarquia Indiana, lib. V cap. XXVI (UNAM digital edition, vol. II, p.418); Bancroft, History of Mexico, vol. II (1883), pp.749-750, citing 'Torquemada, i. 699' as 'the only account extant of the return of the Santa Ana to Acapulco'.
claims.retrieval_note: I did not take this from Bancroft alone. I fetched the UNAM chapter PDF, converted it with pdftotext, and confirmed the running head 'JUAN DE TORQUEMADA' and the chapter marker 'CAP XXVI', with the passage sitting inside the narrative of the viceroyalty of the marques de Villamanrique and dated 'El ano de 1587'. CAVEAT: the UNAM edition modernises Torquemada's orthography, so the Spanish above is the modernised reading, not the 1615/1723 spelling. Bancroft's independent citation to the 1723 edition i.699 brackets it.
claims.game_impact: KEEP, and make it the ending. The player burns her, sails off rich, and the epilogue reveals the Spaniards floated the hulk and sailed her into Acapulco - which is also how the Crown learned exactly what was lost. Flag the Drake misattribution as a period rumour the game can use.

claims.claim: The action was in the bay at Cabo San Lucas, under the lee of Land's End, with the arch rocks as a hazard.
claims.finding: Right water, wrong placement of the fight. (a) NAMES: Pretty calls it 'the cape of S. Lucar'; the harbour 'a great bay called by the Spaniards Aguada Segura'; later 'Aguada Segura, or Puerto Seguro'. Fuller calls it simply 'the port of S. Lucas'. Torquemada calls it 'el puerto de San Lucas'. Bancroft identifies Aguada Segura with 'the bay of San Bernabe, or Puerto del Cabo' - San Bernabe IS the bay at modern Cabo San Lucas. (b) THE ROCKS ARE DOCUMENTED, and better than the game knows: Pretty says the cape 'is very like the Needles at the isle of Wight', and Shelvocke in 1721 says the port is known by three white rocks like the Needles and that you cannot even see the anchorage until you are round them. (c) BUT THE FIGHT WAS NOT IN THE BAY. The action was fought at sea off the headland on 4 Nov; the prize was taken into the harbour on the 5th (Fuller) or 6th (Pretty and N.H.). Cavendish had been 'beating up and downe upon the headland'. (d) UNRESOLVED: Pretty's bay has 'a faire fresh river', and Cabo San Lucas has none, while San Jose del Cabo twenty miles up the coast does. Rogers in 1709 sent a boat and found a river bay with 500 Indians that he supposed was Cavendish's. Fuller's anchorage data ('12 fadoms... a Southeast winde is the woorst') and Rogers's bearings ('from the Southermost Rock about half a Mile') both fit San Lucas bay. I would not call the river question closed.
claims.quote: Pretty: "The 14 of October we fell with the cape of S. Lucar, which cape is very like the Needles at the isle of Wight; and within the said cape is a great bay called by the Spaniards Aguada Segura: into which bay falleth a faire fresh river" / Fuller: "You may anker in the port of S. Lucas on the Cape of California in 12 fadoms water: and a Southeast winde is the woorst." / Shelvocke, 13 Aug 1721: "we found ourselves near Puerto Seguro, which may be readily known by three white rocks, not much unlike the Needles of the Isle of Wight. You will not discover the road until you are round these rocks, and must keep close on board the outermost to fetch into the bay."
claims.source: Pretty, Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, p.323-324; Thomas Fuller of Ipswich (master of the Desire), 'Certaine rare and special notes', ibid. pp.369, 387; George Shelvocke, A Voyage Round the World by the Way of the Great South Sea (1726; ed. of 1757), sect. XIV; Bancroft, Hist. North Mexican States I.144, Hist. Mexico II.747.
claims.retrieval_note: Fuller is an independent second eyewitness in the same Hakluyt volume - I checked he is identified on his own title page as 'Master in the desire of M. Thomas Candish in his foresaid prosperous voyage'. Shelvocke verified by the section heading 'Arrival in Puerto Seguro, in the latitude of twenty-three degrees five minutes North, in the Southermost part of California' and by his later chapter heading 'Transactions in our passage between Puerto Seguro in California, and the river of Canton in China'.
claims.game_impact: CHANGE the geography of the fight: stage the battle OFFSHORE of the headland, with the bay as the destination afterwards (where the prisoners are landed, the treasure divided, the mutiny happens and the ship is burned). That is a better two-act level anyway. KEEP the arch rocks, and upgrade them: Shelvocke's 'you will not discover the road until you are round these rocks' is a ready-made reveal. Use the period names Aguada Segura / Puerto Seguro / San Bernabe on the map, not 'Cabo San Lucas'.

claims.claim: The Desire modelled at 84 ft, 3 masts; Cavendish's other vessels and which were present.
claims.finding: TONNAGE: 120 tons in both Hakluyt editions. But the DNB (1887) says 140 - an unexplained discrepancy you should know about. DIMENSIONS, RIG AND GUNS: no primary source gives any of them. 84 feet and three masts are UNVERIFIED; nothing I read states the Desire's length, her rig, or how many guns she carried. CREW AT THE ACTION: the one hard number is Pretty's 'not past 50 or 60 men at the uttermost in our ship'. Note that BOTH the 1589 and the 1600 folio leave a literal BLANK where the number of surviving Englishmen should be: 'wherein were the number of ___ Englishmen onely living'. That gap is in Hakluyt, not in the OCR. FLEET: Desire 120 tons, Content 60 tons, Hugh Gallant a bark of 40 tons; 123 persons all told out of Plymouth 21 July 1586; plus a 10-ton pinnace built in Brazil and a prize, the George, taken off Arica. PRESENT AT THE ACTION: Desire and Content only. The Hugh Gallant had been sunk at Rio Dolce on 5 June 1587 'for want of men'. The Content vanished the night they left Puerto Seguro, 19 November, and was never heard of again.
claims.quote: Pretty: "Wee departed out of Plimmouth on Thursday the 21. of July 1586. with 3. sayles, to wit, The Desire a ship of 120. tunnes, The Content of 60 tuns, and the Hugh gallant a barke of 40. tunnes: in which small Fleete were 123. persons of all sortes" ... "being not past 50 or 60 men at the uttermost in our ship" ... "wee sunke our rere-admirall called The Hugh Gallant for want of men, being a barke of fortie tunnes." / DNB: "The fleet of three ships, manned by 123 hands all told, consisted of the Desire of 140 tons, the Content of 60 tons, and the Hugh Gallant, a barque of 40 tons."
claims.source: Pretty, Hakluyt (MacLehose) XI, pp.290, 318, 324; C. H. Coote, 'Cavendish, Thomas', Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 9 (1887), p.365.
claims.retrieval_note: The blank is not an artefact. I confirmed it in three places: the MacLehose 1904 reprint, the Google scan of the same reprint (a different OCR run), and the 1600 black-letter folio OCR, all of which run 'wherein were the number of Eng[lish]men onely liuing' with no numeral. Three independent digitisations do not lose the same word in the same spot.
claims.game_impact: CHANGE the ship card to say what is actually known: 120 tons (DNB variant 140), 50-60 men aboard at the action, armament and dimensions NOT RECORDED. If you keep 84 ft and 3 masts, mark them as a reconstruction, not a source figure. ADD the Content as a sullen, half-useless consort - she contributed little to the fight, her people led the mutiny over the division, and she disappeared four days later. That is a mechanic, not a footnote.

claims.claim: Cavendish was the youngest to circumnavigate.
claims.finding: The age is solid; the superlative is not. DNB prints an 1887 text with an 1904 erratum specifying that he was baptised 19 September 1560. So he was 25 at departure (21 July 1586), 27 at the Santa Ana action (4 November 1587), and still 27 when he anchored at Plymouth on 9 September 1588 - he turned 28 ten days later. (Note the MacLehose editor's conflicting and undocumented 'born ... about 1555'; and that the common statement 'he was 28' is off by ten days.) As for 'youngest': I found NO source, period or scholarly, making that claim. In the plain sense it is false - ships' boys on earlier circumnavigations were far younger, and Cavendish himself carried home a Manila boy of about nine. A narrow form could be defended - youngest COMMANDER of a circumnavigation to that date, against Magellan (c.40), Elcano (c.36), Drake (c.37 at departure) - but no source I read asserts it and I am not prepared to certify a superlative from my own arithmetic.

claims.game_impact: CHANGE to a defensible form, or cut. Safe: 'twenty-seven years old at Cabo San Lucas; he brought the Desire home ten days short of his twenty-eighth birthday.' claims.claim: The English 'lay for her twice in life' at this cape - Cavendish 1587 and Woodes Rogers 1709, and was Rogers's station at Cabo San Lucas itself?
claims.finding: Rogers is CONFIRMED and is better material than the game realises - but 'twice' is wrong. (a) ROGERS WAS AT CABO SAN LUCAS. From 2 November 1709 his three ships lay spread six to nine leagues off the cape, able to sweep fifteen leagues of sea; he refitted in the harbour, which HE identifies as Cavendish's; he knew exactly whose ghost he was following. He took the Encarnacion on 22 December about five leagues from the cape, and was shot through the jaw doing it. (b) FOUR DAYS LATER the second, bigger galleon appeared and BEAT HIM OFF after six or seven hours, and his account of why is directly relevant to C-1. (c) 'TWICE' IS REFUTED by Anson's own authorised narrative, which calls the cape a standing ambush station. Shelvocke was in Puerto Seguro in August 1721, though for wood and water, not for the galleon; Anson's squadron resolved in 1742 to stand for Cape St Lucas or Cape Corrientes.
claims.quote: Rogers, 7 Nov 1709: "Sir Thomas Cavendish, in Queen Elizabeth's Time, took the Manila Ship in this Place on the 4th of November." / 21 Dec 1709: "we made the best of our Way into the Harbour call'd by Sir Tho. Cavendish Port Segura" / on the second galleon: "they could perceive the Enemy was in disorder, her Guns not being all mounted, and consequently their Netting-deck and Close Quarters unprovided" ... "she was call'd the Bigonia, of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns, about 40 of which were mounted, with as many Patereroes, all Brass; her Complement of Men on board, as we were inform'd, was above 450, besides Passengers." / Anson: "this being a station where she is constantly expected, and where she has been often waited for and fought with, though generally with little success."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (1712), under 7 Nov, 21-27 Dec 1709 (Cassell reprint 1928, pp. 205, 213-221); [Walter/Robins], A Voyage Round the World ... by George Anson (1748), bk. III.
claims.retrieval_note: Rogers proved to be Rogers by his own first-person detail that no summary would carry: the committee minutes signed on board the Dutchess at Tres Marias 24 Oct 1709, the running heads 'Cruising off Cape St. Lucas', and his account of being shot through the left cheek with part of his jaw dropping on the deck. Anson verified across two editions (1757 and 1853 reprints, IA voyageroundworld00walt_2 and avoyageroundwor01ansogoog) reading identically on both the gun-stowage and the 'often waited for' passages, which rules out an OCR phantom.
claims.game_impact: CHANGE 'twice' to 'again and again'. Anson's sentence is the line to quote. KEEP Rogers 1709 as the second instance but USE THE SECOND GALLEON: Rogers took the small one and was driven off the big one in the same week at the same cape. That single pairing teaches the whole lesson of the level better than anything else in the record - and Rogers's own explanation of why he nearly took her ('her Guns not being all mounted') is the closest thing to period authority the C-1 mechanic has.

nulls: I could NOT establish any primary statement about the Santa Ana's armament. The specific claims circulating online (no cannon; two arquebuses and some rusty flintlocks; she had been disarmed the previous year and her guns added to the defences of Acapulco) all trace to W. Michael Mathes, 'The Capture of the Santa Ana, Cabo San Lucas, November, 1587' (Los Angeles: Dawson's Book Shop, 1969), which prints and translates the Alzola and Sierra declarations. Searched Internet Archive (advancedsearch for 'capture of the santa ana' and creator:mathes - zero copies), the open web, and the bibliography of the San Diego Reader article that reproduces the detail. The work is in copyright and not online. This is the single most important gap in the cluster and I would not certify C-1 without it.

The Alzola and Sierra declarations themselves - Tomas de Alzola's sworn statement at Acapulco the day after he entered port, and Antonio de Sierra's before the Audiencia of Guadalajara on 24 January 1588 - are not available in any free text I could find. Navarrete (1802) read both and summarises them; his footnote confirms they list the people aboard and the sums of money carried, and states flatly that NEITHER mentions Juan de Fuca or his 60,000 ducats. He does not quote their wording on armament.

Henry R. Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast of America in the Sixteenth Century (1929), which uses the Spanish documents, is on Internet Archive (spanishvoyagesto0000henr) but lending-restricted: the _djvu.txt endpoint returns HTTP 500, and the ia-fts and archivelab search-inside endpoints returned nothing. Not consulted.

surprises: THE REAL AUTHORITY FOR THE GAME'S CENTRAL MECHANIC IS 1748, NOT 1587. Anson's narrative states the Manila-to-Acapulco galleon stowed her lower tier of guns in the hold because she was too deep laden to mount them. That is the mechanic the game wants - but it is period practice described 160 years later, and in the same breath it says she mounted them as she drew near Cape San Lucas. The game is right about the world and wrong about the evidence.

ROGERS 1709 IS A BETTER LEVEL THAN CAVENDISH 1587. In one week at the same cape he took the small galleon Encarnacion (20 guns, 193 men) and was beaten off the big one, the Begona - 900 tons, able to carry 60 guns, about 40 mounted plus 40 patereroes, over 450 men - after six or seven hours. His own explanation of why he nearly carried her is 'her Guns not being all mounted'. Small prize taken, big prize lost, same water, same month. The game models the wrong half of this.

SPAIN REMEMBERED IT AS DRAKE. Torquemada, the only source for the ship's survival, attributes the entire 1587 raid to 'el corsario Francisco Draque'. Bancroft notes Torquemada, Cavo and a host of later writers all made Drake the culprit. A superb fog-of-war beat.

JUAN DE FUCA CLAIMED HE WAS ABOARD. Michael Lok's account has the Greek pilot Apostolos Valerianos losing more than 60,000 ducats in the Santa Ana. Navarrete, who had both Spanish declarations in hand, points out that NEITHER mentions him, and uses that silence to help demolish the Fuca story. A documented liar attaching himself to the game's own level.

CAVENDISH CARRIED OFF CHILDREN. Two Japanese lads who could read and write their own language, Christopher (c.20) and Cosmus (c.17), and three boys of Manila aged about 15, 13 and 9. The youngest ended up in the household of the Countess of Essex. Those five went Manila to California to Manila to England - the nine-year-old saw more of the world than most of the crew.

THE TEXT ITSELF HAS HOLES. Hakluyt printed a BLANK for the number of Englishmen alive at the action in both 1589 and 1600, and another BLANK for the prize's total value in Cavendish's own letter to Lord Hunsdon ('it did amount in value to * in Mexico to be solde'). The two most quotable numbers in the episode were never set in type.

THE DATE IS TWO DATES. The English accounts say 4 November 1587 (Old Style). Navarrete, reading Alzola's own sworn declaration, dates the capture 15 November 1587 (New Style). A ten-or-eleven day gap that is itself a period fact worth surfacing.

THE PRIZE SHARE-OUT NEARLY BROKE THE EXPEDITION. On 8 November 'many of the company fell into a mutinie against our Generall, especially those which were in the Content'. Four days after the Content was left astern she vanished for good. The loot screen is the danger, not the fight.

CAVENDISH ARMED HIS PRISONERS AND LEFT THEM A SHIPYARD. He gave Alzola swords, targets, firearms, shot and powder 'for his defence against the Indians', all the ship's sails for tents, and licence to cut planks enough to build a bark. That generosity is why 190 people survived - and the burnt hulk they then floated is why the Crown learned exactly what had been lost.

verdicts.reasoning: The claim survives all four tests. (1) Quotes verbatim: I read the actual page images, not OCR. IA cihm_35668 (1589 Principall Navigations, microform; metadata confirms imprint "Imprinted at London by George Bishop and Ralph Newberie," 1589) BookReader leaf n863 carries the running head "M. Thomas Candish. of the English nation. 812" and the marginal note "The great S. Anna taken, rifled & burnt" beside: "wee espied the goodly shippe comming from the Philippinas called Saint Anna the great , being of seuen hundreth tunnes". Leaf n864 (p.813) ends the narrative "Written by N. H.", confirming their [N.H.] attribution. For Pretty I downloaded IA principalnavigat011hakl (metadata: MacLehose, Glasgow, 1903, v.11) and read leaf n357, printed page number 324 at the foot, running head "THE ENGLISH VOYAGES / A.D. 1587", marginal note "The fight betweene the great S. Anna and us": "called the S. Anna, & thought to be 700 tunnes in burthen." Both quotes are exact and the page locators are right. (2) Context: both sentences are the narrators' direct statement of the captured hull's burthen; not wrenched. (3) Contrary source: I found none. Bancroft Hist. Mexico II.747 (histofmexicovol210bancmiss) reads "the Santa Ana of seven hundred tons, captain Tomas de Alzola"; Chapman, A History of California: The Spanish Period (1921) p.115 "a 700-ton ship"; Hittell, Hist. California I "a vessel of seven hundred tons burden". Crucially, Navarrete's introduction to the Relacion del viage... Sutil y Mexicana (1802), pp. liv-lv, who had before him Alzola's own sworn declaration made at Acapulco the day after his arrival AND Antonio de Sierra's declaration before the Audiencia of Guadalajara of 24 Jan 1588, gives captain, pilot (Sebastian Rodriguez), date (15 Nov 1587) and place but states NO tonnage. So the Spanish side neither confirms nor contradicts; it is silent, and silence is not a negative. The 600-ton figure appears only in Wikipedia-derived tertiary web text (and the themua.org paper that footnotes Wikipedia), and the same snippets carry "600 tons of precious silks and spices", i.e. the cargo, exactly as the researcher diagnosed. The 1589 page I read says "burnt all the rest aswell shippe as goods, to the quantitie of sixe hundreth tunnes of rich marchandise" - the confusion source is confirmed on the leaf. (4) The finding supports the claim directly, and the researcher already states the right hedge (English eyeball estimate, not a register figure). Non-fatal corrections to pass on: (a) "both independent" overstates it - Bancroft is NOT independent (at II.745 n.16 he names Pretty as "the standard authority" and cites the 1589 account), and the two English narratives are from the same ship's company and disagree on other tonnages (Desire 120 vs 140 tunnes; cargo burnt 500 in Pretty p.329 vs 600 in N.H.), so their numbers are not independently reliable; (b) no register tonnage was located anywhere, and Spanish toneladas are not English tons burthen (Navarrete's own note on toneles vs toneladas); (c) their retrieval note contains an error - there is no printed "816" on the facing leaf; the adjacent pages are 811 and 813. The identification by running head and marginal note is nonetheless correct and I reproduced it independently.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Not a refutation, but a weakening of the "two independent narratives + Bancroft" framing. Bancroft is derivative: Hist. Mexico II.745 n.16 states that the standard authority for the voyage is Pretty's narrative in Hakluyt iii.803-25, and that "A brief account was also published in the first edition of Hakluyt, in 1589, 809-13." So his 700 is inherited from the very English texts being corroborated, not an independent datum. Further, the two English narratives are not reliable on tonnages generally: Pretty gives the Desire as "a ship of 120. tunnes" (MacLehose XI p.290) while N.H. 1589 p.809 gives "a hunded and fortie"; Pretty says 500 tunnes of goods were burnt (MacLehose XI p.329) while N.H. says "sixe hundreth tunnes of rich marchandise" (1589 p.812). Finally, the one place a Spanish register figure could be expected - Navarrete's note at Sutil y Mexicana, Introduccion pp. liv-lv, written from Alzola's own declaration at Acapulco and Antonio de Sierra's declaration of 24 Jan 1588 - gives no tonnage. So 700 tons is an English estimate with no Spanish corroboration located.

verdicts.reasoning:
All three quotes check out word for word against texts I fetched myself. I did NOT trust OCR for the 1589 passage: I resolved printed p.812 of cihm_35668 to leaf n863 and read the JPEG (the item's own page_numbers.json is off by four here, mapping 812 to leaf 867, which is actually printed p.816 — a Ralegh assignment; I caught and corrected this). Leaf n863 running head: "M. Thomas Candish. of the English nation. 812", marginal note "The great S. Anna taken, rifled & burnt." The N.H. sentence reads exactly as the finding quotes, including "sixe hundreth tunnes" — which the djvu OCR mangles (it renders "to tbe quantitie of re ... bundzeth tunnes", a marginal note interleaved), so the finding's claim to have read the image rather than OCR is independently corroborated.

MacLehose XI verified as the right book by its title page ("In Twelve Volumes / Volume XI", Glasgow, MCMIV). Pretty's sentence is on p.327 verbatim. The Hunsdon letter runs pp.376-377 under running head "LETTER FROM THOMAS CANDISH a.d. 1588", dateline "Plimmouth this ninth of September 1588", subscription "Thomas Candish", and the asterisk for the suppressed sum is printed: "for it did amount in value to * in Mexico to be solde. Which goods (for that my ships were not able to conteine the least part of them) I was inforced to set on fire." The 122,000 pesos and the marginal "A pezo is 8s" are on p.326 of Pretty's narrative (minor sourcing imprecision in the finding, which runs them together with the 1589 N.H. text at p.812 — they are from the 1598-1600 recension, not from 1589).

Context (test 2): not out of context. Both narratives are describing the actual disposal of the prize at Aguada Segura, and the capacity reason is stated in the sources themselves, not inferred.

Counter-source hunt (test 3): I found a Spanish-side source and it CORROBORATES rather than refutes — Manila Audiencia to Felipe II, 25 June 1588 (Blair & Robertson, The Philippine Islands, vol. 6, pp.311-312): "after having plundered the ship, he burned it, with all the goods which still remained on board." The Spaniards themselves treated the lading as a total loss, "the greatest misfortunes that could happen to this land."

Test 4 (does the finding support the CLAIM, or only something adjacent): it supports the claim directly. Cavendish's own letter gives capacity as the reason; N.H. gives it as "because we were not able to bring it away"; the quantities (40 tons taken, 500-600 burnt) are in the texts.

TWO CORRECTIONS that do not kill the claim but must travel with it: (a) The SHIP did not burn to the water. Pretty's "we saw burnt unto the water" is contradicted by the Spanish record — Bancroft, History of Mexico II, 749-750, following Torquemada and Alzola's declaration, says the cables burned through, she drifted ashore, ballast was thrown out, and "the hulk was found in a condition capable of being repaired ... so as to carry the whole party to Acapulco." Any game text or table saying he burned her to the waterline IS refuted. The cargo claim survives because the Audiencia letter independently confirms the remaining goods were destroyed. (b) 600 tons is the outlier: N.H. 600 in a 700-ton ship; Pretty 500; Bancroft and B&R's editor both adopt 500. The finding reports both honestly, which is to its credit.

Bonus for Aodhan: Hakluyt's blank can be filled from the Spanish side — the Audiencia reckoned the cargo "would have been worth in Mexico two millions [of pesos]." A Manila estimate from investments, not an audited register, but it is the contemporaneous Spanish figure for the exact sum Hakluyt suppressed.

Wording caveat: "could not carry a fraction of her cargo" is literally false — he carried about 7%. Cavendish's "not able to conteine the least part" is a courtier's boast, not a measurement. Recommend "could carry only a small fraction."

One thing I could NOT verify: a web page quotes Alzola's declaration as saying the English sacked the ship "until the twenty-ninth when they had no more space to load," which would be Spanish-side confirmation of the capacity motive. The underlying translation is W. M. Mathes, The Capture of the Santa Ana (Dawson's, 1969), in copyright and not accessible to me. I did not rely on it and neither should the table.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Manila Audiencia to Felipe II, 25 June 1588, in Blair & Robertson, The Philippine Islands 1493-1803, vol. 6, pp.311-312 (CORROBORATES): "after having plundered the ship, he burned it, with all the goods which still remained on board"; and the lading "would have been worth in Mexico two millions [of pesos]" — the figure Hakluyt left blank. CONTRADICTS ONLY THE HULL, NOT THE CARGO: Bancroft, History of Mexico, vol. II, pp.749-750 (1886), following Torquemada and Alzola's declaration via Navarrete: "After taking what he wanted out of the galleon, leaving still some five hundred tons of valuable cargo, and after setting fire to the vessel, he was not particular to see that every plank was burned before he left it ... When her cables burned off she drifted to the shore, and ballast being thrown out, the hulk was found in a condition capable of being repaired, as we are informed by Torquemada, so as to carry the whole party to Acapulco." So Pretty's "burnt unto the water" is false as to the ship. Also Bancroft, History of the North Mexican States I, p.144: "enough of her hulk remained unburned to carry the company to Acapulco."
