(The OCR renders the comma after "gente" as a period; the same file turns many commas into periods, e.g. "sabio. sagaz y prudente.") So the quote is NOT misremembered.
(2) I checked it against the 1723 Madrid original, which they only invoked at second hand. IA item monarquia-indiana.-vol-i_202109, file "Monarquia Indiana. Vol I_djvu.txt" (4.1MB). The 1723 text reads "Quemo el Navio, y dexó alli la Gente, aunque fe vinieron en el cafco, que avia quedado fobre el Agua, que no fe quemo." The UNAM modernisation is faithful. Their caveat about orthography is honest and correct.
(3) I verified the English half independently in Pretty's narrative, Hakluyt (Glasgow ed. vol. XI, pp. 326-27 = Hakluyt 1600, iii.819), IA item principalnaviga07unkngoog: "our Generall caused the kings shippe to be set on fire, which having to the quantitie of 500 tunnes of goods in her we saw burnt unto the water, and then gave them a piece of ordinance and set sayle joyfully homewardes towardes England." The phrase "burnt unto the water" is exact. Pretty also records (same narrative) that 190 Spaniards were put ashore with the ship's sails for tents and "licence to take such store of plankes as should bee sufficient to make them a barke" — i.e. the English expected them to BUILD a bark, which is what makes the survival of the hulk a twist rather than a plan.
(4) I looked for a source that says otherwise. Morga, Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas (1609, Retana ed., IA sucesosdelasisla00morg_0) reports only that "Thomas Escander Yngles... auia tomado en la costa de la Nueua España, (junto á la California) la nao santa Ana" — silence on the burning, not contradiction. Navarrete, Relación del viage... Sutil y Mexicana (1802), p. LVI n.1 (IA relaciondelviage00espi) confirms independently that Alzola gave "una declaración jurídica dada en Acapulco por el mismo capitán Alzóla al día siguiente de su entrada en aquel puerto." Wagner, Spanish Voyages to the Northwest Coast (1929), p. 210, translating the Vizcaíno-expedition relation, carries the same story ("he set fire to her and burned her down to the water's edge. As what was left of her unburned remained afloat on the water..."), and his index records "Acapulco... arrivals at... crew of Santa Ana, 194." I found no source, early or modern, denying that the hulk survived or that the company reached Acapulco.

THE DEFECT. The finding says Torquemada, at lib. V cap. XXVI, "records that she was fired at anchor, that when her cables burned through she drove ashore, that the hulk was found repairable once the ballast was thrown out, and that the marooned company sailed her to Acapulco." Cap. XXVI records NONE of that mechanism. It gives one clause: they came away in the hull, which did not burn. No anchor, no cables, no ballast, no Acapulco. The ballast/Acapulco material is in a DIFFERENT chapter — lib. V cap. XLVIII, inside the Vizcaíno 1602 narrative, 1723 ed. vol. I p. 699 (I located the running head "de la Monarquia Indiana, 699" immediately above it) = UNAM ed. vol. II p. 484, PDF miv2165.pdf. That is exactly the page Bancroft cites as "Torquemada, i. 699" — so Bancroft's citation is right and the finding's is not. Their claim that the UNAM chapter PDF "brackets" Bancroft's i.699 is false: their PDF is the 1723 edition's p. 650 (the 1723 index lists "Marques de Villamanrique. 650"), a different chapter forty-odd chapters away. And the "fired at anchor / cables burned through" element is in NEITHER Torquemada passage; it is Bancroft's own embroidery. Torquemada cap. XLVIII says the sea cast the submerged remnant into the bay, not that burned cables let her drive ashore.

Two smaller slips. "It was Alzola's arrival at Acapulco in her that produced the sworn declaration" — "in her" is an inference; Navarrete says only that Alzola declared the day after entering the port, and Navarrete read TWO declarations, the second by Antonio de Sierra before the Audiencia of Guadalajara on 24 January 1588, which the finding's singular ignores. And the "burnt unto the water" quotation was given with no locator at all.

The Drake error is real and checks out verbatim in both editions of cap. XXVI: "entró por la Mar del Sur el corsario Francisco Draque." (Note that in cap. XLVIII Torquemada calls him only "el inglés, que robó la nao Santa Ana," unnamed.)

ONE LIMITATION TO DISCLOSE. The mechanism of survival rests on a single textual tradition — the Vizcaíno-expedition relation (Fr. Antonio de la Ascensión, which Torquemada worked up), composed c. 1602-15 and reporting what was said at the bay fifteen years after the event. Bancroft says as much: Torquemada "gives the only account extant of the return of the Santa Ana to Acapulco." Navarrete read the Alzola and Sierra declarations and reported nothing from them about the hull. So "she survived" is attested, early and from the site, but by one line of transmission, not by two independent ones.

NET: refuted=false. Both halves of the claim are true and I verified them from the texts myself. But the sources table must cite Torquemada, Monarquía Indiana, lib. V cap. XLVIII (1723 ed. i.699 / UNAM ed. ii.484) for the ballast-jury-rig-Acapulco detail, cite lib. V cap. XXVI (1723 ed. i.650 / UNAM ed. ii.418) only for the bare survival clause and the Draque misattribution, and drop "fired at anchor" and "when her cables burned through" entirely or attribute them to Bancroft's gloss rather than to Torquemada.
verdicts.counter_evidence: The mechanism the finding attributes to lib. V cap. XXVI is actually in lib. V cap. XLVIII. 1723 Madrid ed., vol. I, p. 699 (OCR of the original, long-s normalised): "En esta Bahia fue donde el Ingles, que robó la Nao Santa Ana, que venia de Filipinas los años pasados, hechó en Tierra la Gente, que en la Nao venia, y aviendo robado lo que quiso de ella, le pegó fuego, y se quemó hasta lo que estaba fuera del Agua, y lo que quedó debaxo de ella con las olas, lo hechó la Mar en esta Bahia, y los que alli estaban sin remedio, entraron dentro, y hechando el Lastre a la Mar, quedaron con suficiente Buxél para venir hasta Acapulco con unas Vandolas, que le pusieron." UNAM modernised text, vol. II p. 484: "...y echando el lastre a la mar, quedaron con suficiente bajel para venir hasta Acapulco con unas bandolas que le pusieron." Note what is NOT there: no anchor, no cables. The sea casts the submerged remnant into the bay; "cuando sus cables se quemaron" is Bancroft's invention. Cap. XXVI (1723 i.650 = UNAM ii.418), which the finding cites for all of this, contains only "Quemó el navío y dejó allí la gente, aunque se vinieron en el casco que había quedado sobre el agua, que no se quemó" — survival, yes; mechanism, no; Acapulco, no. Corroboration that cap. XLVIII is the right locator: Bancroft's own footnote cites "Torquemada, i. 699," and the 1723 running head "de la Monarquia Indiana, 699" sits directly above this passage; Wagner 1929 p.210 translates the same passage ("he set fire to her and burned her down to the water's edge"). English side, verbatim and with a locator the finding omitted — Francis Pretty in Hakluyt 1600, iii.819 (Glasgow ed. XI.327): "our Generall caused the kings shippe to be set on fire, which having to the quantitie of 500 tunnes of goods in her we saw burnt unto the water." Pretty also shows the English had given the Spaniards "licence to take such store of plankes as should bee sufficient to make them a barke," which is the detail that makes the hulk's survival an accident rather than the plan. Navarrete 1802, p. LVI n.1, corrects the finding's "Alzola's arrival... in her": he says only "una declaración jurídica dada en Acapulco por el mismo capitán Alzóla al día siguiente de su entrada en aquel puerto," and he read a second declaration too, "ante el Presidente y Oidores de la Audiencia de Guadalaxara a 24 de enero de 1588 por Antonio de Sierra."

claims.claim: The first prize: name, date, place, guns, tonnage, how hard she fought. Game models her as mid-size, ~20 guns, striking after a sharp fight.
claims.finding: Name, date, place and gun count CONFIRMED; tonnage confirmed from Cooke not Rogers; 'sharp fight' OVER-READS the sources. Rogers (1712, p. 294): the prize was 'Nostra Seniora de la Incarnacion Disenganio, Sir John Pichberty Commander; she had 20 Guns, 20 Patereroes, and 193 Men aboard, whereof 9 were kill'd, 10 wounded, and several blown up and burnt with Powder.' Taken at daybreak 22 December 1709 (Old Style; Rogers' journal, and the Committee minute of 24 Dec refers to 'the Prize taken on board the 22d instant'). Place: off Cabo San Lucas; at noon the day before 'The Cape then bore N.N.E. of us, distant about 5 Leagues' (p. 292), and after the action the harbour 'bore N.E. of us, distant about 7 Leagues'. TONNAGE: Rogers gives none. Edward Cooke, who watched from a hill ashore, gives it: 'being a Ship of about 400 Tuns, carrying 20 Guns, and 20 Brass Pedreros, commanded by Sir John Pichberty, a French Gentleman, and Brother-in-Law to Monsieur du Cass' (Cooke I, p. 346). HOW HARD SHE FOUGHT: not hard. Only the DUKE engaged her; the Dutchess was becalmed to leeward. Rogers: 'we gave her several Broad-sides, plying our Small Arms very briskly, which they return'd as thick a while, but did not ply their great Guns half so fast as we. After some time we shot a little a-head of them, lay thwart her Hawse close aboard, and plyed them so warmly, that she soon struck her Colours two thirds down.' Rogers reckons 'We engag'd 'em about 3 Glasses' (~1.5 hours, including the long-range chase-gun exchange); Cooke, watching, says 'The Action lasted not half an Hour, before she was in our Possession.' English loss in the whole action: TWO men. Rogers shot through the left cheek, his upper jaw and teeth carried away; 'the other, Will. Powell, an Irish Land-man, was slightly wounded in the Buttock.'
claims.quote: "This Prize was call'd by the long Name of Nostra Seniora de la Incarnacion Disenganio, Sir John Pichberty Commander; she had 20 Guns, 20 Patereroes, and 193 Men aboard, whereof 9 were kill'd, 10 wounded, and several blown up and burnt with Powder. We engag'd 'em about 3 Glasses, in which time we had only my self and another Man wounded."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), p. 294 (journal entry of 22 December 1709); tonnage from Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (London, 1712), vol. I, p. 346
claims.retrieval_note: Downloaded the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy of the 1712 FIRST edition. Proved identity three ways: (1) OCR of the title page carries the full 1712 imprint 'LONDON, Printed for A. Bell at the Cross-Keys and Bible in Cornhil, and B. Lintot ... M DCC. XII' and the dedication to the named Bristol owners; (2) I downloaded the title-page IMAGE (leaf n6) and read it directly, confirming 'Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1711'; (3) I located this passage via IA's search-inside API, downloaded the page image (leaf n321) and READ IT, confirming the printed page number '294' and the text word for word against the OCR. Independently cross-checked against the 1928 Manwaring reprint (IA cruisingvoyager00roge), which agrees verbatim. Cooke verified by his own 1712 title page naming 'Capt. Edward Cooke' and the Lintot/Gosling imprint.
claims.game_impact: KEEP 20 guns (exact). KEEP 'mid-size' — ~400 tons against the other galleon's ~900. CHANGE the fight: it was short and lopsided, one English ship against a galleon that fired her great guns slowly and struck with her colours two-thirds down, costing the English two casualties. If the level wants drama, the real beat is that the player's own captain takes a musket ball through the face and has to command by writing notes.

claims.claim: The second galleon: name, tonnage, gun count. Game says about 900 tons and 40+ guns.
claims.finding: Both numbers CONFIRMED, independently, by both primary accounts. Rogers (1712, p. 302) — I read this page as an image: 'The Enemy's was a brave lofty new Ship, the Admiral of Manila, and this the first Voyage she had made; she was call'd the Bigonia, of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns, about 40 of which were mounted, with as many Patereroes, all Brass; her Complement of Men on board, as we were inform'd, was above 450, besides Passengers.' Cooke, writing separately: 'The Enemy was a new Ship of above 900 Tuns, could mount at least 60 Guns, but had not now so many.' NAME CAVEAT, and it matters: the form 'Begoña' appears NOWHERE in either primary account. Rogers' only spelling, used once, is 'Bigonia'; Cooke never names her at all, calling her only 'the Admiral of Manila'. I grepped both texts for begon/bigon/bagon/vegon/begoign. So 'Nuestra Señora de Begoña' is a later normalisation, not an English eyewitness reading. Rogers adds the detail that explains her behaviour: '150 of the Men on board this great Ship were Europeans, several of whom had been formerly Pirates, and having now got all their Wealth aboard, were resolved to defend it to the last.'
claims.quote: "The Enemy's was a brave lofty new Ship, the Admiral of Manila, and this the first Voyage she had made; she was call'd the Bigonia, of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns, about 40 of which were mounted, with as many Patereroes, all Brass; her Complement of Men on board, as we were inform'd, was above 450, besides Passengers."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), p. 302; corroborated by Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I, p. 351
claims.retrieval_note: Because the whole detection/clock mechanic rests on this, I did not trust OCR. I used IA's fulltext search-inside endpoint to find the leaf carrying 'Bigonia' (leaf n329), downloaded that page image via the BookReader JPEG API, and READ IT. The image shows the running head 'A Cruising Voyage round the World', the printed page number 302, the marginal year 1709, and the sentence verbatim. Cooke's corroborating sentence came from a physically separate 1712 book (different printer, different author, verified by its own title page).
claims.game_impact: KEEP ~900 tons and 40+ guns — both are exactly right, and the 40 mounted guns were brass, backed by about 40 brass patereros (swivels) and 450+ men. Note she COULD have carried 60; she was under-gunned for her build, which is itself a nice detail. CHANGE the name display or add a note: the English eyewitness spelling is 'Bigonia'. If the game prints 'Begoña' it is using a form no participant wrote.

claims.claim: Did she fight off Rogers' entire squadron? How many English ships engaged, for how long, outcome and damage. The level's 'walk away' lesson.
claims.finding: CONFIRMED, and if anything the game understates it. The action ran over three days off the cape (25–27 December 1709 OS). Night of 25/26: the DUTCHESS engaged her ALONE. 26th: Dutchess and MARQUIS. 27th: all THREE — Duke, Dutchess, Marquis — engaged together, and she beat them all off. Rogers on the Duke's share: 'We engag'd first and last about six or seven Hours.' Outcome: the English broke off by a written council resolution, signed on board the Duke the same day, which Rogers printed in full: 'We having consider'd the Condition of all our 3 Ships, and that our Masts are much damnified in engaging the Manila Ship, do think it for the Interest of the whole to forbear any further Attempts upon her, having no Probability of taking her.' Signed by Rogers, Courtney, Dampier, Cooke, Frye and ten others including Alexander Selkirk. DAMAGE TO THE ENGLISH: Duke took two shot in the mainmast ('which rent it miserably'), had a fire-ball thrown from the galleon's top which blew up a chest of arms and cartouch boxes on the quarterdeck, 11 men wounded, 3 scorched; Rogers himself 'again unfortunately wounded in the Left Foot with a Splinter ... part of my Heel-bone being struck out'. 'The Dutchess had about 20 Men killed and wounded' (Cooke, on board, says 25 killed and wounded), foremast much disabled, a shot in the powder room, leaks. 'The Marquiss had none kill'd or wounded, but 2 scorch'd with Powder' — but her mainmast was disabled and she had fired off nearly all her shot and powder. DAMAGE TO THE GALLEON: almost none. 'we shatter'd her Sails and Rigging very much, shot her Mizon-yard, kill'd two Men out of her Tops, which was all the Damage we could see we did 'em; tho' we could not place less than 500 Shot (6 Pounders) in her Hull.' Rogers' explanation: 'These large Ships are built at Manila with excellent Timber, that will not splinter; they have very thick Sides, much stronger than we build in Europe.' She kept her flag at the maintopmast head the whole time.
claims.quote: "we shatter'd her Sails and Rigging very much, shot her Mizon-yard, kill'd two Men out of her Tops, which was all the Damage we could see we did 'em; tho' we could not place less than 500 Shot (6 Pounders) in her Hull. These large Ships are built at Manila with excellent Timber, that will not splinter; they have very thick Sides, much stronger than we build in Europe."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 297–303 (26–27 December 1709), incl. the Committee minute of 27 Dec 1709; Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I, pp. 347–351
claims.retrieval_note: Page 302 read as an image (see R-2) carries the casualty tallies and the 500-shot sentence directly. The surrounding narrative (pp. 297–303) was read in the 1712 OCR and checked line-by-line against the independent 1928 reprint OCR, which agrees. Cooke's three-day sequence is an entirely independent witness: he was commanding the Marquis and dates each day by weekday as well as date ('Tuesday, December 27'), which matches Rogers' committee minute dated 27 December 1709.
claims.game_impact: KEEP the walk-away lesson — it is real, documented, and signed by fifteen officers. SHARPEN it: the failure was not a gun-count problem but a PENETRATION problem. Six-pounders could not hurt Manila-built timber; 500 hits in the hull produced no visible effect. Boarding was also ruled out (she had a netting-deck, close quarters, false decks, bales packed between the guns, and no man visible above board, with 'above treble the Number aboard'). Model her as functionally immune to the player's shot, not merely tough.

claims.claim: Was the Dutchess present as consort, and did Rogers signal her? Was there a third ship (the Marquis)? Is one AI consort you can signal defensible?
claims.finding: Dutchess present and signalled: CONFIRMED. One-consort model: defensible for the FIRST action only, and WRONG for the second. The squadron off the cape was THREE ships plus a bark used as a despatch vessel. Stations were formally agreed on 2–3 November 1709: 'I was to be the outermost Ship, the Dutchess in the middle, and the Marquiss next the Land; with the Bark to ply and carry Advice from Ship to Ship: The nearest Ship to be 6 Leagues at least, and 9 at most from the Land: By this Agreement, we could spread 15 Leagues ... And to prevent the Ships passing in the Night, we were to ply to Windward all Day, and drive at Night.' Signalling is everywhere in the text: Rogers sent Lt. Frye by yawl to the Dutchess 'to agree how to engage her'; 'We then hoisted a French Ensign, and fired a Gun, which the Stranger answer'd' (a ruse); the two pinnaces tended the chase all night 'showing false Fires'; sentries were posted on a hilltop with orders 'if they saw a Sail in the Offing, to make 3 Wafts with their Colours'; after breaking off, Rogers made 'a Signal to our Consorts to consult what to do'; Cooke names the specific flags — 'the one with a Waift in his Ensign, and the other with a Spanish Jack, the Signals to speak with one another'. CORRECTION the game needs: at the FIRST action the Marquis was NOT at sea — she was in Port Segura refitting, and Cooke watched the capture from a hilltop. So action one really was Duke + Dutchess. At the SECOND action all three fought. The third ship was the Marquis, ex-French prize Havre de Grace taken off Guayaquil, rearmed from 12 to 20 guns; Cooke says she carried 18 at the action, 'six of which were very small, and but a meer Shell of a Ship'.
claims.quote: "I was to be the outermost Ship, the Dutchess in the middle, and the Marquiss next the Land; with the Bark to ply and carry Advice from Ship to Ship: The nearest Ship to be 6 Leagues at least, and 9 at most from the Land: By this Agreement, we could spread 15 Leagues, and see any thing that might pass us in the Day, within 20 Leagues of the Shore."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 204–205 (3 November 1709), and pp. 292–299; Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I, pp. 345, 350–351
claims.retrieval_note: Read in the 1928 Manwaring reprint (clean OCR) and verified against the 1712 first-edition OCR for the same passages; the 1712 copy was itself proven by title-page image (see R-1). Cooke's hilltop view of the first action is at his vol. I p. 345 ('I went up a Hill, and saw our Ships engage and take the lesser of the Manila Ships'), in the 1712 Cooke scan verified by its own title page.
claims.game_impact: DEFENSIBLE for the first galleon: one signalled AI consort (the Dutchess) is exactly right there. NOT defensible for the second: the whole point of that action is that THREE ships could not take her. If the game uses one consort in both levels, add the Marquis for the second action, or the 'walk away' lesson reads as 'you were undermanned' rather than 'she was invulnerable'. Also consider the bark as a scout/advice vessel and the three-ship picket line spread 15 leagues — that is a far better detection mechanic than a single radius.

claims.claim: The Duke: tonnage, guns, crew, length. Game: 102 ft, heavy broadside, slow, toughest hull, biggest hold of the three older ships.
claims.finding: Tonnage, guns and crew CONFIRMED verbatim in Rogers' first journal entry: 'the Duke Burden about 320 Tuns, having 30 Guns and 117 Men; and the Dutchess Burden about 260 Tuns by Measure, 26 Guns and 108 Men'. LENGTH: NOT RECOVERABLE from either primary account. Neither Rogers nor Cooke gives any dimension of the Duke. The only figure I found anywhere is G. E. Manwaring's 1928 editorial estimate, and he explicitly frames it as an analogy, not a measurement — he calls the two ships the equivalent of a 6th rate of the day, with a keel length of about 80 ft and a breadth of about 25 ft. A roughly 80-ft keel is arithmetically compatible with an overall/gundeck length near 100 ft, but no source I retrieved states 102 ft or anything like it. BIGGEST OF THE THREE: supported — Duke 320 tons vs Dutchess 260, and the Marquis was a rearmed French prize carrying 18 guns that Cooke called 'but a meer Shell of a Ship'. TOUGHEST HULL: not directly attested, and cuts against the evidence — the Duke sprang a leak off California on 23 November 1709, and by the homeward leg was so bad that four men could barely keep her free for half an hour at a time. SLOW: NOT supported and partly refuted. Rogers notes the Duke and Dutchess 'did not sail so well as the major part' of the Bristol convoy in 1708, but within the squadron the poor sailers were the Marquis and the Batchelor, which 'sail but very indifferent upon a Wind'; Cooke says the Marquis was 'not so good a Sailer as the Dutchess'. In the first galleon action the Duke outran her consort and, in a flat calm, 'got out 8 of our Ships Oars, and rowed above an Hour'.
claims.quote: "the Duke Burden about 320 Tuns, having 30 Guns and 117 Men; and the Dutchess Burden about 260 Tuns by Measure, 26 Guns and 108 Men: both well furnish'd with all Necessaries on board for a distant Undertaking."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), p. 1 (entry of 2 August 1708); length estimate from G. E. Manwaring's introduction to the 1928 Seafarers' Library reprint, p. xvi
claims.retrieval_note: Found in both the 1712 OCR (which reads '...bout 320 Tuns, having 30 Guns and 117 Men; and') and the 1928 reprint OCR, which agree. The 1712 copy is proven by its title-page image. I then grepped both primary texts for 'keel', 'feet long', 'foot long', 'dimension' and found no dimension of the Duke anywhere; the only hit is Manwaring's 1928 editorial parenthesis.
claims.game_impact: KEEP 320 tons, 30 guns, 117 men — exact. FLAG 102 ft as INVENTED, or at least unsourced: no primary account gives the Duke's length, and the only published estimate is a 1928 editor's ~80 ft keel by analogy. If you need a number, say 'about 80 ft keel (estimated)' or drop the figure. DROP or justify 'slow' — within the squadron she was the better sailer and could row. 'Toughest hull' is not attested and she was in fact the leaky one; 'biggest hold of the three' is fine.

claims.claim: Where: the game puts both actions at Cabo San Lucas. What does Rogers say about his station, the cape, and the watering place?
claims.finding: CONFIRMED for both actions. The council resolution of 24 October 1709 fixed the station by name: they 'do now finally determine to cruize off Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Cape of California ... We resolve with the utmost Care and Diligence to wait here the coming of the Manila Ship belonging to the Spaniards, and bound for Acapulco'. They raised the land 1 November and identified it next day: 'The Westermost Land we set yesterday Noon, we make to be Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Head-land of California', with an observed latitude of 22°55' N the day before (Cooke's table gives the cape as 23°10' N). FIRST ACTION: at noon before the capture 'The Cape then bore N.N.E. of us, distant about 5 Leagues'. SECOND ACTION: Cooke, morning of 27 December, 'Cape St. Luke bearing N.E. by E. distant about two Leagues'. So both fights were within two to five leagues of the cape. HARBOUR AND WATERING PLACE: they used the anchorage Rogers calls by Cavendish's name — 'we made the best of our Way into the Harbour call'd by Sir Tho. Cavendish Port Segura' — anchoring there in 25 fathoms. The watering place was found by boat on 22 November: 'they had found a very good Bay, with a fresh Water River, and that they saw near 500 Indians, who lived there in small Hutts, but had no Recruit for us, besides a little Fish ... which we suppose was the same that Sir Thomas Cavendish recruited at in Queen Elizabeth's Time, Anno 1588.' Water was scarce and slow: on 26 November the pinnace returned with just three barrels of water and two large fish from the Indians.
claims.quote: "we do now finally determine to cruize off Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Cape of California, in such Methods, and with such Signals to each other, as shall be agreed on in our next Committee. We resolve with the utmost Care and Diligence to wait here the coming of the Manila Ship belonging to the Spaniards, and bound for Acapulco; whose Wealth on board her we hope will prompt every Man to use his utmost Conduct and Bravery to conquer."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), p. 201 (Committee at Tres Marias, 24 October 1709), pp. 204, 209, 213, 294; Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I, p. 349 and the Guam run table in vol. II
claims.retrieval_note: All four locating passages grepped out of the 1712 OCR and re-read in the independent 1928 reprint; the 22 December bearing ('The Cape then bore N.N.E. of us, distant about 5 Leagues') and the Port Segura anchorage were confirmed on the page image of p. 294 that I read directly. Cooke's 27 December bearing comes from the separate 1712 Cooke volume; his latitude for the cape (23°10' N) comes from the run table that opens Cooke vol. II, whose header names the ship Marquis and the run from Cape St. Lucas to Guam in 1709.
claims.game_impact: KEEP Cabo San Lucas for both actions — correct and tightly documented. ADD, if you want texture: the base is Port Segura (Cavendish's name, used by Rogers), the watering place is a bay with a freshwater river and about 500 Indians living in huts, and water came off in barrels a few at a time. Watering was a real bottleneck: Courtney's stock was nearly spent by 25 November.

claims.claim: How long did Rogers lie in wait, and what did he know about when the galleon was due? (the ambush phase)
claims.finding: CONFIRMED: about seven weeks, 2 November to 21 December 1709, and they knew the season rather than a date. Intelligence basis, stated in the council minute: they 'examin'd the Opinion of Capt. Dampier, appointed Pilot by the Owners' and had 'been well informed from all the Intelligences we have frequently had from Prisoners since our being in the South Seas'. Rogers also had a historical precedent he took seriously: 'Sir Thomas Cavendish, in Queen Elizabeth's Time, took the Manila Ship in this Place on the 4th of November.' By 9 December he judged they had missed the window: 'We were now something dubious of seeing the Manila Ship, because it's near a Month after the time they generally fall in with this Coast.' CRUCIALLY, what ended the ambush was not patience but VICTUALS. On 20 December Rogers wrote out a bread calculation: 64 days' bread for each ship eight days earlier, 56 left, 14 more squeezed out by rummaging, '70 Days Bread to come', against 9 days to refit plus 50 days' passage to Guam — leaving '11 Days Bread will be left when we come to Guam'. On that arithmetic the council resolved 'to forbear any further Attempts' and make for Guam, and 'At signing this in the Committee we all looked very melancholy and dispirited'. They sighted the galleon the very next morning, 21 December, while beating in to Port Segura to refit.
claims.quote: "We were now something dubious of seeing the Manila Ship, because it's near a Month after the time they generally fall in with this Coast."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 200–201, 205, 210–213 (24 October – 21 December 1709)
claims.retrieval_note: The whole 2 November – 21 December sequence was read continuously in the 1928 reprint OCR and spot-checked against the 1712 OCR at the start (Cape St. Lucas identification), middle (Cavendish, 4 November) and end (the bread minute and the 21 December sighting, which runs straight into page 292 of the 1712 text immediately preceding the page image I read at p. 294). The dates are Old Style throughout: Rogers' own committee minute of 13 February 1708 corresponds to our February 1709, confirming he used the 25 March year.
claims.game_impact: KEEP the ambush phase and make it ~7 weeks. CHANGE the timer's driver: the clock that actually ran out was BREAD, not patience or enemy detection. Rogers quit on a victualling calculation with an 11-day margin to Guam, and the galleon appeared the next morning. A provisions meter that forces the abandon-station decision one beat before the prize appears is both truer and better drama than a countdown. Also give the player a soft prior, not a date: the galleons 'generally fall in with this Coast' about a month earlier, and Cavendish took one here on 4 November.

claims.claim: 'Rescued Alexander Selkirk' - correct? Date and place.
claims.finding: Substantially correct but the word 'rescued' flattens it, and the date needs a style note. Place: Juan Fernandez, the middle bay, approached on the north-east side. Date: 2 February in Rogers' journal — Old Style, and since Rogers reckons the year from 25 March (his own minute is dated '13th of February, 1708' for what we call 1709), this is 2 February 1709 modern style, 13 February 1709 Gregorian. It was the DUKE's pinnace, sent after the yawl failed to return, that brought him off, not Rogers personally: it 'brought abundance of Craw-fish, with a Man cloth'd in Goat-Skins, who look'd wilder than the first Owners of them. He had been on the Island four Years and four Months, being left there by Capt. Stradling in the Cinque-Ports; his Name was Alexander Selkirk a Scotch Man'. Two qualifications: Selkirk had drawn them in himself — ''Twas he that made the Fire last night when he saw our Ships, which he judg'd to be English' — and he was hired on the spot, not merely saved: 'I immediately agreed with him to be a Mate on board our Ship.' He went on to sign the 27 December 1709 council minute after the Begoña action and was later appointed Master of the captured galleon.
claims.quote: "Immediately our Pinnace return'd from the shore, and brought abundance of Craw-fish, with a Man cloth'd in Goat-Skins, who look'd wilder than the first Owners of them. He had been on the Island four Years and four Months, being left there by Capt. Stradling in the Cinque-Ports; his Name was Alexander Selkirk a Scotch Man, who had been Master of the Cinque-Ports."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 91–92 (entry of 2 February 1708/9)
claims.retrieval_note: Grepped both the 1712 and 1928 texts for 'Selkirk' and read the full entry in the 1928 reprint; the 1712 title page itself advertises 'An Account of Alexander Selkirk's living alone four Years and four Months in an Island', which I read on the title-page IMAGE — an independent confirmation of the four-years-four-months figure from the printed sheet. Old Style year-reckoning established by Rogers' own committee minute dated 13 February 1708 (= our 1709) at p. 97.
claims.game_impact: KEEP the episode. CHANGE the framing if the game says Rogers rescued him: a boat's crew from the Duke brought him off after Selkirk lit a signal fire to draw the ships in, and Rogers immediately signed him on as a mate. Date it 2 February 1709 (Old Style) and, if the game prints a modern calendar date, 13 February 1709. Selkirk is then aboard for BOTH galleon actions and signs the resolution to break off — a good continuity hook.

claims.claim: Rogers' dates: the game says '1708-11'.
claims.finding: CONFIRMED on the printed title page of the first edition, which I read as an image: 'Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1711.' The journal bears this out at both ends. Departure: 'August 2. Yesterday about four in the Afternoon we weigh'd from Kingroad near Bristol, on board the Duke frigate' — i.e. sailed 1 August 1708, journal opened 2 August. Return: 'On the 1st of October, about 11 of the Clock we came to an Anchor in the Downs, where several of our Owners came aboard', and then 'Octob. 14. This Day at 11 of the Clock, we and our Consort and Prize got up to [Erith], where we came to an Anchor, which ends our long and fatiguing Voyage.' Both 1711. One trap worth recording: the OCR of the 1712 title page renders the line as 'finish'd in 1712', which is wrong — the type reads 1711. I only caught this by downloading the page image.
claims.quote: "Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1711."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), title page; journal entries of 2 August 1708 (p. 1) and 1 and 14 October 1711 (pp. 313–314)
claims.retrieval_note: Downloaded leaf n6 of the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy as a JPEG via the IA BookReader image API and READ IT. The sheet shows the full title, 'Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1711', the Selkirk advertisement, 'By Captain WOODES ROGERS, Commander in Chief on this Expedition, with the Ships Duke and Dutchess of Bristol', and the imprint 'LONDON, Printed for A. Bell ... and B. Lintot ... M DCC. XII.' This both confirms the date range and proves the file is the 1712 first edition rather than the 1718 or 1726 reissue. The terminal dates were then located in the journal text of both the 1712 and 1928 scans.
claims.game_impact: KEEP '1708-11' exactly as the game has it — it is the author's own title-page formulation. If you ever want precise bookends: sailed from Kingroad, Bristol, 1 August 1708; anchored in the Downs 1 October 1711; moored at Erith 14 October 1711.

claims.claim: What did the prize actually yield, and what became of the treasure?
claims.finding: The FATE is fully documented; the YIELD is not, in either primary account, and I will not supply a figure I could not verify. FATE: the Encarnación was renamed on 6 January 1709/10 — 'now named by us The Batchelor Frigate' — after Alderman Batchelor of Bristol. Thomas Dover was given nominal command by a majority of the council over Rogers' furious written protest, and the quarrel generated duelling protests which Rogers printed in full; Selkirk was made her Master. She sailed with the squadron from California on 10/11 January 1710 for Guam, then Batavia, then the Cape, then the Texel. The Marquis was condemned at Batavia as worm-eaten ('eat to a Honey-comb by the Worms') and sold for 575 Dutch dollars. Goods were sold ashore at Batavia and at the Cape. At the Texel the owner James Hollidge came aboard and 'took Account of what Plate, Gold, Pearl, &c. was in the Ship', and they refused to land gold at Amsterdam for fear of voiding the insurance. The East India Company moved against them: Rogers had to swear an affidavit before a notary 'to justifie our Proceedings to the Queen and Council, in Answer to what the East-India Company had to alledge against us, they being, as we were inform'd, resolved to trouble us, on Pretence we had encroached upon their Liberties in India.' YIELD: Rogers gives no total anywhere in the 1712 book. The only primary number near it is a PRISONER'S CLAIM in Cooke: the prisoners said the Encarnación's cargo 'amounted to two Millions of Dollars' in India and that the other ship was of much greater value — hearsay from captives, not an audit. The only internal valuation Rogers gives is trivia: the plunder-cloth in the Batchelor was appraised at Batavia at about 400 pounds sterling. For the voyage total I found only Manwaring's 1928 editorial statement that the outfit cost under 14,000 pounds and net profits were at least 170,000 pounds, two-thirds to the owners and one-third shared among officers and men by rating, with his footnote that a contemporary petition put the plunder at 800,000 pounds. That is secondary, and the 800,000 figure is an interested party's claim in a petition.
claims.quote: "On the 31st Mr. Hollidge came aboard (the rest of the Owners being gone over for England) and took Account of what Plate, Gold, Pearl, &c. was in the Ship. The same being done aboard the Dutchess, he likewise took a List of our Men to get Protections for them, from being impress'd after our Arrival in the River of Thames."
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 224–227 (Batchelor naming and protests, January 1709/10), pp. 289–290 (sale of the Marquis, Batavia, July 1710), pp. 311–313 (Texel, East India Company, August–September 1711); Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I, p. 346
claims.retrieval_note: I read the Batavia and Texel sections in full in the 1928 reprint and confirmed the Batchelor naming passage, the Marquis sale and the East India Company affidavit against the 1712 OCR. I then searched BOTH primary texts specifically for a total: grepped for pound signs, 'Sale of', 'Cargo', 'Pieces of Eight', five- and six-digit numbers, 'East India Company', 'Owners'. No voyage total exists in either book. I also downloaded and grepped the 1889 Leslie edition (Life Aboard a British Privateer) for a figure and found none, and searched Internet Archive for pre-1929 works on the Rogers prize accounting without result.
claims.game_impact: FLAG any specific treasure figure in the game as UNSOURCED from the primaries. If a number is needed, use Manwaring's net 170,000 pounds against an outfit of under 14,000 and label it as a later editor's figure, or use Cooke's 'two Millions of Dollars' and label it explicitly as what the Spanish prisoners claimed. CHANGE any implication that the treasure was simply banked: the real ending is a command fight over who got the prize, goods sold off piecemeal at Batavia and the Cape, gold kept aboard to protect the insurance, and the East India Company suing the squadron for trespassing on its monopoly before they had even reached England.

nulls: No total value for the voyage or for the Batchelor's cargo exists in either primary account. I grepped the full text of Rogers 1712 and Cooke 1712 (both volumes) for currency symbols, 'Pieces of Eight', 'Sale', 'Cargo', 'Value', and all five- and six-digit numbers. Rogers' only internal valuation is the plunder-cloth at Batavia, about 400 pounds. The oft-cited totals (170,000 pounds net, 800,000 pounds plunder) come from G. E. Manwaring's 1928 introduction and his citation of a petition via Mariner's Mirror 1924, neither of which I could retrieve and read.

No dimensions of the Duke (length, beam, draught) appear in any source I retrieved. Grepped both primary texts for 'keel', 'feet', 'foot long', 'dimension', 'built'. The only figure anywhere is Manwaring's 1928 estimate of an 80 ft keel and 25 ft beam, explicitly offered as an analogy to a 6th rate of the period, not as a measurement of this ship. The game's 102 ft has no source I could find.

The Spanish form 'Nuestra Senora de Begona' does not occur in either eyewitness account. I grepped Rogers 1712, the 1928 reprint, and both Cooke volumes for begon, bigon, bagon, vegon, begoign and bcgon. Rogers writes 'Bigonia' once and only once; Cooke never names her, calling her only 'the Admiral of Manila'. I did not reach a Spanish-language source to settle the true name.

Whether the Begona/Bigonia actually reached Acapulco afterwards is not stated by Rogers or Cooke. Rogers records only the decision 'to keep her company till Night, then to lose her'. Confirming her arrival would need a Mexican or Philippine source I did not consult.

I did not examine any Spanish-side account of either action. Everything here is English, from the two participants who published. Rogers' crew figures for the galleons (193 men, above 450 men) are explicitly secondhand: 'as we were inform'd', from prisoners.
