A deliberate null check.

surprises: The real ambush timer was BREAD, not the enemy. On 20 December Rogers wrote out an arithmetic table in his journal - 70 days' bread in hand, 9 to refit, 50 to Guam, 11 days' margin - and on that basis the council voted to abandon the station. 'At signing this in the Committee we all looked very melancholy and dispirited.' The galleon appeared the next morning. A victualling meter that forces the abandon decision one beat before the prize appears is truer and far better drama than a countdown clock.

The level's lesson is not 'she had more guns'. It is a penetration failure. 500 six-pound shot in the hull produced two dead men in her tops and a shot-away mizzen yard. Rogers' own diagnosis: Manila-built timber 'will not splinter' and the sides are 'much stronger than we build in Europe'. He also records that they deliberately stopped loading bar and partridge shot because 'the Ship's Sides were too thick to receive any Damage by it'. Model her as immune to the player's shot type, not merely high-HP.

Boarding was ruled out by a specific anti-boarding fit-out, not by numbers alone: netting-deck, close quarters, false decks, bales packed between the guns to shield the crew, and nobody visible above board. Rogers notes they could not fire small arms 'till we saw a Man appear, or a Port open'. Cooke records the prisoners' warning that if the English entered 500 men they would lose them all.

She fought with fire. A fire-ball thrown from one of her tops blew up a chest of arms and loaded cartouch boxes on the Duke's quarterdeck; Cooke says stink-pots set the Marquis alight and he 'stunk several Days intolerably'; the Dutchess, about to lash herself alongside, had to cast off for fear of burning. The English considered burning her in return and rejected it only because they had goods of value aboard.

Rogers was shot through the face on day one - jaw and teeth carried away, part of his jawbone swallowed in the night - and commanded by writing notes. On day three a splinter took out part of his heel bone and he spent the rest of the action lying on his back on the quarterdeck. A commander whose ability to issue orders degrades is a better mechanic than a health bar.

The first galleon hung barrels at each yardarm 'that look'd like Powder Barrels, to deter us from boarding 'em' - a pure bluff, and she then struck after a short fight. A deception layer on an enemy's apparent strength is already in the source.

Before the first action Rogers served out a kettle of chocolate because there was no spirits aboard, then called the ship to prayers - 'and before we had concluded were disturb'd by the Enemy's firing at us'. In a flat calm he had eight sweeps run out and rowed the Duke for over an hour to close.

The squadron carried a social failure state. The sailors resented the Dutchess for not engaging the first prize until after she had struck, which poisoned the council, which then refused Rogers' proposal to concentrate the Marquis's men in the two good ships. Rogers believed that refusal cost them the big galleon: had the Duke and Dutchess been together at first, 'we all believe we should have made them have carried this great Ship'. The ships then exchanged formal written protests over who should command the prize. Squadron cohesion as a resource is in the primary text and the game apparently does not model it.
Alexander Selkirk is aboard for all of this. He signs the 27 December 1709 council minute to break off the action, and is afterwards made Master of the captured galleon.

The first prize's captain was a Frenchman, Sir John Pichberty, brother-in-law to Admiral Ducasse. Rogers settled the outstanding Guayaquil ransom with him by bills of exchange for 6,000 dollars payable in London, trusting him 'being we hope a Man of Honour' with no hostage held. A prize fight that ends in a credit transaction is an unusual beat.

The Marquis was not a purpose-built warship at all but a French prize, the Havre de Grace, taken off Guayaquil (Rogers' younger brother John was killed boarding her), rearmed from 12 to 20 guns, and by the action carrying 18, six of them very small. Cooke, her captain, called her 'but a meer Shell of a Ship' and wrote that if the galleon had fired at hulls instead of rigging 'he consequently must have shatter'd us almost to Pieces'. She was later condemned at Batavia as worm-eaten and sold for 575 Dutch dollars.

verdicts.reasoning:
TEST 1 — IS THE QUOTE REALLY THERE, WORD FOR WORD? Yes, and it survives a harder test than they applied. I downloaded their URL (https://archive.org/download/10467991bsb/10467991bsb_djvu.txt, 949,121 bytes) to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-aodhan/29937ecb-e066-4c86-9742-3a2d90c08f3c/scratchpad/rogers.txt and proved the retrieval off the title page itself: "A CRUISING / VOYAGE / ROUND THE / WORLD ... By Captain WOODES ROGERS, / Commander in Chief on this Expedition, with the Ships Duke and Dutchess of Bristol. LONDON ... M DCC. XII." The OCR of the target page is badly mangled (it reads "906'Tuns", "above 456", "r¥6 of the Men", and has dropped the opening clause of the sentence entirely), so this file alone could NOT have supported their quote — their decision to read the page image was the right call. I corroborated the wording from two physically independent printings instead: the 1718 second edition (IA bim_eighteenth-century_a-cruising-voyage-round-_rogers-woodes_1718, lines 24947-24955) and the 1928 Manwaring edition (IA cruisingvoyager00roge, lines 14367-14373, printed page 221). Both give the sentence exactly as they quote it, including "of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns, about 40 of which were mounted, with as many Patereroes, all Brass" and "above 450, besides Passengers". The p. 302 locator checks out: the 1712 file's next running head is "Engaging the bigger Manila Ship. 303". Their Cooke quote is also verbatim — voyagetosouthsea01cook.txt lines 17687-17689, on printed p. 351 (title page verified: "By Capt. Edward Cooke", London, printed for B. Lintot and R. Gosling): "The Enemy was a new Ship of above 900 Tuns, could mount at least 60 Guns, but had not now so many." Their grep claim holds too: "Bigonia" occurs exactly once in the 1712 text. So nothing in the quotation is misremembered.

TEST 2 — CONTEXT. Not out of context, but the context weakens it in a way the finding does not report. Both authors flag the figures as hearsay from the beaten enemy's own officers: Rogers writes "as we were inform'd"; Cooke "as some of the Prisoners told us". And the passage sits immediately before the signed committee minute that Rogers says was drawn up "to prevent false Reflections hereafter" — i.e. the surrounding pages are, by Rogers' own account, a defence of his decision to break off from a galleon worth a fortune. A big, heavily-gunned, pirate-manned enemy is exactly what that document needs to be true. This is the tell: the cheap reading is also the one that makes the failure respectable.

TEST 3 — A SOURCE THAT SAYS OTHERWISE. There is one, and it is the Spanish side. Cesáreo Fernández Duro, "Armada española desde la unión de los reinos de Castilla y de León", tomo VI (Madrid: Sucesores de Rivadeneyra, 1900), p. 95 — retrieval proved by the 1900 imprint, the tomo VI signature marks, the running heads "94 ARMADA ESPAÑOLA"/"EN LAS INDIAS. 95", and the index line "WOODES ROGERS. 93, 94, 95" — states of the same ship, in the same action: "la filipina, Nuestra Señora de Begoña, montaba 24 como la primera, de modo que duplicaban los enemigos su fuerza en artillería y la tenían mucho mayor en gente." Twenty-four guns mounted, with the English having DOUBLE her artillery and far more men. He adds that Fernando de Angulo "sólo disponía de 30 soldados", his crew being Indian sailors and passengers largely sick. That is the mirror image of Rogers' 40 guns, 450-600 men and "150 ... Europeans, several of whom had been formerly Pirates". Duro is describing the right ship and the right fight: he puts the Almiranta's capture on 1 January 1710 and the Capitana fight on 4-5 January (New Style = Rogers' 22 and 25-26 December, Old Style), has the Begoña reach Acapulco with eight dead, and footnotes a primary document (declarations of the Guayaquil hostages Jiménez and de la Puente, Dirección de Hidrografía, Miscelánea, tomo I, b. 2). A modern Spanish compilation citing AGI legajos (Filipinas 129 N.124, 332 L.11, Escribanía 419A) independently gives "20 cañones y 20 pedreros (podía montar 60 cañones)" — again roughly half Rogers, with the same guns-to-pedreros ratio, which looks like a real documentary disagreement rather than noise. (I treat that site as a finding aid only, per rule 5; Duro carries the weight.) Duro gives NO tonnage at all, so ~900 tons rests solely on the English testimony.

TEST 4 — DOES THE FINDING SUPPORT THE CLAIM? Partly. What is established is "Rogers and Cooke wrote that she was about 900 tons with about 40 of 60 possible guns mounted". That is not the same as "about 900 tons and 40+ guns, CONFIRMED". The finding's load-bearing word is "independently", and it is wrong: Rogers and Cooke were officers in the same three-ship squadron who both attribute the numbers to the same post-action interrogation of Spanish prisoners. One informant chain, two publishers. They already diverge where the chain was soft — Rogers "above 450" men, Cooke "600" — which shows the figures were estimates passed round a quarterdeck, not a register. Two further corrections to their framing: calling "Nuestra Señora de Begoña" a "later normalisation" overstates it, since Duro in 1900 names the ship so from Spanish documents — it is her actual Spanish name, and Rogers' "Bigonia" is the garbling, not the other way round; and Rogers' "the Admiral of Manila" conflicts with the Spanish designation, where the Begoña was the Capitana and the captured Encarnación the Almiranta.

VERDICT. The quotation work is clean and the tonnage figure is honestly sourced, so this is not a kill. But "both numbers CONFIRMED, independently" does not hold: the gun count is a contested attacker's estimate that the Spanish record halves, and the tonnage has no corroboration outside the one English informant chain. Since the gun count is said to drive a game mechanic, the difference between a 40-gun galleon and a 24-gun galleon with 30 soldiers aboard is material, and the table must say whose number it is. Downgrade to PARTLY, phrased as: English eyewitness accounts give about 900 tons and about 40 of 60 guns mounted; the Spanish side (Fernández Duro 1900, from documents) gives 24 mounted and a skeleton crew.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Cesáreo Fernández Duro, Armada española desde la unión de los reinos de Castilla y de León, tomo VI (Madrid, 1900), p. 95, on the same engagement off Cabo San Lucas: "la filipina, Nuestra Señora de Begoña, montaba 24 como la primera, de modo que duplicaban los enemigos su fuerza en artillería y la tenían mucho mayor en gente. El general español D. Fernando de Ángulo sólo disponía de 30 soldados, componiendo su equipaje marineros indios y pasajeros enfermos en gran parte" — 24 guns mounted (not 40), the English with twice her artillery, and a garrison of 30 soldiers rather than Rogers' 450-600 men including 150 European ex-pirates. Duro footnotes the declarations of the Guayaquil hostages (Dirección de Hidrografía, Miscelánea, tomo I, b. 2) and gives no tonnage for her at all. Separately, a Spanish compilation citing AGI Filipinas 129 N.124 / 332 L.11 and Escribanía 419A gives her as "20 cañones y 20 pedreros (podía montar 60 cañones)", again about half the Rogers figure. Rogers' and Cooke's numbers are also not independent of each other: both are explicitly hearsay from the same post-action prisoner interrogation ("as we were inform'd"; "as some of the Prisoners told us"), and they already disagree on the crew (above 450 vs 600).

Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (1712), vol. I — retrieval proved by title page ("A VOYAGE TO THE South Sea, AND Round the World. Perform'd in the Years 1708, 1709, 1710, and 1711") — is the finding's own second witness and contradicts "DAMAGE TO THE GALLEON: almost none".

(a) p. 348, Monday 26 Dec: "We could perceive many Shot plac'd in her betwixt Wind and Water, which oblig'd them to pump often." Hull penetration at the waterline, bad enough to keep her pumps going. Rogers never mentions it.

(b) p. 352: "We had set the Ship several Times a-fire on the Quarters and Bows; but they put it out, and did the same by us. We shot their Mizen Yard, most of their Rigging, and two Suits of Sails almost to Pieces; but they had the good Fortune that all their Masts stood"; p. 353: "we also shot their Ensign half down, and thought they had struck, but they some Time after hoisted it again."

So the galleon was set on fire more than once, lost two suits of sails, and her ensign was shot down far enough that the English believed she had surrendered. Cooke's considered verdict is "their Ship so strong, that I believe our Shot in some Places did but little Damage" (p. 350) — "in some places," not "almost none."

(c) Rogers himself hedges in the very sentence the finding quotes: "which was all the Damage we could SEE we did 'em" (p. 302). That is a statement about English visibility from alongside a close-quartered ship with "not a Man to be seen above-board," not a statement about the galleon's actual condition. Converting it to a flat "almost none" is exactly the cheap reading the game wants.

(d) A Spanish-side tradition (todoavante.es, "Galeón de Manila 1709-1710", citing AGI legajos plus Fernández Duro, Fish and Marley; and the Wikipedia "1709 in piracy" line) puts the Begoña's losses at roughly 8 dead and 28 wounded, against Rogers's "two Men out of her Tops." I could NOT establish that figure from any authority — the todoavante page gives casualties only for the Encarnación, and I found no reachable AGI relación or scholarly citation for it. Registering it as an unresolved counter-signal, not as evidence. But it means the "almost none" figure is the one number in the finding that rests on a single interested witness's own hedged eyeball estimate and has a live contrary tradition against it.

Lesser defects: the finding says "Cooke, on board, says 25 killed and wounded" of the Dutchess — Cooke commanded the MARQUIS (Rogers p. 216: "Capt. Courtney in the Dutchess, and Capt. Cooke in the Marquiss"); he visited the Dutchess at 8 p.m. on the 26th and recorded 7 killed and wounded at that point (p. 348), reaching 25 after the 27th (p. 349). Cooke also records that the council vote was carried "by the Majority of Voices" against Courtney and himself, who "were for carrying of him by Boarding, and design'd to make another Attempt" (p. 351) — the squadron did not unanimously judge her unbeatable. And the cited Cooke range pp. 347-351 is short: the minute is on p. 352 and the fire/ensign detail on pp. 352-353.
verdicts.reasoning:
TEST 1 — IS THE QUOTE REALLY THERE, WORD FOR WORD? Yes, exactly. I downloaded their URL (https://archive.org/download/10467991bsb/10467991bsb_djvu.txt), proved retrieval by the title page ("A CRUISING VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD... By Captain WOODES ROGERS") and found the passage at p. 302. The 1712 OCR is line-broken, so I cross-checked two further independent copies: the 1718 London edition (bim_eighteenth-century_...rogers-woodes_1718, retrieval proved by its own title page) and the 1928 Manwaring reprint (cruisingvoyagero00roge_0). All three carry the sentence identically: "She kept a Spanish Flag at her Main-top-mast Head all the time she fought us; we shatter'd her Sails and Rigging very much, shot her Mizon-yard, kill'd two Men out of her Tops, which was all the Damage we could see we did 'em; tho' we could not place less than 500 Shot (6 Pounders) in her Hull. These large Ships are built at Manila with excellent Timber, that will not splinter; they have very thick Sides, much stronger than we build in Europe." Not a word misremembered. Every other quoted fragment also checks verbatim: "We engag'd first and last about six or seven Hours" · "but eleven Men wounded, 3 of whom were scorch'd with Gun-powder" · "part of my Heel-bone being struck out" · "The Dutchess had about 20 Men killed and wounded" · "The Marquiss had none kill'd or wounded, but 2 scorch'd with Powder" · "which rent it miserably" · the fire-ball out of her top blowing up "a Chest of Arms and Cartouch Boxes". The committee minute is verbatim and dated "December 27. 1709", with all fifteen signatories as listed, Selkirk included; Cooke prints the same fifteen names independently. Page range 297-303 is correct.

TEST 2 — OUT OF CONTEXT? Partly, and this is the one real flaw. The 500-shot/no-splinter sentence is genuinely about the galleon's invulnerability, so it is not misapplied. But the finding promotes Rogers's explicitly sight-limited phrase into a flat statement of fact ("DAMAGE TO THE GALLEON: almost none"). Rogers wrote "all the Damage we could SEE." Read one level down and the hedge is doing work: the English were alongside a ship whose crew was entirely below the netting, and they could not assess her.

TEST 3 — A SOURCE THAT SAYS OTHERWISE? Yes, and it is the finding's own corroborating witness. Cooke, in the Marquis, reports waterline shot holes forcing the galleon to pump, the galleon set on fire several times, two suits of sails shot to pieces, and her ensign shot half down so that the English thought she had struck. That is materially more damage than "almost none." A Spanish-side tradition of 8 dead / 28 wounded exists but I could not run it to an authority, so I register it as UNVERIFIED counter-signal only, not as proof.

TEST 4 — DOES IT SUPPORT THE CLAIM? For the core of the claim, yes, and robustly. Three English ships; the sequence is independently double-attested. Cooke dates by weekday as well as date, and his weekdays are calendrically correct for the Julian calendar (25 Dec 1709 OS = Sunday; I checked by converting to 5 Jan 1710 NS, a Sunday), which is a strong retrieval and dating check. Cooke p. 347: night of 25/26, "At Twelve at Night, the Dutchess got up along the Side of the Manila Ship, and began to engage her," the Marquis two leagues off and unable to close — Dutchess alone. Monday 26th: Marquis closes at 2 p.m., Dutchess rakes her, Duke still three leagues to leeward — two ships. Tuesday 27th: "Before Day the Duke join'd us; and being all three provided... made Sail to engage again... The Enemy fir'd at us all three at once" — all three, and she beat them off. Rogers's council minute of 27 Dec, the withdrawal, and the English damage tally are all exactly as reported. So: yes, she fought off the whole squadron; three ships; the Duke's own share six or seven hours; the English broke off by written resolution.

CONCLUSION. I am not killing this — the central historical content is as well attested as 1712 material gets, verbatim in three editions of Rogers and independently in Cooke. But the CONFIRMED verdict as written does not hold in full, because one element that will directly drive level design — the galleon as effectively undamageable — is an over-read of a hedged sentence and is contradicted by the second witness the finding itself cites. Downgrade to PARTLY. For publication the galleon-damage line should read: Rogers reported only the damage the English could see (sails and rigging shattered, mizen yard shot away, two men killed in her tops) while estimating no fewer than 500 six-pound shot in her hull; Cooke adds hull penetration at the waterline that kept her pumping, repeated fires, and her ensign shot down and rehoisted. Her masts all stood and she reached Acapulco. Spanish casualty figures I could not establish.

verdicts.counter_evidence:
(1) QUOTE IS NOT VERBATIM. Their quotation opens "we do now finally determine to cruize off Cape St. Lucas". Every edition I checked reads "and do now finally determine". 1928 Manwaring reprint (the item at THEIR url, cruisingvoyager00roge, line 13287): "from Prisoners since our being in the South Seas, and do now finally | determine to cruize off Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Cape of | California". A second, independent 1928 scan (cruisingvoyagero00roge_0, line 13067) reads the same. The 1718 edition (bim_eighteenth-century_a-cruising-voyage-round-_rogers-woodes_1718, line 22587) reads "and do nom [now] finally determine to crix [cruize] off Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Cape of California". The rest of their long quote IS word-for-word correct, including "every Man to use his utmost Conduct and Bravery to conquer", but the subject has been silently substituted inside quotation marks.

(2) WRONG EDITION ATTACHED TO THE PAGE NUMBERS. They cite "A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), p. 201 ... pp. 204, 209, 213, 294" but their url is the 1928 G. E. Manwaring reprint (IA metadata year 1928; its own preface: "This edition of Woodes Rogers's 'Cruising Voyage round the World,' is printed from the original and scarce edition of 1712"). Pages 201, 204, 209 and 213 are Manwaring's running heads, not 1712's. In the genuine 1712 first edition (IA 10467991bsb, title page verified: "A CRUISING VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD: First to the South-Seas... Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1712") the same passages sit at: council resolution pp. 274-275 (running head "Description of Tres Marias 275"); Nov 1-2 "Southermost Head-land" pp. 278-279 ("Cruizing off Cape St. Lucas 279"); Nov 22 watering place p. 286; the Cape bearing p. 292; Port Segura anchorage p. 294. The 1718 edition shares the 1712 pagination (same "Description of Tres Marias. 275" head).

(3) RETRIEVAL NOTE MISSTATES ONE LOCATOR. They say the 22 December bearing and the Port Segura anchorage "were confirmed on the page image of p. 294". Only the anchorage is on p. 294; "time it was Noon: The Cape then bore N.N.E. of us, distant about 5 Leagues" is on 1712 p. 292 (= 1928 p. 213). 1928 p. 294 is Batavia, October 1711 ("we sold her to Capt. John Opey, Commander of the Oley Frigate"), nowhere near California. They also describe the 1928 reprint as an "independent" check on the 1712 OCR, but the 1928 reprint is the file their url serves.

(4) UNREPORTED COUNTER-EVIDENCE IN THEIR OWN SECOND WITNESS. Cooke, vol. I pp. 335-336, explicitly disputes which headland the cape is: "The Entrance is about a League to the Eastward of a round, sandy, bald Headland, which some take to be Cape St. Lucas, because it is the Southermost Land; but I believe that to be Cape St. Lucas which bears E. by S. from this bald Head, distant about three Leagues, and is the Eastermost Point." So Cooke's 27 December bearing of "two Leagues" is measured to a point he himself puts ~3 leagues from the southern tip. Cooke also gives Puerto Seguro as "inhabited by about 200 Indians" with "The Brooks have good Water", against Rogers's boat report of "near 500 Indians" and "a fresh Water River" — the identification of the November watering bay with Puerto Seguro rests on Rogers's own hedge ("which we suppose was the same that Sir Thomas Cavendish recruited at"), not on agreement between the two eyewitnesses. None of this is wrong in the finding, but it is omitted, and the finding presents harbour and watering place as one established thing.

WHAT DOES HOLD, verified by me directly: the resolution text and station (1712 pp. 274-75); "Nov. 2. The Westermost Land we set yesterday Noon, we make to be Cape St. Lucas, the Southermost Head-land of California" and "We had an Observation Lat. 22. 55" (1712 pp. 278-79); the 22 Nov watering report verbatim incl. "Anno 1588" (1712 p. 286); "3 Barrels of Water, and 2 very large Fish from the Indians" on 26 Nov; "The Cape then bore N.N.E. of us, distant about 5 Leagues" (1712 p. 292); "we made the best of our Way into the Harbour call'd by Sir Tho. Cavendish Port Segura" and "got to an Anchor in Port Segura in 25 Fathom Water" (1712 pp. 292, 294); Rogers's protest of 9 Jan. calling the prize "safe at Anchor in a Bay near Cape St. Luke, on California". Cooke vol. I p. 349 is correct to the page: "Tuesday, December 27. in the Morning, had a small Easterly Breeze, Cape St. Luke bearing N. E. by E. distant about two Leagues" (running heads at p. 346 and p. 350 bracket it). Cooke vol. II opens: "A JOURNAL [and T]ABLE of our Voyage, in the Ship Marquis, from Cape St. Lucas in the Island of California, in the Latitude of 23 Deg. 10 Min. North; to the Island Guam... Perform'd in the Year 1709" — exactly as they describe.
verdicts.reasoning:
The historical substance survives all four tests and I confirmed it independently against five texts: the 1712 first edition (IA 10467991bsb), the 1718 edition, two separate 1928 Manwaring scans, and Cooke vols I and II. Both fights were within 2-5 leagues of Cabo San Lucas, the station was fixed by name on 24 October 1709, and the anchorage/watering material is accurately reported. Cooke's p. 349 bearing and the 23 deg 10 min figure in the vol. II run table are correct to the page and the header, which is a strong retrieval check and not something they could have bluffed.

But the CONFIRMED verdict as written does not hold up, on two counts that matter for a published sources table. First, the quotation is not word-for-word: "we do now finally determine" where every edition reads "and do now finally determine". One word, no change of meaning, but it is a silent substitution inside quotation marks, and the refutation brief treats that as disqualifying. Second, the citation apparatus is edition-confused: the work is cited as the 1712 London edition while the url serves the 1928 Manwaring reprint, and four of the five page numbers (201, 204, 209, 213) are Manwaring's pagination, not 1712's. The 1712 locations are pp. 274-75, 278-79, 286, 292, 294. Their own retrieval note compounds this by placing the Cape bearing on p. 294 when it is p. 292, and by calling the 1928 reprint an independent check when it is the file their url returns. A referee checking p. 201 of a 1712 Rogers finds nothing about California.

Third, a softer point: Cooke, whom they cite as the corroborating witness, openly disagrees about which headland is Cape St. Lucas and gives 200 Indians and "Brooks" against Rogers's 500 and a "fresh Water River". That does not break the geography at game resolution, but it means the harbour-equals-watering-place identification rests on Rogers's own supposition and should be stated as such.

Verdict: PARTLY. Fix the quoted word, re-cite to one edition consistently with that edition's pages, and the finding is sound.

Retrieval verified independently. Their URL (archive.org/download/cruisingvoyager00roge) is NOT the 1712 first edition they cite: it is the 1928 Cassell edition edited by G. E. Manwaring ("CASSELL AND COMPANY LT", "G.E.MANWARING, F.R.Hist.S.", and the editor's own note that the text "is printed from the original and scarce edition of 1712"). I separately downloaded the actual 1712 first edition (IA id 10467991bsb, long-s OCR: "Cavendifh", "Cruifing Voyage") and checked every passage in both.

TEST 1 — the designated quote. EXACT. 1928 text: "We were now something dubious of seeing the Manila Ship, / because it's near a Month after the time they generally fall in / with this Coast." 1712 text, p. 288: "e were. now. fomething dubious of-feeing the Manila Ship, becaufe it's neara Month after the time they generally fall in with this Coatt." Word for word.

Also exact: the 24 Oct 1709 committee minute ("examin'd the Opinion of Capt. Dampier, appointed Pilot by the Owners of the Ships Duke and Dutchess in Bristol, and have been well informed from all the Intelligences we have frequently had from Prisoners since our being in the South Seas"); the 7 Nov entry ("Sir Thomas Cavendish, in Queen Elizabeth's Time, took the Manila Ship in this Place on the 4th of November"); the whole bread arithmetic (64 / 8 spent / 56 / 14 more / "70 Days Bread to come" / 9 days to fit + 50 days passage = 59 / "11 Days Bread will be left when we come to Guam"); and "At signing this in the Committee we all looked very melancholy and dispirited".

TEST 2 — context. Sound. The chronology holds: 2 Nov "We agreed on Signals and Stations"; 3 Nov stations concluded; 14 Dec "to cruize but 8 Days longer... because our Provisions grow short"; 20 Dec resolve; 21 Dec "about 9 a Clock the Man at Mast-head cry'd out he saw a Sail" while standing in for Port Segura. 2 Nov to 21 Dec is 49 days, exactly seven weeks. Old Style confirmed from the text itself: the Juan Fernandez minute is dated "the 13th of February, 1708" for what is our Feb 1709.

TEST 3 — contrary source. I checked the only independent published journal of the same cruise, Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (London, 1712), vol. 1 (IA voyagetosouthsea01cook; title page verified). Cooke CORROBORATES rather than contradicts: "Tuesday, November 2. all the Captains met aboard the Marquis, and agreed about our cruizing Stations" (p. 332), and on 13 December "We were much concern'd to have no Tidings of the Manila Ship, the usual Time of her coming being elaps'd" plus a provision count of "only three Months Meat, at short Allowance, and but two Months Bread for the three Ships" (pp. 334-35). That is a second, independent witness to both the start date and to "season, not date", and to victuals as the operative constraint.

TEST 4 — WHY I STILL DOWNGRADE. Two defects, one of them a real quotation error:

(a) MISATTRIBUTED QUOTATION. The finding states: "On that arithmetic the council resolved 'to forbear any further Attempts' and make for Guam." That phrase is not in the 20 December minute, in either edition. The 20 December resolve reads: "...finding it too little to continue our Cruize longer here for the Manila Ship, do therefore now agree to get a Harbour, and there to recruit with the utmost dispatch, and sail for the Island of Guam, or any other Place where we can revictual." The words "to forbear any further Attempts" come from a DIFFERENT minute a week later: "At a Committee held on board the Duke, after we had engag'd the bigger Manila Ship, December 27. 1709... do think it for the Interest of the whole to forbear any further Attempts upon her, having no Probability of taking her, but to do our endeavours to secure the Prize we have already took." Different date, different object (the Begoña, not the ambush), and opposite import: it resolves to stay and secure the prize, not to make for Guam. The likely route of the error is Manwaring's 1928 introduction, which uses the phrase in quotation marks about the Begoña fight. A historian publishing this would be quoting a 27 December decision as if it were the 20 December one.

(b) WRONG-EDITION PAGINATION. The source line reads "(London, 1712), pp. 200-201, 205, 210-213". Those are the 1928 Cassell pages (running heads 200-01 council minute, 205 Cavendish, 211-13 bread minute and sighting). In the actual 1712 first edition the same passages sit at approximately pp. 274-75 (24 Oct minute), 283 (Cavendish), 288 (9 Dec doubt), 289-91 (bread minute and resolve), 291-92 (21 Dec sighting). Their own retrieval note half-admits this ("page 292 of the 1712 text"), which contradicts the "pp. 210-213" in the citation. A reader sent to the 1712 edition at p. 213 lands in the Pacific crossing, nowhere near the ambush.

CONCLUSION: the substantive answer to the claim — about seven weeks, 2 Nov to 21 Dec 1709 OS, season rather than date, Dampier plus prisoner intelligence, the Cavendish 4 November precedent, the 9 December judgement that the window had closed, and victuals (not patience) ending the cruise one morning before the galleon appeared — is verbatim-verified in the 1712 original and independently corroborated by Cooke. But the verdict as written contains a quotation attached to the wrong committee minute and a citation whose page numbers belong to a different edition than the one named. PARTLY, not CONFIRMED. Fix: strike the "forbear any further Attempts" phrase (or re-date it to 27 December and note it concerns the Begoña), quote the 20 December resolve's actual words, and either cite the 1928 Manwaring edition by its own pagination or give true 1712 pages (~274-75, 283, 288-92).
verdicts.counter_evidence: 1712 first edition, p. 291, the 20 December resolve in full: "WE the Officers present in a Committee on board the Dutchess, having farther considered our short Store of Bread and Bread-kind, and finding it too little to continue our Cruize longer here for the Manila Ship, do therefore now agree to get a Harbour, and there to recruit with the utmost dispatch, and sail for the Island of Guam, or any other Place where we can revictual." No "forbear" anywhere in it. The quoted phrase belongs to a later minute: "At a Committee held on board the Duke, after we had engag'd the bigger Manila Ship, December 27. 1709. WE having consider'd the Condition of all our 3 Ships, and that our Masts are much damnified in engaging the Manila Ship, do think it for the Interest of the whole to forbear any further Attempts upon her, having no Probability of taking her, but to do our endeavours to secure the Prize we have already took." Independent corroboration of the substance from the other eyewitness, Edward Cooke, A Voyage to the South Sea (London, 1712), 1:332, 334-35: "Tuesday, November 2. all the Captains met aboard the Marquis, and agreed about our cruizing Stations"; and on 13 December, "We were much concern'd to have no Tidings of the Manila Ship, the usual Time of her coming being elaps'd," with "but two Months Bread for the three Ships."

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to break this four ways and could not. It survives.

TEST 1 — IS THE QUOTE REALLY THERE, WORD FOR WORD?
Yes, and I proved it the hard way rather than trusting their report. I downloaded the BSB copy's OCR (https://archive.org/download/10467991bsb/10467991bsb_djvu.txt, 949,121 bytes) and it does render the line as "Begun in 1708, and finifh'd in 1712" — so on OCR alone their quote would be a misquote and I would have refuted them. I therefore pulled the title leaf myself as an image (BookReader API, id=10467991bsb, server ia800101, page=n6, scale=2) and READ it. The type unambiguously reads:
  "Begun in 1708, and finiſh'd in 1711."
The OCR trap they flagged is real and I reproduced it independently. Their quote is verbatim; the machine text is wrong.

RETRIEVAL VERIFIED (not just a 200): the leaf I read shows the full title "A CRUISING VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD", "First to the SOUTH-SEAS, thence to the EAST-INDIES, and homewards by the Cape of GOOD HOPE", the Selkirk advertisement ("Alexander Selkirk's living alone four Years and four Months in an Island"), "By Captain WOODES ROGERS, Commander in Chief on this Expedition, with the Ships Duke and Dutchess of Bristol", and the imprint "LONDON, Printed for A. Bell at the Cross-Keys and Bible in Cornhil, and B. Lintot ... M DCC. XII." That is the 1712 first edition, not the 1718 or 1726 reissue. (Incidental: the OCR also drops "Spanish" from "from the best Spanish Manuscript Draughts" — the leaf has it. Same OCR unreliability.)

TEST 2 — CONTEXT / IS A TITLE PAGE DOING WORK IT WASN'T ASKED TO DO?
A title page could in principle be a publisher's blurb rather than the voyage's own record, so I went one level down and found FOUR independent attestations of the same terminal dates:
(a) 1712 first edition, internal half-title to the journal (as reprinted verbatim in the 1928 Cassell/Manwaring edition, "printed from the original and scarce edition of 1712"): "Begun August 1. 1708. and Finished October 14. 1711."
(b) 1712 first edition, running marginal years printed in the text itself: the sequence runs 1708 → 1709 → 1710 → 1711, and "1711." is printed as the marginal/running year on p. 426, immediately before the 1 October and 14 October entries. The year is on the page, not inferred.
(c) 1718 edition (IA id bim_eighteenth-century_a-cruising-voyage-round-_rogers-woodes_1718), half-title: "Begun Auguſt [1]708. and Finiſh'd October 14. 1711." Its title-page OCR garbles the start year ("Begun in 47565") but independently returns "1711" for the end. A second press, same dates.
(d) 1928 Manwaring introduction, p. xxv: the ships "arrived in the Downs" on 1 October and "on the 14th came to an anchor at Erith", finishing a voyage "of over three years" — arithmetic consistent with Aug 1708 → Oct 1711.

TEST 3 — DOES ANYTHING SAY OTHERWISE?
Nothing I found. I checked the 1712, 1718 and 1928 texts and Manwaring's editorial apparatus; all agree. There is no Spanish-side or later-scholarship correction at issue here, because this is not a contested narrative claim (like a treasure figure or a casualty count) — it is the voyage's own dated log, printed with marginal years, corroborated across three separate printings. The terminal quotes check out verbatim too: "On the 1ſt of October, about 11 of the Clock we came to an Anchor in the Downs, where ſeveral of our Owners came aboard" appears in both the 1712 and 1718 texts; and "Octob. 14. This Day at 11 of the Clock, we and our Consort and Prize got up to Eri[th], where we came to an Anchor, which ends our long and fatiguing Voyage" closes the journal, followed by "FINIS."

TEST 4 — DOES IT SUPPORT THE CLAIM OR ONLY SOMETHING ADJACENT?
It supports the claim directly, not adjacently. The game asserts Rogers' dates are "1708-11"; the source's own summary of itself, at both ends of the journal, is 1 August 1708 to 14 October 1711.

TWO DEFECTS WORTH RECORDING, NEITHER FATAL:
1. CITATION MISMATCH (should be fixed before publication). Their source line reads "(London, 1712) ... journal entries of 2 August 1708 (p. 1) and 1 and 14 October 1711 (pp. 313–314)". Those page numbers are the 1928 Cassell/Manwaring pagination, not the 1712 first edition's. In the 1712 edition the October entries fall on pp. 426–428 (I read the printed page number 426 off the scan). The 1928 index confirms its own "Erith, 314" and "Kingroad, Bristol, 2". So the page locators are attributed to the wrong edition.
2. SILENT MODERNIZATION INSIDE QUOTATION MARKS. Their departure quote gives "on board the Duke frigate". The 1712 first edition reads "on board the Duke-Frigot, whereof Capt. Woodes Rogers was Commander". "Duke frigate" is the 1928 Manwaring spelling, which they did also consult — so it is a real quotation, just from the other edition than the one cited. Same root cause as defect 1.

Neither defect touches the dates. The claim stands: refuted = false, no downgrade. The headline quote "Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1711." is genuine, I read it off the type myself, and the game's "1708-11" is exactly what the source says.
verdicts.counter_evidence: No counter-evidence to the claim itself. The only adverse finding is a citation defect in their write-up: the page locators "pp. 313–314" and "p. 1", and the quotation "on board the Duke frigate", come from the 1928 Cassell/Manwaring reprint, while the source line attributes them to the 1712 first edition. In the 1712 edition the October entries are on pp. 426–428 (printed page number read off the scan) and the text reads "on board the Duke-Frigot". Separately, a trap for anyone re-checking this: the OCR of the 1712 BSB scan renders the title line as "Begun in 1708, and finifh'd in 1712" — I confirmed the machine text is wrong and the type reads 1711, so the OCR must not be used as the authority here.

claims.claim: The action took place off the Philippines; the game's plan treats it as open blue water with no cape.
claims.finding: Date and water are right; the "no cape" framing is wrong. Both eyewitness accounts put the action off Cape Espiritu Santo, the NE point of Samar (Walter spells the island "Samal"), which was Anson's deliberate landfall-interception station because it "is the first land they always make at the Philippine Islands." Walter: the Centurion "usually kept from ten to fifteen leagues distant" from the cape and was repeatedly SEEN FROM THE LAND, which put Manila on the alert. Pascoe Thomas, who was aboard, logs the sighting at sunrise on 20 June 1743 O.S. with the cape bearing SW½W about seven leagues off, the sail six leagues to windward in the SE. Walter adds that Anson deliberately fought from LEEWARD specifically to deny the galleon a run to the land: the Centurion came abreast "keeping to the leeward of them with a view of preventing their putting before the wind, and gaining the port of Jalapay, from which they were about seven leagues distant" (Jalapay = Palapag, on the north coast of Samar). So this is coastal water under a headland, with a lee shore and a friendly port as a live tactical factor for the Spaniard, not featureless blue water. Date: 20 June 1743 Old Style = 1 July 1743 New Style.
claims.quote: "the Centurion came abreast of the enemy within pistol-shot, keeping to the leeward of them with a view of preventing their putting before the wind, and gaining the port of Jalapay, from which they were about seven leagues distant." (Walter, p. 379) / "she bore from us about South-East ... and about six Leagues distant from us; at the same Time Cape Spiritu Sen[to] bore from S. W. half West distant about seven Leagues." (Pascoe Thomas, p. 280)
claims.source: Richard Walter, A Voyage Round the World in the Years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV, by George Anson, Bk III ch. viii, pp. 375-379 (1748 1st edn and the later octavo collated); Pascoe Thomas, A True and Impartial Journal of a Voyage to the South-Seas (London, 1745), pp. 280-281
claims.retrieval_note: Two independent editions of Walter downloaded and grepped. The 1749 octavo file opens with the title page "A VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD, In the Years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV. BY GEORGE ANSON, Esq; Now LORD ANSON". The 1748 first-edition file (bim_eighteenth-century_..._1748) opens "VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD In the Years MDCCXL, I, II. UI. IV. BY GEORGE ANSON, Eq; Commander in Chief of a Squadron of His Majesty's Ships, sent upon an Expedition to the South-Seas" and carries the identical action text (I diffed the Covadonga passage word for word across the two). Thomas's file proves itself at line 73-74: "By PASCOE THOMAS, Teacher of the Mathematicks on board the CENTURION".
claims.game_impact: Keep the Philippines; drop "open blue water, no cape." The scenario's real geometry is: a cruising station held off a named cape for a month, the enemy sighted to windward at six leagues, and a leeward fighting position chosen to cut him off from a port seven leagues away. A lee shore + a windward enemy + a port to deny is a far better encounter than an empty-ocean duel.

claims.claim: The engagement lasted an hour and a half, and was "the only pure artillery fight."
claims.finding: Duration: close, slightly long. The eyewitness log gives one hour twenty minutes; Walter's narrative implies about the same (half an hour on the bow, then "near an hour longer" alongside). "Pure artillery fight" is REFUTED by both accounts. Anson put about thirty picked marksmen in the tops before the action, and both witnesses make musketry the decisive arm: the topmen cleared the galleon's tops at the first volley, then shot down nearly every officer on her quarterdeck and disabled the Spanish general with a musket ball in the breast, which is what broke the Spanish will to fight. Thomas records that after the boarding party took her he found fifty-odd swords and nearly as many muskets flung down on the poop, "scarce one of the Muskets discharged." Grape, not round shot, is what Walter credits with sweeping the decks. Neither ship boarded, but both rigged spritsail yards fore and aft as a boarding threat, and Thomas says that bluff plus the sight of the Centurion's lower-deck ports hauled up is what demoralised the Spaniards before a shot was exchanged.
claims.quote: "Thus the action proceeded for at least half an hour; but then the Centurion lost the superiority arising from her original situation, and was close along-side the galeon, and the enemy continued to fire briskly for near an hour longer" (Walter, p. 379). / "The Fight continued one Hour and twenty Minutes, an Hour of which the Spaniards behaved very well, and fought bravely." (Thomas, p. 283). / "the galeon's decks lay open to her topmen, who, having at their first volley driven the Spaniards from their tops, made prodigious havock with their small arms, killing or wounding every officer but one that appeared on the quarter-deck, and wounding in particular the General of the galeon himself." (Walter, p. 379)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 377-380; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, pp. 281-286
claims.retrieval_note: Thomas's figure found by reading his dated journal entry under the heading "JUNE, 1743. The 20th" through to the surrender, confirming the number is his own log and not a later summary. Walter's two-part duration confirmed identical in the 1748 first-edition OCR (p. 379) and the later octavo.
claims.game_impact: Change the duration to "about an hour and twenty minutes" (or keep ~1.5h as a rounding, but do not cite it as precise). DELETE "the only pure artillery fight." This fight was decided by marksmen in the tops plus grape at pistol-shot. If the game needs a label, it is the only fight won by sustained aimed fire rather than by boarding.

claims.claim: The Covadonga carried about 30 guns and fought hard.
claims.finding: Both numbers in the game are too low, and "fought hard" needs qualifying. Walter: 36 guns mounted for action PLUS 28 pedreros (four-pound swivels) in gunwale, quarters and tops, and 550 men. Thomas, who boarded her and inventoried her arms, says she had ports for sixty-four guns but mounted only about forty, seventeen of them brass twelve-pounders and no two alike, plus twenty-eight brass patereroes on swivels, each loaded with seventy musket balls or equivalent in old iron, nails, flints and quartered slugs. Thomas puts her complement at 644 effective men, passengers included, not 550. Crucially, she could not fight her lower tier at all: she was so lumbered that the lower-deck guns could not be cleared. Walter's own chapter on the Manila trade explains the system: outbound from Manila the galleon stows her lower tier in the hold, and homeward from Acapulco her lower tier "is (or ought to be) always mounted before she leaves the port" - Montero's had not been. As to fighting hard, Thomas (favourable to the enemy on this point) says the Spaniards behaved very well for an hour; but he also records that her soldiers were men entered at Acapulco, "many of which were poor heartless Mortals, and others of them Felons condemned for their Crimes to their Galleys at Manila," who abandoned their quarters and tumbled down the hatchways in heaps. Tonnage: NOT given by either source as a burthen figure - see A-6 for the measured dimensions, which are the real surprise.
claims.quote: "The galeon was much larger than the Centurion, and had five hundred and fifty men, and thirty-six guns mounted for action, besides twenty-eight pedreroes in her gunwale, quarters and tops, each of which carried a four pound ball." (Walter, p. 381). / "She had Ports for mounting sixty-four Guns, but had, I think, to the best of my Remembrance, but forty, and was so lumbered that she could not fight all of them; seventeen of those were Brass, I think all twelve Pounders, but no two of them alike" (Thomas, p. 288). / "her lower tire is (or ought to be) always mounted before she leaves the port" (Walter, p. 246)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 246-247, 381; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, pp. 288-291
claims.retrieval_note: Walter's gun/crew sentence verified character-for-character in the 1748 first-edition file as well as the later octavo, so it is not a later editorial inflation. Thomas's count is independent and from a man who went aboard the prize in the boarding party and personally secured the arms on the poop.
claims.game_impact: Change "about 30 guns" to "36-40 guns mounted (ports for 64), plus 28 four-pound swivels." The real mechanic hiding here is that she could not open her lower tier because she was stuffed with cargo - a rich prize is a weak prize. Make the galleon's broadside a function of how much treasure she is carrying.

claims.claim: Casualties on both sides and the treasure taken.
claims.finding: Walter: the galleon had 67 killed in the action and 84 wounded; the Centurion had only two killed, and a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded, of whom all but one recovered. Thomas's independent arithmetic (644 aboard before the fight, minus 580 accounted for as released, escaped or still detained) gives 64 "slain outright in the Fight, or had since died of their Wounds" - a close match. Thomas puts the galleon's wounded at about seventy, of whom above sixty recovered under the surgeon of the Tryal. Treasure: Walter's first estimate on the day was "near a million and a half of dollars"; the ascertained cargo, once counted, was 1,313,843 pieces of eight and 35,682 oz of virgin silver, besides some cochineal. Thomas logs the physical transfer: 112 bags and 6 chests of dollars sent across on the afternoon of the action alone, each bag reckoned at 1,000 dollars and each chest at 3,000-4,000. Walter's grand total for the whole voyage is "not much short of 400,000l." of treasure taken by the Centurion, plus an estimated 600,000l. of enemy shipping and merchandise burnt or destroyed.
claims.quote: "She had sixty-seven killed in the action, and eighty-four wounded, whilst the Centurion had only two killed, and a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded, all of whom but one recovered: Of so little consequence are the most destructive arms, in untutored and unpractised hands." (Walter, p. 381). / "it was found that she had on board 1,313,843 pieces of eight, and 35,682 oz. of virgin silver, besides some cochineal, and a few other commodities" (Walter, p. 384)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 381, 384; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, pp. 286-287, 300
claims.retrieval_note: Both the casualty sentence and the treasure figures were located in the 1749 octavo and then re-found verbatim in the 1748 first-edition OCR, which rules out an OCR artefact in the digits (the 1748 scan renders "sixty-seyen" and "eighty-four" legibly in the same sentence).
claims.game_impact: Use these exact figures: 67 dead / 84 wounded against 2 dead / 17 wounded, and 1,313,843 pieces of eight + 35,682 oz of virgin silver. The casualty ratio of roughly 35:1 is the single most striking number in the cluster and should drive the reward, not just flavour text.

claims.claim: Centurion attrition: the crew shrinks on a timer and reloads get slower the longer you dither. Was the crew at the Covadonga so thin that he worked the guns in an unusual way?
claims.finding: YES, and the specific detail exists and is far better than a timer. Numbers first. Thomas's appendix: 510 men of all sorts left England in the Centurion on 19 Sept 1740; dead to 30 Sept 1741 were 172 seamen, 46 invalids, 69 marines, 2 bombardiers and 3 agents' servants, total 292, leaving 218 alive. Walter independently gives 292 buried out of the Centurion and 214 remaining. The dying was concentrated in about four months: scurvy appeared soon after passing Strait Le Maire, 43 died aboard the Centurion in April 1741, "near double that number" in May, and by the time they reached Juan Fernandez in mid-June, after losing above two hundred men, they "could not at last muster more than six fore-mast men in a watch capable of duty." 167 sick were carried ashore in hammocks, twelve or fourteen dying in the boats on first exposure to the air. Across the three ships that got into the Pacific, 961 men sailed from England and 626 were dead by September 1741, leaving 335. By the time of the Covadonga action Anson had 227 hands aboard, near thirty of them boys, against a complement of 400. THE DETAIL: because he had not enough hands to quarter a full crew to every gun, he put only two men to each gun on the lower tier, whose sole job was to LOAD, and formed the rest into roving gangs of ten or twelve who moved continuously about the decks running out and firing whichever guns were loaded. The side effect was that instead of broadsides with intervals he kept up a continuous fire gun by gun - which specifically defeated the Spanish practice of lying down on the decks while a broadside was given and then rising to work their own guns. He also pulled thirty of his best marksmen out of the gun crews entirely and put them in the tops. The captured Spaniards, once aboard and seeing how slenderly she was manned, "could not help expressing themselves with great indignation to be thus beaten by a handful of boys."
claims.quote: "As he had not hands enough remaining to quarter a sufficient number to each great gun, in the customary manner; he therefore, on his lower tire, fixed only two men to each gun, who were to be solely employed in loading it, whilst the rest of his people were divided into different gangs of ten or twelve men each, who were continually moving about the decks, to run out and fire such guns as were loaded. By this management he was enabled to make use of all his guns; and instead of whole broad-sides with intervals between them, he kept up a constant fire without intermission" (Walter, p. 378). / "he himself had but two hundred and twenty-seven hands on board, of which near thirty were boys" (Walter, p. 371). / "we buried no less than forty-three men on board the Centurion, in the month of April" ... "after the loss of above two hundred men, we could not at last muster more than six fore-mast men in a watch capable of duty" (Walter, pp. 100, 102). / "Left England in the Centurion, of all Sorts, Sept. 19, 1740 — 510 ... Total of Dead to that Time — 292 ... Remained alive at that Time — 218" (Thomas, Appendix)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 100-102, 112-113, 159-160, 370-371, 378, 382; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, p. 277 and Appendix, "An Account of what Men left England with us in the Centurion"
claims.retrieval_note: The gun-gang passage was found in the 1749 octavo at p. 378 and then located verbatim in the 1748 first-edition scan, so the wording is original to the published Voyage. Thomas's mortality table was too garbled in OCR to trust, so I pulled the actual page image from the Internet Archive BookReader (leaf 0375 of the 1745 scan, located by matching the word coordinates in the item's djvu.xml) and read the figures off the plate: 510 / 172 / 46 / 69 / 2 / 3 / 292 / 218. The crop is saved at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-aodhan/29937ecb-e066-4c86-9742-3a2d90c08f3c/scratchpad/mort_s.png.
claims.game_impact: REPLACE THE TIMER WITH THE GUN GANGS. The historical mechanic is: crew loss does not reduce how many guns you have, it changes HOW you can work them. Below a manning threshold, the Centurion stops firing broadsides and switches to two-men-per-gun loaders plus roving fire gangs - lower peak damage per volley, but continuous uninterrupted fire, and it specifically negates an enemy whose drill is to shelter from broadsides. Add the marksman trade-off: pull thirty hands out of the gun crews into the tops and you lose gun output but gain officer kills. Keep the 227-of-400 figure and the "near thirty were boys" detail.

claims.claim: Centurion modelled as a 60-gun fourth rate with two gun decks, 144 ft, slowest, heaviest broadside, largest hold.
claims.finding: Rate, guns and length all check out against period sources. Walter's squadron list: "the Centurion of sixty guns, four hundred men, George Anson, Esq; Commander." She still carried sixty in the Pacific - Walter laments having to "fight our sixty-gun ship with no more than thirty hands." Falconer's Universal Dictionary of the Marine (1769), art. RATE: "Ships of the fourth rate mount from 60 to 50 guns, upon two decks, and the quarter-deck. The lower tier is composed of 24 pounders, the upper tier of 12 pounders" - so fourth rate and two gun decks are correct by period usage (Falconer is 25 years after the voyage, so treat the calibres as indicative, not as Centurion's 1740 establishment). Charnock's dimension table, read off the page image, gives her: Gun Deck 144 ft 1 in, Keel 117 ft 5 in, Breadth 40 ft 1.5 in, Depth 16 ft 5 in, 1005 tons, 350 men, 48 guns as later rated, annotated "b.f.60" (built for 60), built 1732 at Portsmouth by J. Allen. So 144 ft is right to the inch. CAUTION on "largest hold": her depth in hold was 16 ft 5 in, and the Covadonga's measured 18 ft - the prize had the deeper hold. Against the other ships a game of this period would field (Golden Hind, Desire, Duke and Duchess) a 1005-ton fourth rate is comfortably the biggest, so the relative claim survives, but do not say she had the largest hold in the fight she is famous for.
claims.quote: "the Centurion of sixty guns, four hundred men, George Anson, Esq; Commander" (Walter, p. 14). / "had we been necessitated ... to fight our sixty-gun ship with no more than thirty hands" (Walter, p. 132). / "Ships of the fourth rate mount from 60 to 50 guns, upon two decks, and the quarter-deck. The lower tier is composed of 24 pounders, the upper tier of 12 pounders" (Falconer, Universal Dictionary of the Marine, 1769, art. RATE). / Charnock table row: "Centurion, b.f.60 | 144 1 | 117 5 | 40 1½ | 16 5 | 1005 | 350 | 48 | Sir J. Allen | Built 1732, Portsm. J. Allen."
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 14, 132; William Falconer, An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (London, 1769), art. "RATE"; John Charnock, An History of Marine Architecture, vol. 3 (London, 1802), p. 253 (dimension table, 50-gun class)
claims.retrieval_note: Charnock's OCR mangles the numeric columns, so I did not trust it. I located the row's word coordinates in the item's djvu.xml (leaf 0307, full-res 9248x12697), fetched the half-scale BookReader JPEG, cropped the Centurion row and the column headers separately, and read them visually. The header plate reads: Rates | Ships Names | Establishment, when | Length of Gun Deck | Keel | Breadth | Depth | Tons | Men | Guns | Surveyors | When and where built, and Builders Names - which is what lets the figures be assigned to the right columns. Crops at .../scratchpad/row_a.png and hdr_b.png. Falconer verified by its own title page ("By WILLIAM FALCONER") plus the RATE article's internal structure running first through sixth rates.
claims.game_impact: Keep 60 guns, fourth rate, two gun decks, 144 ft. Add 1005 tons and built Portsmouth 1732 if you want precision. Soften or drop "largest hold" - her hold was 16 ft 5 in, shallower than her own prize's 18 ft.

claims.claim: Anson's dates given as "1740-44".
claims.finding: Correct. The squadron weighed from Spithead on 10 September and from St Helens on 18 September 1740 (Thomas's muster table dates the Centurion's departure from England 19 September 1740). The Centurion anchored at Spithead on the evening of 15 June 1744. Walter closes the book with the elapsed time explicitly.
claims.quote: "ON the 18th of September, 1740, the squadron ... weighed from St. Helens with a contrary wind" (Walter, p. 14). / "By the twelfth of June they got sight of the Lizard; and the fifteenth, in the evening, to their infinite joy, they came safe to an anchor at Spithead ... Thus was this expedition finished, when it had lasted three years and nine months." (Walter, p. 417)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 14, 417; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, Appendix
claims.retrieval_note: Both endpoints read in continuous context (departure in Bk I ch. ii, arrival in the final paragraph before FINIS), not from an index or a chapter summary. The 1740 departure date cross-checks against Thomas's independent table heading "Left England in the Centurion, of all Sorts, Sept. 19, 1740".
claims.game_impact: Keep "1740-44". If you want a single line: sailed 18 September 1740, home 15 June 1744, three years and nine months.

claims.claim: "His real enemy was scurvy, not Spain" - defensible as a one-line blurb?
claims.finding: Strongly defensible, and the sources give a sharper version than the blurb. Pascoe Thomas titles his own mortality table "An Account of what Men left England with us in the Centurion, and how many we lost by Sickness, inclusive of those 4 lost in Engagements 'till our Return." FOUR men lost in action over the whole circumnavigation, against 292 dead by September 1741 alone and, on Thomas's estimate, about 380 of the 510 who left England dead by the time she came home. Those four are fully accounted for by the sources: one man at Paita, two killed at the Covadonga, and one of the seventeen wounded there who did not recover. Walter's squadron-wide figure is the same story: of 961 men who left England in the three ships that got into the Pacific, 626 were dead by September 1741, leaving 335 - "a number greatly insufficient for the manning the Centurion alone." Walter also notes that Spanish naval force never materialised, and that a Manila squadron fitted out to attack the Centurion on her station was abandoned before it sailed because "the Commerce and the Governor disagreed." One honest caveat: scurvy did not act alone. Walter blames the Admiralty delay and the resulting Cape Horn passage "in the most tempestuous season of the year" as "the source of all the disasters," and the Centurion's dead include 69 of 79 marines and 46 of 50 invalid pensioners - men sent to sea half-dead by a manning policy Anson himself had protested.
claims.quote: "An Account of what Men left England with us in the Centurion, and how many we lost by Sickness, inclusive of those 4 lost in Engagements 'till our Return." (Thomas, Appendix). / "the three ships together departed from England with nine hundred and sixty one men on board, of whom six hundred and twenty-six were dead before this time" (Walter, p. 160). / "on board the Centurion, out of fifty invalids and seventy-nine marines, there remained only four invalids, including officers, and eleven marines" (Walter, p. 160)
claims.source: Walter, Voyage Round the World, pp. 12-13, 100-102, 159-160, 376; Pascoe Thomas, True and Impartial Journal, Appendix
claims.retrieval_note: The decisive phrase "inclusive of those 4 lost in Engagements" was read off the page image (leaf 0375) rather than the OCR, because the OCR dropped it. The four are then reconcilable against the narrative: one man lost at Paita (Thomas), two killed at the Covadonga and one of the wounded who died (Walter), which is an internal consistency check rather than an assumption.
claims.game_impact: Keep the blurb, and consider the harder version: four men killed by the enemy in four years, roughly 380 killed by the voyage. If you want a second line, the squadron figure (961 sailed into the Pacific, 626 dead inside a year) is even starker.

nulls: COVADONGA'S TONNAGE/BURTHEN. Neither Walter nor Pascoe Thomas states her burthen in tons. I grepped both texts for "tons", "tuns", "burthen" and "tunnage": Walter gives tonnage for the victualling pinks, the Carmelo, the Teresa, the Santa Teresa de Jesus, the Carmin, Chinese junks and the Centurion's careening hulk, but never for the galleon - only "much larger than the Centurion", which her measured dimensions contradict (see surprises). Thomas gives linear dimensions, not tons. I did NOT consult modern scholarship (Schurz 1939, Williams 1999) for a tonnage figure because it would be in copyright and could not be quoted, and because I would be unable to verify what document it rests on. If a tons-burthen number is needed, it should be computed from the measured dimensions and labelled as a computation, or sought in the Admiralty survey of the prize (ADM 106 / ADM 95) which I did not search.

CENTURION'S ARMAMENT BY CALIBRE IN 1740-43. I could not find a period source stating what weight of gun she actually carried on each deck during the voyage. Walter says sixty guns and nothing more; Charnock's table gives numbers and dimensions, not calibres; Falconer's 24pdr/12pdr figure for fourth rates is from 1769 and cannot be back-projected to the 1733 Establishment without checking the Establishment itself, which I did not retrieve. Treat any per-deck calibre in the game as unverified.

THE SPANISH SIDE. I made no attempt to find Montero's own report, the Manila government's account, or any AGI/AGN document on the loss of the Covadonga. Everything above is from the two English eyewitness publications. Thomas notes that Montero expected to be "called to a strict Account at Manilla" - if that proceeding survives it would be the obvious counter-source, and it is not something I searched for.

PHILIP SAUMAREZ'S AND PIERCY BRETT'S JOURNALS. Saumarez commanded the prize and his manuscript journal is the third great eyewitness source for this action. I did not look for it. It is not on the Internet Archive under an obvious title and was published only in extract in modern editions, so it is outside what I could verify in free full text.

WHICH LIEUTENANT WAS WOUNDED. Walter says "a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded" without naming him, and Thomas's account of the Centurion's own casualties does not appear in the surviving OCR of his journal. I searched Thomas for "our Loss", "on our Side", "wounded" and "two Men" and found no corresponding passage. Unresolved.
