surprises: THE GALLEON WAS SMALLER THAN THE CENTURION, AND ANSON HAD HER MEASURED TO PROVE IT. Pascoe Thomas's appendix prints dimensions of the Cabadonga "taken by Orders of the Commodore, by John Shepherd Carpenter of the Tryall": Length of the Ship on the Gun-Deck 124 ft 00 in; Breadth from Outside to Outside 38 ft 02 in; Depth of the Hold 18 ft 00 in; Length from the fore part of the Lion to the after part of the Taffarel 154 ft 00 in. Against Charnock's Centurion (gundeck 144 ft 1 in, breadth 40 ft 1½ in, depth 16 ft 5 in) the galleon was TWENTY FEET SHORTER and two feet narrower, though deeper in the hold. Walter's famous line that "the galeon was much larger than the Centurion" is not supported by Anson's own carpenter's survey. I read these figures off the page image (leaf 0374 of the 1745 scan) because the OCR dropped the breadth. This looks like a durable small correction to the standard account, and it changes the encounter: the game should NOT model the Covadonga as a bigger ship.

AMMUNITION AND HITS ARE ON RECORD. Thomas, again from Shepherd's survey: "During the Engagement we shot about 141 Great Shot thro' the Hull and Masts of the Prize ... We expended 341 Round Shot, beside Abundance of Grape, Double-headed, and Small-shot", and the Centurion "receiv'd between 20 and 30 Shot in our Hull, Boats, &c." A 41 percent hit rate at pistol shot over eighty minutes, and a 12:1 ratio of hits taken to hits given. That is a ready-made gunnery model, and far more interesting than abstract damage.

THE GALLEON CHOSE TO FIGHT BECAUSE SHE THOUGHT ANSON WAS DYING. The Spanish had intelligence of the Centurion from Guam, including men who had been Anson's prisoners and who described her as weak and "almost defenceless". Montero bore down from six leagues to windward - the one position from which he could certainly have escaped - because he intended to take her. What changed his mind, too late, was seeing the Centurion haul up her ports and run out her lower-deck guns: "for till they saw that, they never imagined we had Men sufficient to fight them." The general had told his officers "That he did not doubt but to have the Honour to introduce Commodore Anson to his Table that Day to Dinner." An information/bluff mechanic is sitting right there: the enemy acts on a stale report of your strength, and you choose when to reveal it.

THE CENTURION ALMOST BLEW UP AT THE MOMENT OF VICTORY. Seconds after the galleon struck, a lieutenant whispered to Anson that the ship was on fire near the powder-room. Cartridges had blown up between decks and fired oakum in the after hatchway next to the after powder-room; Thomas says the flash also set off three lower-deck guns on the off side. Walter notes the escape route was gone too - the galleon had just fallen aboard the Centurion's starboard quarter. A near-catastrophe at the instant of the payoff.

THE PRIZE WAS A LOGISTICS CRISIS. 550 (Walter) or above 500 (Thomas) prisoners for 227 captors - "above double the number of his own people". They were stowed in the hold behind a square partition of thick planks with two hatchways left open for air and sentries over them; Walter says that after a month's confinement "they were reduced to mere Skeletons". Meanwhile the prize was crewed by roughly thirty Englishmen guarding near three hundred Spaniards. Holding a prize is a harder problem than taking her, and no treasure-hunt game models it.

THE FIRE THAT ALMOST LOST ANSON THE PRIZE. The mats with which the galleon had stuffed her netting caught fire at the very start of the action, probably from the Centurion's wads, and blazed "half as high as the mizen-top". Anson was alarmed not for the enemy but for the money - he feared she would burn and that she might drive aboard him. Her colours were in fact singed off the ensign staff, which is why she had to strike the royal standard at the main topgallant masthead, and Anson ordered cease fire so the man sent aloft to do it would not be shot down.

ANSON RAN A MARKSMANSHIP SCHOOL. Walter digresses to explain why the Centurion's small-arms fire was so deadly: the crew were taught no more of the manual exercise than the shortest method of loading with cartridges, were "constantly trained to fire at a mark, which was usually hung at the yard-arm", and "some little reward was given to the most expert". He concludes they were "more than a match for double their number, who had not been habituated to the same kind of exercise." This is a training-investment mechanic with a documented payoff, and it is the explicit cause of the 35:1 casualty ratio.

THE GAME'S "DITHERING" TIMER HAS A REAL ANALOGUE, BUT IT IS NOT ATTRITION - IT IS MISSING THE SECOND GALLEON. Anson expected two Acapulco ships. The one he had bottled up in Acapulco the previous year sailed early and alone and reached Manila before he got on station. Walter: Anson "had great reason to regret his lost of time at Macao, which prevented him from taking two rich prizes instead of one." Delay cost him a second Covadonga, not his crew.

verdicts.counter_evidence:
ANSON'S OWN OFFICIAL DISPATCH CONTRADICTS WALTER ON EVERY CASUALTY NUMBER IN THE FINDING.

The London Gazette of 16 June 1744 printed Anson's letter to the Duke of Newcastle, written from the Centurion at St Helens. I found it reprinted verbatim in three separate 1744 periodicals plus Barrow's 1839 life, which used the Admiralty papers:

Gentleman's Magazine, June 1744, p. 335 ("From the London Gazette, June 16. Extract of a Letter from George Anson, Esq..."): "She was called the Nuestra Senora del Caba Donga, Don Geronimo Montero Admiral; had 42 Guns, 17 of which were Brass, and 28 brass Pedereroes; 550 Men, 5[8] of which were slain, and 83 wounded ... having received only 15 Shot through my Hull, which killed me two Men, and fifteen wounded ... in guarding 492 Prisoners".

The ambiguous digit is settled by the Scots Magazine, June 1744 (same Gazette extract, clean OCR): "550 men, 58 of which were slain, and 83 wounded ... which killed me 2 men, and wounded 15." (https://archive.org/download/sim_edinburgh-magazine-and-literary-miscellany_the-scots-magazine_1744-06_6/..._djvu.txt, lines 6596-6612). The London Magazine, June 1744, prints the same sentence. Barrow, Life of George Lord Anson (Murray, 1839), pp. 74-75, quotes it as "fifty-eight of whom were slain, and eighty-three wounded" (Barrow's own text garbles the English loss as "killed sixteen men and wounded fifteen", which the three Gazette reprints correct to "two men... fifteen wounded").

So Anson: galleon 58 slain / 83 wounded; Centurion 2 killed / 15 wounded.
Walter: galleon 67 killed / 84 wounded; Centurion 2 killed + "a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded" (= 17).

Walter inflates the galleon's dead by nine and the English wounded by two. The finding presents Walter's numbers as the casualties, with no mention that the commander's own return says otherwise.

THE THOMAS "CLOSE MATCH" RUNS THE WRONG WAY. I confirmed Thomas's arithmetic at p. 300 verbatim: 395 + 72 + 6 + 12 escaped + 95 detained = 580, "and this taken from six Hundred and forty-four, their whole Complement at first, leaves sixty-four for the Number of those who were slain outright in the Fight, or had since died of their Wounds." But 64 is the LARGER category (killed plus died of wounds) and it is SMALLER than Walter's 67 killed-in-action alone. That is logically impossible if Walter is right. Thomas's 64 fits Anson's 58 slain plus six subsequent deaths almost exactly. Thomas corroborates Anson, not Walter. The finding reads the near-identity of 64 and 67 as agreement while ignoring its direction. Thomas's hearsay figure at p. 285 is lower still: "I had heard that we had killed them above fifty Men, and wounded as many more."

THOMAS ALSO CONTRADICTS THE TREASURE COUNT, AND THE FINDING USED HIM ONLY WHERE HE AGREES. Thomas, Appendix pp. 4-5: "An Account of the Treasure taken from on board the Ship Nuestra Signora de Cabadonga ... Spanish Dollars secured in 256 Boxes 1,278,546. Wrought Plate and Virgin Silver 1324 l. Troy. The Ship and remaining Part of her Cargo amounted to 6000 Dollars ... amounts to 313,121 l. 7 s. 7 d." His narrative at p. 303 repeats it: the search ended late August 1743 and "found upon Account in Specie one Million two Hundred seventy-eight Thousand five Hundred forty-six Dollars, and one Thousand three Hundred twenty-four Pounds and half Troy of wrought Plate and Virgin Silver; this being all the Treasure, except some Jewels, &c. not valued, which we got in this Prize." That is 35,297 dollars fewer than Walter, and 1,324.5 lb troy = c. 15,890 oz of plate-and-silver against Walter's 35,682 oz. Thomas's total for all three specie prizes is c. 353,324 l., against Walter's "not much short of 400,000 l." Thomas is openly sceptical of official numbers elsewhere (p. 301 on the prize-money division: "in the Log-Book it is set down only twenty Thousand three Hundred and twenty, which I think must be a Mistake"). The finding cites Thomas at pp. 286-287 and 300 and never mentions his appendix.

ONE SILENT ALTERATION IN WALTER. Anson's dispatch reads "35,682 Ounces of Virgin Silver and Plate." Walter prints "35,682 oz. of virgin silver," dropping "and plate." The finding reproduces Walter's wording, so the sources table would state as the register a category Anson did not state.

LOCATOR ERROR. The casualty quote is on p. 380, not p. 381. In the 1749 fifth edition they link (voyageroundworld00walt_1) the page markers run 379 / 380 / 381 and the sentence sits between the 380 and 381 markers; same in the 1748 first edition (voyageroundworld00walt_0), where it is also p. 380. Their p. 384 for the treasure passage is correct in both editions.

WHAT SURVIVES. Both quotes are genuinely verbatim in the linked text (allowing for long s): "She had sixty-seven killed in the action, and eighty-four wounded, whilst the Centurion had only two killed, and a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded, all of whom but one recovered: Of so little consequence are the most destructive arms, in untutored and unpractised hands" and "it was found that she had on board 1,313,843 pieces of eight, and 35,682 oz. of virgin silver, besides some cochineal, and a few other commodities". "Near a million and a half of dollars" is on p. 380 and is also in Anson-via-Barrow. And the 1,313,843 / 35,682 figures ARE Anson's own official numbers, so the specie total is well founded as the official register. Thomas's 112 bags and 6 chests at pp. 286-287 checks out verbatim, with one omission from the finding: Thomas also lists "one Bag of Plate" in the same transfer.
verdicts.reasoning: Tests 1 and 2 pass: I fetched their URL (proved it is Walter's Voyage Round the World, 5th edition, Knapton 1749, from the title page and dedication to the Duke of Bedford) and both quoted sentences are there word for word, in context, answering the question asked. Test 3 breaks the finding. Anson's own official report, printed in the London Gazette of 16 June 1744 and found by me in three independent 1744 reprints plus Barrow 1839, gives 58 slain and 83 wounded on the galleon and 2 killed and 15 wounded on the Centurion. Walter's 67/84 and his "a Lieutenant and sixteen wounded" are the compiler's later, higher figures, not the established casualties. Test 4 also breaks: the finding's claim that Thomas's arithmetic independently corroborates Walter is an over-reading in the agreeable direction. Thomas's 64 covers killed plus died-of-wounds, a wider category than Walter's 67 killed-in-action, so it cannot support 67; it supports Anson's 58. And Thomas, invoked as the corroborating witness, separately contradicts the treasure count in his own appendix (1,278,546 dollars; 1,324.5 lb troy of plate and silver; 313,121 l. for the Covadonga; c. 353,324 l. for all three prizes against Walter's near-400,000 l.) and the finding does not mention it. Walter's specie figure does hold up strongly, because it is Anson's own official number, so the claim is not dead. Downgrade to PARTLY: publish the treasure figures as Walter-and-Anson's official register, with Thomas's lower independent count noted, and do not publish 67/84 or 2-and-17 as the casualties without stating that Anson's dispatch says 58/83 and 2-and-15. Also fix the locator: p. 380, not p. 381.

verdicts.counter_evidence:
I tried to break this four ways and it held, but three qualifications belong in the sources table.

RETRIEVAL PROVED. Their Thomas URL returns the right item: title page reads "By PASCOE THOMAS, Teacher of the Mathematicks on board the CENTURION" (refut_thomas.txt, head). The 1748 Walter first edition (IA bim_eighteenth-century_a-voyage-round-the-world_anson-george-anson-bar_1748) carries "By RICHARD WALTER, M.A. Chaplain of his Majesty's Ship the Centurion, in that Expedition."

TEST 1, VERBATIM. The gun-gang quote is word for word in the 1748 FIRST EDITION, not a later smoothing: "he had not hands enough remaining to quarter a sufficient number to each great gun, in the customary manner; he therefore, on his lower tire, fixed only two men to each gun, who were to be solely employed in loading it, whilst the rest of his people were divided into different gangs of ten or twelve men each, who were continually moving about the decks, to run out and fire such [guns] were loaded. By this management he was enabled to make u[se] of all his guns; and instead of whole broad-sides with intervals between them, he kept up a constant fire without intermission" (1748 ed., anson1748.txt lines 36782-36794; brackets = OCR dropout only). "he himself had but two hundred and twenty-seven hands on board, of which near thirty were boys" is verbatim at 1748 p. 372 (line 36403-04; they cited p. 371, a one-page slip). "handful of boys", "forty-three men ... in the month of April", "six fore-mast men in a watch capable of duty", "a hundred and sixty-seven persons, besides twelve or fourteen who died in the boats" all verbatim.

TEST 2, CONTEXT. Correct. The passage sits in Anson's preparation on 20 June O.S. 1743 as the Centurion closed the galleon off Cape Espiritu Santo. The tops detail immediately precedes it and is also 1748-original: "He picked out about thirty of his choicest hands and best marksmen, whom he distributed into his tops."

TEST 3, THE TABLE. I did not take their word for the plate. I located leaf 0375 independently by splitting the item's djvu.xml into 410 OBJECT blocks and finding the one containing "Bombardiers", pulled the BookReader JPEG (4490x6481), cropped the table by mapping the OCR word coordinates at DPI 800 down by 2x, and read it. It says exactly: Left England in the Centurion, of all Sorts, Sept. 19, 1740 — 510 / Seamen 172 / Invalids 46 / Marines 69 / Bombardiers 2 / Agents Servants 3 / Total of Dead to that Time 292 / Remained alive at that Time 218. Arithmetic closes both ways. Their reading is right. Crop at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-aodhan/29937ecb-e066-4c86-9742-3a2d90c08f3c/scratchpad/r_table.png.

TEST 3b, INDEPENDENT WITNESS — THIS IS THE STRONGEST THING THEY MISSED. Pascoe Thomas, published 1745, THREE YEARS BEFORE Walter, and not an Anson apologia, describes the same gunnery from the deck: "we then kept a continual Fire upon her of both great and small Arms, not firing in set Broadsides and Vollies, and leaving the Intervals of loading again, but every one firing as fast as his Gun would come to bear, or he could take sure Aim; by this Means there was no Cessation of Shot constantly poured in among them: The first Volley our People from the Tops gave upon theirs drove them out of their Tops" (refut_thomas.txt, p. 282). Thomas also records the thin crew being concealed: "the hauling up our Ports and running out our Lower-deck Guns; for till they saw that, they never imagined we had Men sufficient to fight them" (p. 281). This defeats the obvious objection that Walter is Anson's self-serving official narrative (Glyn Williams calls the Walter narrative an apologia for Anson's conduct rather than an impartial memoir).

QUALIFICATIONS THE TABLE SHOULD CARRY:
(a) The specific ARRANGEMENT — two loaders per lower-tier gun, roving gangs of ten or twelve — rests on Walter ALONE. Thomas corroborates the effect (continuous fire, no loading intervals, marksmen in the tops) but not the administrative scheme. Do not present the two-men-per-gun detail as doubly attested.
(b) The two eyewitnesses do not agree on the headcount. Thomas has 224 "Men and Boys in the whole of different Nations" leaving the Grand Ladrone in April 1743 (p. 277), against Walter's 227; and Walter's own figures imply 506 left England (292 buried + 214 remaining), not Thomas's 510. Thomas's 218 alive at 30 Sept 1741 against Walter's 214 at "beginning of September" is a genuine conflict, since the later date should give the lower number. These are two conflicting musters that happen to agree on 292. Small, but the finding presented 292/214 as independent corroboration of the 510 table when it actually implies a different departure figure.
(c) The "handful of boys" line is Walter's, and it is exactly the kind of flattering anecdote an apologia invents. Thomas's independent record of Spanish surprise at the lower-deck ports supports the substance but not the quotation.
verdicts.reasoning:
I could not break it. The quote is verbatim in the 1748 first edition, the context is the Covadonga action itself, the mortality table reads off the plate exactly as they said (I re-derived the leaf and re-cropped it rather than trusting their crop), and the mechanism is independently corroborated by Pascoe Thomas writing in 1745, before Walter. The verification was unusually honest: they flagged that Thomas's OCR was garbage and went to the image, which is the correct move and their reading of it is correct.

Where the finding is vulnerable is TEST 4, and the finder half-saw it themselves. The claim as worded bundles a game mechanic with a historical question. The historical question — was the crew so thin that he worked the guns unusually — is CONFIRMED on two independent eyewitnesses. The mechanic — "crew shrinks on a timer and reloads get slower the longer you dither" — is contradicted by the same sources, in two ways.

First, timing. The dying was not a drip you could run on a dither-timer. It was a single catastrophe concentrated in April–June 1741 off Cape Horn and before Juan Fernandez (43 in April, "near double that number" in May, 167 landed sick in mid-June), which is TWO FULL YEARS before the Covadonga on 20 June 1743. By 1743 the crew was being rebuilt, not shrinking: Thomas records roughly twenty Dutch, Persians and Lascars entered at Macao bringing the total to about 224. A timer that drains the crew while the player loiters in the Pacific misdescribes the actual curve, which was set by one bad decision about when to round the Horn.

Second, direction. Both witnesses say the thin crew produced FASTER fire, not slower. Walter has Anson expecting to "procure very signal advantages" from it; Thomas says there was "no Cessation of Shot". A mechanic where attrition degrades reload speed inverts what the sources report. The finder said so explicitly ("far better than a timer"), so this is not over-reading on their part — it is the claim's framing that is wrong, not their answer.

I am leaving the verdict CONFIRMED rather than downgrading, because the question actually asked was answered correctly and fully from primary text, and refuting a finding this well evidenced would be a false negative of exactly the kind the historian cannot afford. But the sources table should carry the three qualifications in counter_evidence, above all that the two-men-per-gun arrangement is Walter-only, and that Walter is Anson's semi-official apologia.

I re-did every step independently and the SHIP-SPEC half of this finding is excellent. What fails is the scope: the claim has seven elements and the finding carries four.

WHAT SURVIVED (I verified each myself, not from their write-up):

1. Walter p. 14. Downloaded the 1748 first edition (IA bim_eighteenth-century_a-voyage-round-the-world_anson-george-anson-bar_1748, md5 8a19de1f01bdbf30fbc113296907d469; title page reads "By RICHARD WALTER, M.A. Chaplain of his Majesty's Ship the Centurion"). Their quote fails a naive grep because the text is long-s. Searching "ixty guns" finds it: "the Centurion of ſixty guns, four hundred men, George Anſon, Eſq; Commander". The printed marker "( 14)" sits 28 lines above. Verbatim, correct page.

2. Walter p. 132. "had we been neceſſitated (as we muſt have been, had the enemy appeared) to fight our ſixty-gun [ſhip] with no more tha[n] thirty hands", with the printed "( 132 )" marker directly above. The IA OCR mangles "ſhip" to "wn" and "than" to "tka"; I confirmed their reconstruction against the Gutenberg/Masefield edition (#47130), which reads "to fight our sixty-gun ship with no more than thirty hands." Their ellipsis hides only "(as we must have been, had the enemy appeared)" - no distortion.

3. Falconer 1769, art. RATE. Title page verified ("By WILLIAM FALCONER, Author of The Shipwreck... MDCCLXIX"). Article verbatim: "Ships of the fourth rate mount from 60 to 50 guns, upon two decks, and the quarter-deck. The lower tier is compofed of 24 pounders, the upper tier of 12 pounders". Their truncation drops only "and the cannon on the quarter-deck and fore-caftle are 6 pounders." Bonus corroboration they missed: the same article gives "The complement of a 50 gun Ihip is 350 men", matching Charnock's 350 for Centurion.

4. Charnock. I located leaf 307 (confirmed 9248x12697, page number "253" present), pulled the half-scale BookReader JPEG and cropped the row myself. It reads exactly as they reported, to the inch: "Sold. | Centurion, b.f.60 | 144 1 | 117 5 | 40 1½ | 16 5 | 1005 | 350 | 48 | Sir J. Allen | Built 1732, Portsm. J. Allen." Headers confirmed: Rates / Ships Names / Establishment / Gun Deck / Keel / Breadth / Depth / Tons / Men / Guns / Surveyors / When and where built.

I should add that they were RIGHT to distrust the OCR, and I walked into the trap to prove it. The plain _djvu.txt renders the line as "Sold. Centurion, b.f.60 144 11117 5 4 1116 5 7 7 * 480 Built at Portsmouth, 1727." I initially flagged "1727" as a refutation of their 1732. The image shows "Built at Portsmouth, 1727" belongs to the OXFORD row above; Centurion's cell reads 1732. Their method was necessary, not fussiness. They also correctly avoided the other trap on that same page: the first row is a DIFFERENT Centurion (146 0, "Re-b. 1774, Harw. Barnard & Co."), the 1774 fifty. And a point in their favour they undersold - the Rates column on p. 253 literally reads "4th.", so Charnock himself classes her a fourth rate; they attributed that only to Falconer.

WHY IT STILL CANNOT STAND AS CONFIRMED:

"largest hold" is not merely a caution, it is contradicted in the primary source, and more bluntly than they realised. Walter, p. 380-81: "The galeon was much larger than the Centurion, and had five hundred and fifty men, and thirty-ſix guns mounted for action". That is the compiler of the voyage saying the ship Centurion is famous for taking was the bigger vessel, full stop. Their own Charnock figure (depth in hold 16 ft 5 in) points the same way. Separately, their "the Covadonga's measured 18 ft" is itself unsourced - it is NOT in Walter, and they cite nothing for it. So the one number they used to qualify the claim is the one number in their finding I could not verify.

"slowest" has zero evidence in the finding. I went looking and the only support I could find is Masefield's 1911 Everyman introduction: "As she was built more to carry cannon than to sail, she was a slow sailer" - an editor's assertion with no authority given, not a period source, and not cited by them. Against it stands Walter's own narrative, p. 177: "the Centurion ſo much outſailed the two prizes, that we ſoon ran them out of fight". The primary text presents her as a ship that outruns her consorts.

"heaviest broadside" is never evidenced either, though it is safe by trivial inference (60 guns against 18-30 on Golden Hind, Desire, Duke, Duchess; Masefield gives 13 twenty-four-pounders plus 13 nine- or twelve-pounders a side).

Net: 60 guns, fourth rate, two gun decks and 144 ft are solid and I would stake the sources table on them. "Slowest" rests on a 1911 editor against the primary narrative. "Largest hold" is true only if the comparison set is the player roster and false against the galleon - which is exactly the comparison a player will make. PARTLY, not CONFIRMED, and the table should state which ships the comparative stats are measured against.
verdicts.counter_evidence:
Walter, A Voyage Round the World (London, 1748), pp. 380-81, on the captured galleon: "The galeon was much larger than the Centurion, and had five hundred and fifty men, and thirty-ſix guns mounted for action, beſides twenty-eight pedreroes in her gunwale, quarters and tops". This refutes "largest hold" against the one ship Centurion is famous for fighting, independently of the 18-ft depth figure the finder asserted without a citation (that figure is not in Walter and I could not source it).

On "slowest", Walter p. 177: "we all immediately gave her chace; but the Centurion ſo much outſailed the two prizes, that we ſoon ran them out of fight, and gained conſiderably on the chace". The only support for "slow sailer" I could locate is John Masefield's 1911 Everyman introduction (Gutenberg #47130, Introduction, p. vii): "As she was built more to carry cannon than to sail, she was a slow sailer" - editorial, unsourced, and 160 years after the fact.

Corroborating detail the finding missed, in its favour: Charnock vol. 3, p. 253 heads the rate column "4th.", so Charnock independently classes Centurion a fourth rate. Also note the plain OCR at that URL misassigns "Built at Portsmouth, 1727" to the Centurion row (it belongs to Oxford above) - anyone re-checking this from the _djvu.txt rather than the page image will wrongly conclude the 1732 date is an error.

I re-fetched their URL and proved the retrieval before trusting it: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-aodhan/29937ecb-e066-4c86-9742-3a2d90c08f3c/scratchpad/walter_anson.txt opens with the title page "A VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD, In the Years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV. BY GEORGE ANSON, Esq; ... COMPILED From his PAPERS and MATERIALS, By RICHARD WALTER, M.A., Chaplain of his Majesty's Ship the Centurion ... The Fifth Edition. LONDON ... MDCCXLIX."

TEST 1 — quotes verbatim. Both check out word for word.
Departure, under the page header "( 14 )" at the head of Chap. II: "ON the 18th of September, 1740, the squadron, as we have observed in the preceding chapter, weighed from St. Helens with a contrary wind". Their ellipsis elides only "as we have observed in the preceding chapter,". Accurate.

Their supporting 10 September detail is also in the text, p. 10: "The last detachment of these marines came on board the 8th of August, and on the 10th the squadron sailed from Spithead to St. Helens, there to wait for a wind."

TEST 2 — context. Neither quote is lifted from an index or chapter summary. The departure sentence opens the narrative chapter and is corroborated eight pages earlier ("at last, on the 18th of September, he weighed from St. Helens", p. 11). TEST 3 — a source that says otherwise. I checked the independent eyewitness, Pascoe Thomas (IA bim_eighteenth-century_a-true-and-impartial-jou_thomas-pascoe_1745; retrieval proved by title page "By PASCOE THOMAS" and the imprint line "Commencement in the Year 1740 ... conclusion in 1744"). The OCR of the muster table is garbage ("Sept. e e,, F 510"), so I pulled the page scan itself (leaf n375, Appendix p. 8) and read it: "Left England in the Centurion, of all Sorts, Sept. 19, 1740 ——— } 510". On his p. 347 (leaf n366, read from the scan, not OCR) Thomas ends: "The 14th at Eleven in the Morning we anchored at the Back of the Isle of Wight, and in the Evening weigh'd, and again anchored at Spithead. Thus concluding our tedious and perilous Voyage." That is 14 June 1744, not Walter's 15th. The likely cause is sea-day versus civil-day reckoning. It is a one-day disagreement inside June 1744 and does not touch the year range.

TEST 4 — does it support the CLAIM. Yes, directly, not adjacently. The claim is only the date range "1740-44", and both endpoints are nailed to the year: 18/19 September 1740 out, 14/15 June 1744 home, with Walter's own "three years and nine months" and both title pages ("In the Years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV"; "Commencement in the Year 1740 ... conclusion in 1744") agreeing independently.

Caveats for the sources table, none of them fatal: (a) the page numbers 14 and 417 are from the FIFTH edition (Knapton, 1749), not the first of 1748, so the edition must be named with the pagination; (b) their stated arrival of 15 June is Walter's and is contradicted by Thomas's 14 June, so if the table ever states a day, it should cite which witness; (c) all dates are Old Style (Julian), eleven days behind Spanish reckoning, which matters only if English and Spanish dates are juxtaposed elsewhere in the table.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Pascoe Thomas, A True and Impartial Journal (London, 1745), p. 347, read from the page scan: "The 14th at Eleven in the Morning we anchored at the Back of the Isle of Wight, and in the Evening weigh'd, and again anchored at Spithead. Thus concluding our tedious and perilous Voyage." This puts the Centurion at Spithead on 14 June 1744, one day earlier than Walter's 15th. It qualifies their arrival detail, not the 1740-44 range.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding survives all four tests. (1) QUOTE: I downloaded the Thomas 1745 OCR, proved retrieval by the title-page line "By PASCOE THOMAS, / Teacher of the Mathematicks on board the Centurion", then fetched the page image (leaf n375, ia800502) because the OCR of the table heading is badly garbled. The image reads verbatim: "An Account of what Men left England with us in the Centurion, and how many we loft by Sicknefs, inclufive of thofe 4 loft in Engagements 'till our Return." Their quote is word-for-word correct. The table: 510 left England 19 Sept 1740; dead to 30 Sept 1741 = Seamen 172, Invalids 46, Marines 69, Bombardiers 2, Agents Servants 3, Total 292, Remained alive 218; then "not above 130 ... returned alive; so that out of the 510 ... about 380 perifhed on the Voyage." All three Walter quotes verify verbatim at pp. 159-160 of the 1749 edition (IA voyageroundworld00walt_1, lines 7617-7646), including "the three fhips together departed from England with, nine hundred and fixty one men on board, of whom fix hundred and twenty-fix were dead before this time", "a number, greatly infufficient for the manning the Centurion alone", and "out of fifty invalids and feventy-nine marines, there remained only four invalids, including officers, and eleven marines". (2) CONTEXT: not strained. Both passages are deliberate stocktakings of loss; neither is answering a different question. (3) INDEPENDENT CHECK OF THE FOUR: I grepped every "killed/kill'd/slain/wounded" in both texts. Walter has "no other lofs than that of one man killed on the fpot, and two wounded" at Paita, and at the Covadonga "the Centurion had only two killed, and a Lieutenant and fixteen wounded, all of whom but one recovered" = 1+2+1 = 4 exactly. The only other violent death in the Centurion is an accident off Tinian ("the jeers broke again, and killed one of our people"), which is not an engagement. No British combat death is concealed anywhere in either book. (4) CONTRARY SCHOLARSHIP: I found and read a genuinely new peer-reviewed article built on the Spanish side - C. Nathan Kwan, "The World Around Anson's Voyage: Inter-imperial Impacts of the Expedition," Itinerario (2026), doi 10.1017/S0165115326100862, using AGI Filipinas 256/293 and Spanish-language scholarship (Pinzon Rios, Guerra Moscoso, Barros van Buren). It contains zero instances of the words scurvy/mortality/death as a corrective, describes Anson's force in passing as scorbutic, confirms Pizarro's squadron failed at the Horn and never engaged, and records not one British casualty inflicted by Spain in the whole Pacific. That is the Spanish side agreeing with the English one on the only point that matters here. DEFECTS I DID FIND, none fatal: (a) "69 of 79 marines" silently blends two sources - Walter p.160 gives 11 marines remaining of 79 (= 68 lost), while 69 is Thomas's separate figure for marines dead to 30 Sept 1741; (b) Walter says 214 remained aboard the Centurion where Thomas's table says 218, a discrepancy the finding does not flag; (c) the Paita death is attributed to Thomas but I located it in Walter, not Thomas; (d) "abandoned before it sailed" overstates Walter, who writes "fome of thefe veffels actually weighed" before the enterprise was laid aside; (e) the finding says the OCR dropped the key phrase - it did not, it garbled it ("inclufroe of thofe 4. bt in Engagements"), though going to the image was still the right call. These are errors in the connective prose, not in the evidence, and none touches the load-bearing contrast. The blurb is defensible as written.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Two qualifications the finding should carry, neither of which breaks it. FIRST, the honest limit of "not Spain": Spain defeated Anson's primary mission without firing a shot. Kwan shows from Mexican and Spanish records that Anson's mere appearance off Acapulco triggered a Council of War on 28 February 1742 which voted unanimously to hold the galleon Nuestra Senora del Pilar in port and to send word to Manila not to despatch a galleon at all; Anson waited, got nothing, and left for China in April 1742. Walter himself concedes the intelligence failure at pp. 12-13: the Admiralty delay meant "the enemy had been fo well informed of our defigns" that a man arriving from Panama days before Anson left Portsmouth could relate most of the particulars of the plan to Anson's face. So Spain was a real and effective adversary by intelligence, prudence and withdrawal; it simply never killed anybody. "His real enemy was scurvy, not Spain" is true about what destroyed his men and false if read as "Spain was not a serious opponent." SECOND, a correction to the finding's Manila detail: it says a Manila squadron "was abandoned before it sailed." Walter actually says some of those vessels weighed before the plan was dropped, and Kwan shows from AGI Filipinas 256 N.1 that after the Covadonga was taken the Philippines armed the Pilar and two other ships and did send them to Canton to retake the Centurion - they reached Macao on 12 April 1744, after Anson had gone, and bought the Covadonga back for the price he had sold her at. Spain mounted two naval efforts against the Centurion; both missed her. THIRD, a precision point on "scurvy" specifically: Walter records deaths before any scurvy - 2 lost on the run to Madeira, "many died" of calentures and fluxes between Madeira and St Catherine's, and 28 buried at St Catherine's with the sick rising from 80 to 96. Scurvy is overwhelmingly the killer (43 buried in April alone off the Horn), but it is not the whole of the disease mortality, which the finding already concedes.

claims.claim: The galleon made her landfall HIGH on the California coast and ran down the outer coast of Baja California to round the cape for Acapulco.
claims.finding: True as the 16th/early-17th-century practice; false as the 18th-century practice. Morga (1609) has the ship stand north to 42 deg, sight the coast between 40 and 36 deg, then run south in sight of land to Cenizas, Cedros, and Cabo San Lucas. Cabrera Bueno's 1734 derrotero still prints a whole chapter for that coasting route starting at Cape Mendocino in 41-41.5 deg. But Cabrera Bueno's PRIMARY recommended route corrects longitude off the senas without ever seeing land, then runs ESE to about 32 deg and SE to make Cedros/Cenizas (28-30 deg N). Anson's compilers (1748) say the galleon deliberately avoided the upper coast. Schurz (1917) states flatly that by the eighteenth century landfall was made well down the coast, between Point Conception and Cape San Lucas. So the 'high landfall' is a 1565-c.1700 picture, not an Anson-era one.
claims.quote: "When the ships are near the coast, and in general they sight it between from forty degrees to thirty-six, the cold is very great, and the crews suffer and die of it. ... After this the coast is discovered, which is very high land, and a clean coast, and without losing sight of it, the ship runs along it ... decreasing the latitude, and entering a warmer temperature the island of Cenizas is sighted, and afterwards that of Cedars; from thence they go on to sight the cape of San Lucas, which is the mouth of California." (Morga, 1609, Stanley trans. 1868, pp. 356-57.) Against this, Anson/Walter 1748: "After falling in with these Signs, as they denominate them, they steer to the southward, without endeavouring to fall in with the coast, till they have run into a lower latitude; for as there are many islands, and some shoals adjacent to California, the extreme caution of the Spanish Navigators makes them very apprehensive of being engaged with the land" (p. 243). And Schurz 1917, p. 107: "by the eighteenth century they generally made their landfall well down the coast, somewhere between Point Conception and Cape San Lucas."
claims.source: Antonio de Morga, Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas (1609), trans. H. E. J. Stanley, The Philippine Islands, Moluccas, Siam, Cambodia, Japan, and China (Hakluyt Society, 1868), pp. 356-57; Joseph Gonzalez Cabrera Bueno, Navegacion especulativa y practica (Manila, 1734), Quinta Parte, cap. I and cap. IV ('Derrota desde el Cabo de Mendocino, hasta el Puerto de Acapulco por la Costa'); [Richard Walter], A Voyage Round the World ... by George Anson (London, 1748), p. 243; W. L. Schurz, 'The Manila Galleon and California', Southwestern Historical Quarterly XXI:2 (Oct. 1917), pp. 107, 109-11
claims.retrieval_note: Morga: title-page block in the OCR reads 'THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS, MOLUCCAS, SIAM, CAMBODIA, JAPAN, AND CHINA, AT THE CLOSE OF THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY. BY ANTONIO DE MORGA ... BY THE HON. HENRY E. J. STANLEY. LONDON: PRINTED FOR THE HAKLUYT SOCIETY. M.DCCCLXVIII' - correct work, correct translator. Cabrera Bueno: title page confirmed verbatim, 'NAVEGACION ESPECVLATIVA, Y PRACTICA ... COMPVESTA POR EL ALMIRANTE D. IOSEPH GONZALEZ Cabrera Bueno, Piloto mayor de la Carrera de Philipinas ... Impresa en Manila ... Ano de 1734', and the chapter heading 'Derrota defde el Cabo de Mendocino, hafta el Puerto de Acapulco por la Cofta' located in situ. Anson: title block 'A voyage round the world, in the years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV' (1748) and the passage sits inside the chapter on the Manila navigation. Schurz: JSTOR Early Journal Content header plus masthead 'THE SOUTHWESTERN HISTORICAL QUARTERLY Vol. XXI October, 1917 No. 2'.
claims.game_impact: Decide the game's DATE first. For a Cavendish-era (1587) game, keep the high landfall and the run down the outer coast. For an Anson/Woodes Rogers era game (1700s), change it: the galleon corrected her longitude by floating weed (the 'senas') WITHOUT seeing land, ran south offshore, and only closed the coast at the very southern tip. The high landfall is then an anachronism.

claims.claim: The prevailing wind and current on the outer Baja coast are NW setting SE, giving the galleon wind and current astern and the weather gauge.
claims.finding: Confirmed by a 1609 primary and by two nineteenth-century sailing directions, with one textual trap you must not walk into. Findlay's Directory (1886), the parent text of the US Hydrographic Office book, says north-westerly winds blow steadily for eight months, and that the currents set in the direction of the prevailing wind at half a knot to one knot, with an easterly set always to be guarded against. Morga in 1609 independently names NW, NNW and N winds on that coast. The TRAP: the US Hydrographic Office second edition (1893), p. 1, prints 'northeasterly'. I checked the page image, not just the OCR: the printed word really is 'northeasterly'. It is an error. The same book elsewhere says San Lucas Bay shelters 'from northwesterly winds', speaks of 'the strong NW. winds' on Cortez Shoal, and is otherwise a near-verbatim paraphrase of Findlay, who prints 'north-westerly'. Do not cite HO 1893 p. 1 for wind direction. Two documented complications: Nov-Feb brings SE gales, and summer brings short, strong SE gales specifically near Cabo San Lucas; and at the cape itself the current turns east, into the gulf.
claims.quote: "Winds.-Along this coast north-westerly winds blow steadily for eight months of the year ... Near Cape San Lucas, short but strong S.E. gales occur during the summer months, sometimes extending as far North as Magdalena Bay. ... The Currents along this coast set in the direction of the prevailing wind, from half a knot to 1 knot per hour. At all times an easterly set should be guarded against." (Findlay 1886, pp. 178-79.) "From Cape San Lucas to San Diego, or from 23 deg to 32 deg N., the general direction of the wind is from West to North" (Commander James Wood, in Findlay, pp. 1174-75). "the true wind, which blows almost without intermission along the line of coast from the northward ... a strong current accompanying the wind" (Capt. Sherard Osborn, in Findlay, p. 1240). "Off cape San Lucas the current sets to the eastward. The Narragansett experienced quite a strong easterly current off the southern extremity of the peninsula." (US Hydrographic Office, 1893, p. 34.)
claims.source: A. G. Findlay, A Directory for the Navigation of the North Pacific Ocean, 3rd ed. (London: R. H. Laurie, 1886), pp. 177-79, 1174-75, 1240; United States Hydrographic Office, West Coast of Mexico and Central America, from the United States to Panama, including the Gulfs of California and Panama, 2nd ed. (Washington: GPO, 1893), pp. 1-2, 29-30, 34; Morga/Stanley 1868, p. 357
claims.retrieval_note: Findlay: title page in OCR reads 'FROM PANAMA TO BEHRING STRAIT, AND JAPAN; ITS WINDS, CURRENTS, AND PASSAGES, BY ALEXANDER GEORGE FINDLAY, F.R.G.S. ... LONDON: PUBLISHED BY RICHARD HOLMES LAURIE ... 1886'; running heads 'CAPE SAN LUCAS. 177' and 'THE WINDS OF THE NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN. 1174' pin the page numbers. HO 1893: OCR title block reads 'UNITED STATES HYDROGRAPHIC OFFICE ... WEST COAST OF MEXICO AND CENTRAL AMERICA, [FROM] THE UNITED STATES TO PANAMA, INCLUDING THE GULFS OF CALIFORNIA AND PANAMA. SECOND EDITION. WASHINGTON: GOVERNMENT PRINTING [OFFICE] 1893.' For the 'northeasterly' anomaly I did NOT trust the OCR: I located the word in the djvu.xml word-coordinate layer, computed the page object (page 0015 = leaf n14), downloaded the full-resolution BookReader JPEG, cropped the paragraph and read it as an image. The printed word is 'northeasterly'.
claims.game_impact: Keep the wind and current astern from the NW. Two free upgrades: (1) a November SE gale is documented and is the one weather that makes San Lucas Bay a death trap, so it can flip the whole tactical situation; (2) the current turns EAST off the cape, which sets a ship toward the land and into the gulf mouth - that, not a straight SE drift, is what the final approach feels like.

claims.claim: Six months at sea, with grass on her bottom and a crew on short water.
claims.finding: The six months is right and well attested from two independent sides. The water is wrong. The fouling I could not establish at all. Morga (1609) gives five months usually, frequently six or more; Anson's compilers (1748) say the voyage is rarely of less than six months. But Anson also explains, in detail, that the galleon did NOT run short of water: she carried it in earthen jars slung in the shrouds and stays and recruited it by catching rain on mats rigged along the gunwale between 30 and 40 deg N, a method that 'hath never been known to fail them'. The killer on the Manila-Acapulco run was scurvy, not thirst. On hull fouling I found nothing in any period source read here; the claim is unsupported, not disproved.
claims.quote: "the port of Acapulco is entered, without any port having been touched at or a landing made since the channel of Capul of the Philippines during the whole voyage, which usually lasts five months, a little more or less, and frequently six months or more time." (Morga/Stanley 1868, p. 357.) "from the time the Manila ship first loses sight of land, she never lets go her anchor till she arrives on the coast of California, and very often not till she gets to its southermost extremity: And therefore as this voyage is rarely of less than six months continuance ..." (Anson/Walter 1748, p. 240.) "their only method of recruiting their water is by the rains, which they meet with between the latitudes of 30 and 40 North, and which they are always prepared to catch: For this purpose they take to sea with them a great number of mats ... this method of supplying their water ... hath never been known to fail them, so that it is common for them when their voyage is a little longer than usual, to fill all their water jars several times over." (Anson/Walter 1748, p. 241.) On the state of the crew, Schurz quotes a bystander at Navidad in 1734: "It is not possible that these men are China sailors, because we are accustomed to see in those of so difficult a navigation the aspect of dead men, or of mortified penitents."
claims.source: Morga/Stanley 1868, p. 357; Anson/Walter, A Voyage Round the World (1748), pp. 240-41; Schurz, SWHQ XXI:2 (1917), p. 121
claims.retrieval_note: Anson: the file's table of contents includes 'Our cruise off the port of Acapulco for the Manila ship' and the running pagination brackets (240), (241), (243), (244), (245) appear in the OCR around the quoted text, so the page locators are from the book's own printed page numbers, not inferred. Morga verified as above.
claims.game_impact: Keep six months. CHANGE 'crew on short water' - replace with scurvy and beri-beri. Anson is explicit that water was the one thing they reliably had. A galleon arriving with a dying crew but full water jars is both truer and more interesting. DROP or flag 'grass on her bottom' as invented unless you find a source; I could not.

claims.claim: Cabo San Lucas: the anchorage, the bay, the lee of the cape, the depth, and whether a ship could lie in wait there out of sight of a vessel passing down the outer coast.
claims.finding: The anchorage is exactly as the game needs, and the continuity of the description across three centuries is striking. Cavendish's own 1587 rutter and the 1886/1893 pilots agree to the fathom and on which wind is fatal. San Lucas Bay lies NE of the cape, shelters from NW winds, is wide open from south round to east, and the bank is so steep that you can lose an anchor over the edge. BUT the 'lie in wait out of sight' half is not supported and is partly contradicted. Cabrera Bueno does say the bay lies BEHIND the Frailes and only opens when you haul NE, and the ridge between bay and ocean carries a hill named Vigia - lookout. Yet Cavendish did not hide: he watered and then 'lay off and on' in the open from the cape for three weeks, and Anson records that the Spaniards deliberately kept a watch at the cape for exactly such a cruiser.
claims.quote: "San Lucas Bay, lying northward and eastward of the cape ... affords good shelter from north-westerly winds, but is exposed to the sea from South around to East, rendering it an exceedingly unsafe anchorage during the wet season, when S.E. gales are both frequent and heavy. The soundings are very irregular, and the anchorage, by reason of its great depth in the centre, is completely a lee shore. The best anchorage is in the N.W. part, in 6 or 7 fathoms, a quarter of a mile from the beach. At less than a quarter of a mile N. by E. 3/4 E. of the cape, a depth of 218 fathoms, rocky bottom, was found." (Findlay 1886, p. 177.) "be sure to have the lead on the bottom when the anchor is let go, as the bank is very steep" (HO 1893, p. 30). Cavendish's own 1587 note: "You may anker in the port of S. Lucas on the Cape of California in 12 fadoms water: and a Southeast winde is the woorst." (Hakluyt, Principal Navigations, MacLehose ed., XI, p. 373.) And Cabrera Bueno 1734: "luego se descubrira la Baia de San Bernabe que esta detras de ellos que es muy buen Puerto, y hondable ... es muy buen Puerto para el Verano, para el Invierno no lo aseguro, porque es desabrigado del Sueste, y Sursueste." Against concealment: "wee watered in the river and lay off and on from the saide cape of S. Lucar untill the fourth of November, and had the windes hanging still Westerly." (Francis Pretty, in Hakluyt XI, p. 324.)
claims.source: Findlay 1886, pp. 177-78; US Hydrographic Office 1893, pp. 29-30; Cabrera Bueno 1734, Quinta Parte cap. IV (ff. c. 311-12); Francis Pretty, 'The admirable and prosperous voyage of ... Master Thomas Candish', in Hakluyt, Principal Navigations (MacLehose ed., Glasgow, 1904), XI, pp. 324, 369, 373
claims.retrieval_note: Hakluyt vol. XI verified by its own table of contents ('The prosperous voyage of M. Thomas Candish esquire ...') and by the running head 'CANDISH'S CIRCUMNAVIGATION' with the date band '1587.'; printed page numbers 323, 324, 368, 370, 371, 372, 373 appear as standalone lines in the OCR and I used them to pin each quotation to its page. Findlay/HO verified as in T-2.
claims.game_impact: Keep the anchorage exactly as the pilots give it: NW corner, 6-7 fathoms, quarter mile off, bank falls to 218 fathoms a quarter mile from the cape, SE wind is the one that kills you. That is a free, authentic hazard mechanic. CHANGE the ambush premise: historically the English did not hide behind the cape, they cruised openly off it for weeks and the Spanish posted a lookout there. Either make the lookout a game element (the hill is literally called Vigia) or accept that concealment is invention.

claims.claim: The arch rocks at Land's End (El Arco) are real, and a hazard to a sailing vessel.
claims.finding: The arch is real and described in both pilots in near-identical words: it pierces the eastern side of the western Fraile, the 303-foot sugarloaf rock. But as a NAVIGATIONAL hazard it is the opposite of what the game assumes. Both pilots say the Frailes may be approached close-to and that there is nothing hidden. Cabrera Bueno in 1734 uses the three white rocks as the positive MARK for finding the anchorage. The real dangers at that corner are the vertical bank that eats anchors, the sea that breaks heavily on the coast between Cape Falso and Cape San Lucas even in fine weather, and SE weather.
claims.quote: "Los Frailes are two high, rugged rocks, with numerous smaller ones near them; the western one, connected with the wedge-shaped ridge by a narrow strip of low sand beach, is 303 ft. high, of sugar-loaf shape, with an archway on its eastern side, through which the sea rushes with great force. The eastern rock is 251 ft. high, very steep, and is the Cape San Lucas proper" (Findlay 1886, p. 177). "The navigator has no hidden dangers to fear; all are above water. After rounding the Frailes from the westward, he may safely stand for the houses, dropping his anchor in 15 fathoms." (Findlay 1886, p. 178.) "Between cape Falso and cape San Lucas the coast is a succession of sand beaches and bold rocky bluffs, against which the sea breaks heavily, even in the finest weather." (HO 1893, p. 29.) "This fantastically formed headland, when once seen, is not likely to be forgotten." (HO 1893, p. 29.)
claims.source: Findlay 1886, pp. 177-78; US Hydrographic Office 1893, pp. 29-30; Cabrera Bueno 1734, Quinta Parte cap. IV
claims.retrieval_note: HO 1893 identified by its printed title block and by the running head 'LA TINAJA POINT TO CAPE SAN LUCAS. 29' / '30 WEST COAST OF LOWER CALIFORNIA.' bracketing the quoted text, which fixes the pages. Findlay fixed by running head 'CAPE SAN LUCAS. 177' and '178 LOWER CALIFORNIA.'
claims.game_impact: Keep the arch, it is real and both pilots single it out. CHANGE its function: it is a LANDMARK, not a hazard. If you want a hazard at that corner, use the steep-to bank (anchor lost over the edge: Findlay reports HMS Sulphur going from 10 fathoms to no bottom at 88) and the heavy breaking sea on the Falso-San Lucas beach.

claims.claim: The galleons touched at or near Cabo San Lucas for water and refreshment, which is WHY the English lay there.
claims.finding: This is the game's load-bearing premise and it is fully, explicitly documented - but only for the eighteenth century. Anson's 1748 compilation states the reason in so many words, including that the cape is a station where the galleon has 'often been waited for and fought with'. The Jesuits kept refreshments ready and, by the captain's own written instructions, lit signal fires and sent intelligence about enemies on the coast. HOWEVER: in 1609 Morga states that the galleon touched NOWHERE between the Philippines and Acapulco. Schurz shows the regular calls at Bahia San Bernabe began only in 1734, after Montero put in there with one day's water left and the viceroy then ordered all Philippine ships to call. So for a 1587 game the watering stop is NOT yet a Spanish routine - though the bay was already called Aguada Segura, the Safe Watering Place, and Cavendish watered in it; and Spilbergen in 1615 sailed for Cape San Lucas expressly to watch for the galleon.
claims.quote: "when they draw near its southern extremity, they venture to hale in, both for the sake of making Cape St. Lucas to ascertain their reckoning, and also to receive intelligence from the Indian inhabitants, whether or no there are any enemies on the coast ... For this purpose there are refreshments, as fruits, wine, water, &c. constantly kept in readiness for her; and there is besides care taken at Cape St. Lucas, to look out for any ship of the enemy, which might be cruising there to intercept her; this being a station where she is constantly expected, and where she has been often waited for and fought with, though generally with little success. ... the Captain of the galeon is ordered to fall in with the land to the northward of Cape St. Lucas, where the inhabitants are directed, on sight of the vessel, to make the proper signals with fires; and on discovering these fires, the Captain is to send his launch on shore with twenty men, well armed, who are to carry with them the letters from the Convents at Manila to the Californian Missionaries, and are to bring back the refreshments which will be prepared for them, and likewise intelligence whether or no there are any enemies on the coast." (Anson/Walter 1748, pp. 243-45.) Cabrera Bueno 1734 on the same bay: "al Nordeste de la Playa ay un Carrizal, a donde ay mucha agua, lena, y Pescado." Against the early date, Morga 1609: "the port of Acapulco is entered, without any port having been touched at or a landing made since the channel of Capul of the Philippines during the whole voyage" (p. 357). Burney on 1587: "This Bay was called by the Spaniards Aguada Segura, (the Safe Watering Place). There is in it a fresh water river, and wood is plenty; and it is protected from all winds, except the South East." (Burney, II, p. 87.)
claims.source: Anson/Walter, A Voyage Round the World (1748), pp. 243-45; Cabrera Bueno 1734, Quinta Parte cap. IV; Morga/Stanley 1868, p. 357; James Burney, A Chronological History of the Discoveries in the South Sea or Pacific Ocean (London, 1806), II, pp. 86-89; W. L. Schurz, SWHQ XXI:2 (1917), pp. 119-22; H. H. Bancroft, History of Mexico III (San Francisco, 1883), p. 26
claims.retrieval_note: Burney vol. II identified by its table of contents ('Voyage of Thomas Cavendish round the World', 'Expedition of Sebastian Vizcaino to California') and by running heads 'VOYAGE OF THOMAS CAVENDISH' / 'ROUND THE WORLD' with printed page numbers 86-89 in the OCR. Bancroft identified by the title block 'THE WORKS OF HUBERT HOWE BANCROFT' and running heads 'A DUTCH FLEET AT ACAPULCO. 81' etc.; the Spilbergen passage is on p. 26 by its running head 'OPENING OF THE SEVENTEENTH CENTURY'.
claims.game_impact: The premise SURVIVES, and Anson gives you better material than the game currently uses. But date-gate it. Post-1734: the galleon is ordered to close the land north of the cape, watch for signal fires, and send a launch with twenty armed men to collect refreshments AND intelligence about you. That is a whole scenario. Pre-1700: she touched nowhere, and the English lay at the cape because it was her unavoidable landfall and departure point, not because she watered.

claims.claim: The galleon's track pinched against the land at the cape, so an ambusher could cut the corner.
claims.finding: Confirmed from three independent directions, and from a primary eyewitness. Anson's compilers say the galleon 'ventures to hale in' at the southern extremity and that the captain's instructions ORDER him to fall in with the land north of Cape San Lucas. Cabrera Bueno's printed derrotero tells the pilot to coast the land all the way to the cape. And the 1587 eyewitness saw the Santa Ana doing exactly that. One honest qualification: Cabrera Bueno also prints an escape hatch - run SE by S to 22 deg and pass outside without ever seeing the cape - so a nervous captain had a legal alternative, and in 1786 Basco recorded deciding in advance not to put into Monterey although ordered to.
claims.quote: "y se ira costeando siempre la tierra gruesa hasta el Cabo de San Lucas ... el que huviere de tomar Puerto en este Cabo se arrimara al Medano blanco dicho, y se ira costeando, y luego se veran tres Farallones muy juntos blancos, y tajados, y se arrimara a ellos, y desde este Paraje se ira la buelta del Nordeste" (Cabrera Bueno 1734). The eyewitness: "betwene seven and 8 of the clocke in the morning one of the company of our Admirall which was the trumpeter of the ship going up into the top espied a sayle bearing in from the sea with the cape" (Francis Pretty, Hakluyt XI, p. 324). The alternative, same book: "y si quisieres pasar por fuera y no verlo, governaras al Sueste quarta al Sur hasta altura de 22. grados, por que el esta en 22. grados y medio" (Cabrera Bueno 1734).
claims.source: Cabrera Bueno, Navegacion especulativa y practica (1734), Quinta Parte caps. I and IV; Anson/Walter 1748, pp. 243-44; Francis Pretty in Hakluyt, Principal Navigations (MacLehose ed.), XI, p. 324; Burney II, p. 87
claims.retrieval_note: Cabrera Bueno verified by the 1734 Manila title page transcribed in full from the OCR (author, office of piloto mayor of the Philippine run, dedicatee Fernando de Valdes y Tamon as Governor of the Philippines), and the quoted passages located inside the correctly headed chapters 'Derrota desde Cavite a S. Bernardino ... y de alli a Acapulco' and 'Derrota desde el Cabo de Mendocino, hasta el Puerto de Acapulco por la Costa'. The 1734 OCR is poor (long-s and f confusion); I read the surrounding sentences in full rather than keyword-matching, and the sense is unambiguous.
claims.game_impact: KEEP the pinch; it is the best-supported thing in the cluster. Upgrade it: the pinch is not an accident of geography, it is written into the captain's ORDERS. Consider adding Cabrera Bueno's offshore bypass as a rare AI choice - a galleon that stands off and passes outside at 22 deg, never seeing the cape, and the ambush simply fails.

claims.claim: Fort San Diego at Acapulco: built 1617, its armament and its arcs of fire.
claims.finding: 1617 is right as a COMPLETION date, not as the fort's origin, and it is the wrong fort if the game is set after 1776. Works ran 1615-1617 under Viceroy Diego Fernandez de Cordoba, Marques de Guadalcazar, to the design of the engineer Adrian Boot; the fort's own dedicatory inscription over the gate carried the year 1616 and Boot's name; the five caballeros (Rey, Principe, Duque, Marques, Guadalcazar) were finished by 1617. But Acapulco was already defended before that: Purchas's account of Spilbergen's visit in October 1615, quoted by Bancroft, says 'The Castle had seuentie Brasse Pieces'. Armament thereafter: Schurz says some forty or more brass cannon of large bore for most of its history, over eighty guns in the later eighteenth century; Bancroft records that at the 1794 repairs it had only ten brass and fifty-eight iron guns serviceable. Position: NE of the town, on a hill about 422 varas (c. 370 m) from it, commanding the town and the galleon's anchorage, pentagonal and irregular, with one caballero facing south close to the shore. ARCS OF FIRE: I could not establish these from any period source. The decisive point for the game: the 1617 fort was wrecked by the earthquake of 21 April 1776 - Bancroft: 'Acapulco was almost entirely destroyed' - and rebuilt 1778-1783 as the present pentagon to Miguel Constanso's project.
claims.quote: "To the northeast of the town was situated the Castle of San Diego, which protected the town and the anchorage ground of the galleons from the incursions of foreigners. During most of its history there were mounted on its bastions some forty or more brass cannon of large bore. But, whatever its actual strength, it had almost as forbidding a reputation among the enemies of Spain as did the formidable works of Cartagena and San Juan Ulua" (Schurz, 'Acapulco and the Manila Galleon', SWHQ XXII:1 (1918), p. 21; his footnote adds 'In the latter eighteenth century the castle contained over 80 guns'). "The Castle had seuentie Brasse Pieces, hauing intelligence eight moneths before of their comming." (Purchas, His Pilgrimes, I.ii.84, quoted in Bancroft, History of Mexico III, p. 25 n.56.) "This fort, called San Diego de Acapulco, of more modern construction, underwent in 1794 some repairs. It then had only ten brass and fifty-eight iron guns in good condition, and more that were unserviceable." (Bancroft, History of Mexico III, p. 420.) The gate inscription, as transcribed in a modern study of the fort, ends: "se hizo esta fortificacion. Ano de 1616, Yngeniero Adrian Boot." For the raid itself, Anson/Walter 1748, p. 246: "When the galeon arrives in this port, she is generally moored on its western side to the two trees marked in the plan".

claims.game_impact: DATE-GATE the fort. If the finale is set before 1776, you want Boot's 1615-17 irregular pentagon with its five named caballeros and roughly forty brass guns. If after 1776, that fort was in ruins and the one standing is Constanso's 1778-83 rebuild. INVENT NOTHING about arcs of fire - no period source I found gives them. Two authentic free details for the raid: the galleon moored on the WESTERN side of the harbour to two trees, and in 1742 the governor posted a guard on the island at the harbour's mouth specifically against boat attack.

nulls: ARCS OF FIRE for the Castillo de San Diego: not established. Looked in Schurz 1918 (the dedicated article on Acapulco), Bancroft History of Mexico III (all 45 'Acapulco' hits), and Anson/Walter 1748 (who had a captured Spanish plan but printed no bearings). The 2013 UAEM architectural study gives the pentagon's geometry and says one caballero faced south near the shore, but no fields of fire. Anson's engraved plan of the port and citadel exists in the 1748 book and might settle it; I did not read the plate image.

HULL FOULING / 'grass on her bottom': no period evidence found. Searched Anson/Walter 1748 for foul, weed, bottom, sheathing, worms; searched Schurz 1917 and 1918; searched Morga. Anson describes the galleon's slowness but attributes it to cautious orders and seamanship, never to a foul bottom.

A PRE-1929 PRINTED SOURCE for the 1615-1617 construction of the Castillo de San Diego: not found. Bancroft dates Acapulco's fortification efforts to Cerralvo after the 1624 Dutch visit and to Palafox in 1642, and says nothing about 1615-17 or Adrian Boot. Purchas's 1615 'Castle' with seventy brass pieces shows an earlier work existed. The 1615-17 dates rest on the 2013 UAEM study and on the fort's gate inscription dated 1616 as transcribed there.

WHETHER AGUADA SEGURA (1587) IS BAHIA SAN BERNABE AT CABO SAN LUCAS OR SAN JOSE DEL CABO: unresolved. Burney (II, 87 n.) states it was 'Since named the Bay de San Bernabe', and Cavendish's 12-fathom anchorage with 'a Southeast winde the woorst' matches the San Lucas Bay pilot descriptions exactly (San Jose Bay has a 40-50 fathom hole and you anchor in 13-15). But Pretty's 'faire fresh river' fits the Rio San Jose, 16 miles east, far better than San Lucas Bay, where Findlay and HO both say the water comes from WELLS in an arroyo. Cabrera Bueno describes San Bernabe's water as a carrizal, a reed bed, not a river. I did not resolve this and the game should not assert it.

WHY the Santa Ana was standing in for the cape in November 1587: not established. Pretty says only that she was 'bearing in from the sea with the cape'. No source read here states her intention. The inference that she was coming in to water is natural but unproven for that date, and Morga's 1609 statement that the galleon touched nowhere cuts against it.

A LATER EDITION of the US Hydrographic Office book correcting 'northeasterly' to 'northwesterly': not checked. I verified the 1893 second edition reads 'northeasterly' from the page image, and established the error by internal inconsistency and by comparison with Findlay 1886, from which the HO text is clearly derived. I did not locate the 1880 first edition or any later edition on Internet Archive.

surprises: THE HILL ABOVE THE AMBUSH ANCHORAGE IS CALLED 'VIGIA' - LOOKOUT. Findlay and the HO both name the summit of the wedge ridge between the Pacific beach and San Lucas Bay as Vigia Hill (527 ft in Findlay, 627 ft in HO - the two books disagree). Anson independently records that a watch was kept at Cape San Lucas for enemy cruisers. The lookout is a better game mechanic than concealment: the ambusher's problem is not being seen from the hill, and the galleon's launch comes ashore for intelligence about exactly that.

ANSON PRINTS THE GALLEON CAPTAIN'S STANDING ORDERS FOR THE CAPE, AND THEY ARE A SCENARIO ALREADY WRITTEN. Fall in with the land NORTH of the cape; the shore people light signal fires; the captain sends his launch with TWENTY ARMED MEN carrying letters from the Manila convents to the California missionaries; the launch brings back refreshments and intelligence whether there are enemies on the coast; only if all is clear does he proceed for the cape and then Cape Corrientes. A game whose finale is a cutting-out raid is ignoring a ready-made boat action at the cape.

THE GALLEON CAUGHT HER DRINKING WATER IN THE RAIN WITH MATS. Anson, p. 241: jars (not casks) hung in the shrouds and stays, and mats rigged sloping along the gunwale draining into a split bamboo into a jar, worked between 30 and 40 deg N. It never failed, and on a long passage they filled the jars several times over. Visually extraordinary, and it kills the 'short water' trope.

CAVENDISH'S OWN 1587 ANCHORING NOTE IS IDENTICAL TO THE 1886 AND 1893 PILOTS. 'You may anker in the port of S. Lucas on the Cape of California in 12 fadoms water: and a Southeast winde is the woorst.' Three hundred years later Findlay and the Hydrographic Office say 6-12 fathoms, sheltered from NW, exposed south through east, SE gales fatal. A game could literally put the Elizabethan rutter line on screen as the player's anchoring information and it would be correct.

THE FRAILES WERE MISTAKEN FOR FRIGATES UNDER SAIL. Cabrera Bueno 1734: three white rocks on the way down from Cedros 'que parecen Fragatas a la Vela, que son los que enganaron al Navio S. Geronymo el ano de 1699'. A false-contact mechanic with a date and a ship's name attached.

THE CAPE GOT ITS OWN SIGNAL AND REFRESHMENT SYSTEM ONLY AFTER 1734. Schurz: Montero's galleon reached Bahia San Bernabe in 1734 with ONE DAY'S water left and several down with beri-beri, 'whose only remedy is to go ashore'; they took aboard 100 sheep and hogs, 40 cattle, game birds, fruit and vegetables, and at Navidad people said these could not be China sailors because China sailors look like dead men. The viceroy then ordered all Philippine ships to call there. The game's premise has a birth date.

THE 1617 FORT WAS DESTROYED BY AN EARTHQUAKE IN 1776 AND REBUILT 1778-83. If the finale is set in the Anson/Woodes Rogers century the fort is Boot's; if it is set later, the pentagon the player sees is Miguel Constanso's rebuild. The game should not quietly use one fort for all dates.

SPILBERGEN'S WATERING PARTY AT SALAGUA WAS AMBUSHED BY A PARTY SAID TO HAVE BEEN COMMANDED BY SEBASTIAN VIZCAINO (Bancroft, Hist. Mex. III, p. 26) - the same Vizcaino who charted the coast the galleons ran down. The Spanish counter-ambush is historically attested and under-used.

verdicts.reasoning:
RETRIEVAL AND QUOTES: all four quotes check out word for word, which is rare. Findlay retrieval re-proved independently (title page at line 246: "BY ALEXANDER GEORGE FINDLAY, F.R.G.S." / "PUBLISHED BY RICHARD HOLMES LAURIE" / "1886"; running heads "CAPE SAN LUCAS. 177" and "1174 THE WINDS OF THE NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN" pin the pages). The Winds paragraph sits under the running head "178 LOWER CALIFORNIA" and the Currents sentence straddles 178/179, exactly as cited. Morga/Stanley re-proved via Hakluyt Society title page; p.357 running head "AND FROM NEW SPAIN. 357" confirms "the ship runs along it with the north-west, north-north-west, and north winds, which are usually met with on this coast ... decreasing the latitude". HO 1893 p.34 Narragansett quote verbatim, page pinned by the following head "GULF OF CALIFORNIA. 35".

THE TRAP: their handling is correct and I can harden it beyond what they did. The HO 1893 p.1 word really is "northeasterly", and it is demonstrably a second-edition typesetting error, because the FIRST edition settles it. US HO, The West Coast of Mexico and Central America (1887), p.7, prints the same paragraph word for word with "northwesterly": "The prevailing winds along the coast are from a northwesterly direction, and they may be said to blow steadily from that direction for eight months of the year." They did not cite the first edition; it closes the question.

WHY IT STILL DOES NOT HOLD AS CONFIRMED. The claim has three clauses and the evidence covers two.

(1) Unsupported third clause. Nothing cited addresses "the weather gauge". That is a relational tactical state between two vessels, not a property of a wind regime, and no source in the finding speaks to it. Worse, the one primary that observes the actual interception zone in the actual interception season contradicts its reliability. Woodes Rogers off Cabo San Lucas, 22 Dec 1709: "At Day-break we saw the Chase upon our Weather-Bow ... the Dutchess a-head of her to Leeward" and then "We had no Wind, but got out 8 of our Ships Oars, and rowed above an Hour" (A Cruising Voyage round the World, pp. 214-15). The 26 Dec action against the Begoña: "the Wind veering at once, put our Ship about ... the Enemy lay driving" (pp. 218-19). And on California itself: "The Wind at this Time of the Year generally blowing over Land" (p. 229). Who held the weather gauge there was a function of relative position and of calms, not of a prevailing NW.

(2) Season mismatch they did not flag. They disclose the Nov-Feb exception as a "complication", but do not note that Nov-Feb IS the galleon's arrival window at the southern end of the run. Morga, p.357, has the voyage "usually lasts five months, a little more or less, and frequently six months or more"; departures were mid-year, so Baja landfall and the run to Acapulco fell roughly Oct-Jan. Findlay p.178 puts "winds from S.E. to S.W." and "moderate S.E. gales" in Nov-Feb and "Heavy northers, blowing from North to N.E." in Dec-Jan. The eight-month steady NW regime is largely the off-season for the thing the claim is about.

(3) Current qualifications missed. Findlay's own currents chapter, pp. 1216-17, section "COAST OF CALIFORNIA", says the drift "follows the general trend of the coast" and reaches "a maximum of 22 miles off the entrance to the Gulf of California" (good for the claim) but also: "Under the shelter of the projecting headlands, and frequently close in-shore, there are counter-currents, and reversed tides, by which small vessels can advantageously work their way against its general influence", and "On approaching the southern parts of California, and in the latitudes of the peninsula, it assumes a higher temperature and a more westerly course". So inshore counter-currents, and an offshore westward bend in the peninsula's own latitudes. Both Findlay p.179 and HO 1893 p.1 also record a rare adverse winter set: "A very slight N.W. current has sometimes, though rarely, been found in the winter season."

NET: the meteorological core (prevailing NW wind, coastal current setting with it at half to one knot, wind and current astern for a southbound galleon) is solidly confirmed by a 1609 primary and two sailing directions, with the HO 1893 misprint correctly caught. The tactical corollary is not evidenced and is contradicted at the point of use. PARTLY, not CONFIRMED. Drop "and the weather gauge", or support it separately, and state the season.
verdicts.counter_evidence: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage round the World (1712; 1928 repr.), off Cabo San Lucas: "At Day-break we saw the Chase upon our Weather-Bow, about a League from us, the Dutchess a-head of her to Leeward near about half as far ... We had no Wind, but got out 8 of our Ships Oars, and rowed above an Hour" (pp. 214-15); "the Wind veering at once, put our Ship about ... the Enemy lay driving" (pp. 218-19); "The Wind at this Time of the Year generally blowing over Land" (p. 229). Findlay 1886, pp. 1216-17: "Under the shelter of the projecting headlands, and frequently close in-shore, there are counter-currents, and reversed tides, by which small vessels can advantageously work their way against its general influence"; "On approaching the southern parts of California, and in the latitudes of the peninsula, it assumes a higher temperature and a more westerly course." Findlay 1886, p. 179 and HO 1893, p. 1: "A very slight N.W. current has sometimes, though rarely, been found in the winter season." CORROBORATING, not countering: US Hydrographic Office, The West Coast of Mexico and Central America (1st ed., 1887), p. 7, prints "northwesterly" in the paragraph the 1893 2nd ed. renders "northeasterly", proving the 1893 reading a typo.

I could not break the claim. I found MORE support than the researcher had, including the Spanish side they did not cite, plus two real counterweights and three transcription defects.
