TEST 1 — ARE THE QUOTES THERE? Two of three are verbatim-exact; the Cabrera Bueno quotes are NOT clean.
• Anson: EXACT. "however, when they draw near its fouthern extremity, they venture to hale in, both for the fake of making Cape St. hucai [Lucas] to afccrtain their reckoning, and alfo to receive intelligence from the Indian inhabitants ... and this laft circumftance, which is a particular article in the Captain's inftruftions". And: "the Captain of the galeon is ordered to fall in with the land to the northward of Caps St. LncaSy where the inhabitants are diredlcd, on fight of the veffel, to make the proper fignals with fires".
• Pretty: EXACT, on the page that ends with the printed "324": "betwene seven and 8 of the clocke in the morning one of the company of our Admiral[l] which was the trumpeter of the ship going up into the top espied a sayle bearing in from the sea with the cape".
• Cabrera Bueno quote 1: present but MIS-TRANSCRIBED. The 1734 text reads "y Ce [se] irá coíleando ficmpre la tierra grueíla baila el Cabo de San Lucas ... el que-huvieic de tomat Puerto en eíle Gabo fe arrimara al Megano blanco dicho, y fe irá coíleando, y luego fe verá tics Farallones muy juntos blancos, y tajados, y fe arrimará á ellos, y defde eíle Paraje fe irá la buelta del Nordeílc". The book says MEGANO, not "Medano", and "tierra gruessa", not "gruesa". Modernising "Megano"→"Medano" inside quotation marks is exactly the kind of slip a referee catches against the scan.
• Cabrera Bueno quote 2 (the escape hatch): the OCR at that spot is wrecked and the words "pasar por fuera" are NOT legible in the file they cite. It reads: "y (¡ qut'fcr? paíar 'pQt &c¿J)y no vef l|govcrnarás al Sal eíjc guaría al Surjuíla altura de 22. grados, por queeleíU en 11. grados, y medios y jie allí te podüaur metiendo en tierra conio te pareciere". The sense ("...y no ver l[o], governarás al Sueste quarta al Sur hasta altura de 22 grados, porque él está en 22 grados y medio") is clear, and the final "11." is plainly OCR for 22. But it was reconstructed and presented as verbatim without saying so. Note also that this edition spells latitudes out in words in the adjacent coast derrota ("veinte y dos grados, y medio"), so numerals here need the page image to settle.

TEST 2 — CONTEXT. One misattribution of weight. The "coast the thick land all the way to Cape San Lucas" sentence is in the COAST derrota, "Derrota defde el Cabo de Mendocino, hafta el [Puerto de Acapulco por la Costa]". The escape hatch is in the galleon's OWN chapter, "Derrota defde Cavite á S. Bernardino [y de allí a Acapulco]", where the instruction from Isla de Cerros/Guadalupe is 30 leagues SSE then SE until "vendrás a dar con el Cabo de S. Lucas" — with the offshore option attached, and a cross-reference sending the reader to the coast chapter only "fi quifires faver con mas individualidad los paraxes, y feñas de eíla Coila". So the escape hatch sits in the primary chapter and the coast-hugging sentence in the supplementary one. That is the reverse of the weighting the finding implies. Also, the second half of quote 1 is conditional — "el que huviere de tomar Puerto en este Cabo" — i.e. directions for a ship that intends to anchor in San Bernabé, not a general route statement. Only the first clause is unconditional.

TEST 3 — A SOURCE THAT SAYS OTHERWISE. I went looking for the Spanish side to contradict Anson. It corroborates him instead. Venegas, Noticia de la California (Madrid 1757), II, p. 460: "y folo en Manila fe dió orden, que el Galeón tocaífe en el Cabo de San Lucas. Afsi lo hizo el que vino el año figuiente ... porque llegando el Capitán Montero á Manila de vuelta, antes de la falida de la Nao, fe añadió efte artículo en fu inftruccion de viage." A Spanish Jesuit source, printed independently of Anson, says an article was ADDED TO THE CAPTAIN'S SAILING INSTRUCTION ordering the galleon to touch at Cape San Lucas. That is Anson's "particular article in the Captain's inftruftions" confirmed from the other side of the war. Venegas II also records a galleon actually taken there: a man "havia hecho la carrera de Philipinas, y fido llevado prifionero á Batavia, quando fué aprefada la Nao de Philipinas en el Cabo de San Lucas" (Part III §XV, p. 342) — a second successful ambush at the cape besides 1587. And Burney (chronologicalhis02burn, pp. 86-87) independently narrates the ambush geometry: Cavendish "quitted the coast of New Spain, and steered for the South Cape of California, with the determination to wait there for the arrival of the ship which was expected from the Philippine Islands ... on this station, keeping sight of the Cape, they continued to cruize till the 4th of November ... a strange sail was discerned from the mast head, standing in for the Cape."

THE TWO REAL COUNTERWEIGHTS, both omitted by the finding:
(a) Venegas II, Part III §XV (p. ~334): "Por temor de ellos, embió orden el Virrey a Loreto en aquel mifmo tiempo, para que el Barco de California faliefíe a cruzar, efperar, y avifar á la Nao de Philipinas, que fe apartaífe mucho de las Coftas, infeftadas de enemigos, que la efperaban." When enemies were known to be on station the viceroy sent a boat out from Loreto to warn the galleon to keep WELL OFF the coast. So the pinch was defeasible by standing Spanish counter-play, not just by a nervous captain's discretion. Also vol. 1, p. ~215: a warship was ordered out "a efperar otra vez la Nao de Philipinas, cuya navegación fiempre era expueíla á dar en manos de enemigos" — i.e. convoy was the other answer.
(b) Anson's own sentence, which the finding quotes around: Cape St. Lucas is "a flation where (lie is conftantly expefled, and where flie has been often waited for and fought with, though generally with little fuccefs." The compilers themselves put the ambusher's expected yield at the cape as LOW. For game design that number matters, and the finding dropped it.

PAGINATION CORRECTIONS: the "ordered to fall in with the land to the northward" sentence straddles the foot of p. 244 and p. 245, not pp. 243-44 (the "venture to hale in" sentence is the one on 243). Burney is pp. 86-87, not p. 87.
verdicts.reasoning:
The claim survives all four tests and is better evidenced than the researcher realised, so I will not kill it. But the supporting apparatus has three publishable defects, so it should read PARTLY rather than CONFIRMED.

What holds. Both halves of T-7 are documented verbatim and from independent directions. The galleon's track did close the land at the cape: Anson/Walter say the Spanish deliberately stayed off the coast ("without endeavouring to fall in with the coaft, till they have run into a lower latitude ... very apprehenfive of being engaged with the land") and then "when they draw near its fouthern extremity, they venture to hale in" — the pinch is at the cape specifically, which is precisely the claim's geometry. And an ambusher could use it: Anson calls the cape "a flation where (lie is conftantly expefled, and where flie has been often waited for and fought with"; Pretty is a 1587 eyewitness of a sail "bearing in from the sea with the cape" after three weeks of lying off and on; Burney 1803 narrates the same as a deliberate wait-on-station. Crucially, I went hunting for Spanish evidence to contradict the English compilers and found the opposite: Venegas (1757), a Jesuit source with no stake in Anson, records that an article was added to the galleon captain's sailing instruction at Manila ordering him to touch at Cape San Lucas, and records a galleon actually taken at the cape. The Spanish side ratifies the English side. That is the hardest test the finding could have faced and it passed.

Why PARTLY and not CONFIRMED. Three things need fixing before this goes into a published sources table.

First, the quote fidelity. The 1734 book reads "Megano blanco" and "tierra gruessa"; the finding prints "Medano blanco" and "tierra gruesa" inside quotation marks. One letter, but it is a silent modernisation of an archaic reading presented as verbatim, and a referee checking the scan will find the mismatch. Worse, the escape-hatch quote sits on a stretch of OCR that is genuinely wrecked — the words "pasar por fuera" are not legible in the file cited, and "22. grados" appears once as "11. grados". The researcher reconstructed a readable sentence and presented it as a transcription. The reconstruction is almost certainly right on sense, but it must be marked as reconstructed or verified against the page image.

Second, the weighting of Cabrera Bueno is backwards. "Cabrera Bueno's printed derrota tells the pilot to coast the land all the way to the cape" is true of the coast derrota (Cape Mendocino to Acapulco por la Costa), while the galleon's own chapter (Cavite to Acapulco) explicitly licenses running SE by S to 22 degrees and passing outside without ever seeing the cape. The finding treats the coasting sentence as the rule and the bypass as a footnote; the book puts the bypass in the primary galleon chapter. Also the second half of the quoted passage is conditional on intending to anchor ("el que huviere de tomar Puerto en este Cabo"), so it is directions into San Bernabé, not a statement of the through route.

Third, two omissions that cut against the game design the claim feeds. Venegas shows the viceroy's standing counter-measure: send a boat out from Loreto to warn the galleon to keep well off the coast when enemies were known to be waiting, or convoy her in. And Anson's own sentence finishes "though generally with little fuccefs" — the compilers rate the cape ambush as frequently attempted and usually fruitless. A sources table that says "an ambusher could cut the corner" without that rider will mislead whoever sets the probability.

Minor: the Anson citation should be pp. 243-45 (the instruction sentence runs from the foot of 244 onto 245), and Burney pp. 86-87. The Basco/Monterey 1786 item in the qualification is about a different landfall and does not bear on the cape; it should be dropped or relabelled.

Net: the claim is sound and I could not refute it. The verdict should be PARTLY pending the transcription corrections and the addition of the two counterweights.

claims.claim: ships.js draws St George's cross as the national colours of Drake's Golden Hind, 1579, flown 'off the ensign staff right aft'.
claims.finding: The DEVICE is right, the FLAG and the POSITION are not. Perrin, the Admiralty Librarian and the standard authority, states that English ships of this period flew the St George's cross as a MASTHEAD flag, and that the stern ensign, a different flag, was striped. On merchant and private ships: 'the English merchant ships were in the habit of flying the St George's flag at one or more mastheads' (p. 129). And on the ensign: 'The field of the ensign had, since its introduction about 1574, been of striped design' (p. 115), with a footnote that 'In the earlier ensigns, towards the end of Elizabeth's reign, the stripes were sometimes diagonal, and different designs appear to have been used to distinguish individual ships.' A plain St George's cross on the ensign staff aft in 1579 conflates the two flags. Perrin also records (p. 59) that Drake flew a striped flag on the bowsprit on his last voyage, 1595-96. Note the game's own index.html comment says 'at her mastheads', which is correct; ships.js then draws it aft.
claims.quote: "The field of the ensign had, since its introduction about 1574, been of striped design"
claims.source: W. G. Perrin, British Flags: Their Early History, and Their Development at Sea (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1922), p. 115; and p. 129 (ch. V (iv), Merchant Ships)
claims.retrieval_note: Downloaded the full djvu text (681 KB) and proved identity three ways before using it: the title page reads 'BRITISH FLAGS / THEIR EARLY HISTORY, AND THEIR DEVELOPMENT AT SEA ... BY W. G. PERRIN, ADMIRALTY LIBRARIAN ... CAMBRIDGE AT THE UNIVERSITY PRESS 1922'; the preface is signed 'W. G. PERRIN. January 1922'; and the OCR'd contents list (ch. III 'THE UNION FLAGS AND JACKS' p. 54, ch. V 'COLOURS OF DISTINCTION' with sub-sections at pp. 110, 124, 126, 129, 136) matches the running heads found in the body at those page numbers, so I located each quotation by its own running head rather than trusting a page estimate.
claims.game_impact: Keep the red cross on white, but move it to the mastheads and put a striped ensign (red/white, variable) on the staff aft, or simply give her no stern ensign. Change the ships.js comment: St George's was the masthead flag, not the ensign.

claims.claim: ships.js draws St George's cross as the colours of Cavendish's Desire, 1587.
claims.finding: Same correction as F-1a, and with an unexpected bonus: the Spanish side of the Santa Ana action independently describes Cavendish's colours. Fernandez Duro, extracting the sworn declarations of Tomas de Alzola (master of the Santa Ana) and Antonio de Sierra, writes that the English flagship came up to windward 'con banderas blancas y rojas, tocando los clarines' - with white and red flags, trumpets sounding. Plural banderas, white and red: that fits St George at the mastheads plus a red-and-white striped ensign exactly, and it is the best single piece of evidence for this level. The device is right; a single plain cross flown aft is still the wrong flag in the wrong place.
claims.quote: "Llegó la capitana inglesa por barlovento, con banderas blancas y rojas, tocando los clarines"
claims.source: Cesáreo Fernández Duro, La Armada Invencible, t. I (Madrid: Est. tipográfico 'Sucesores de Rivadeneyra', 1884), p. 153, extracting the declarations of Tomás de Alzola and Antonio de Sierra; with Perrin, British Flags, pp. 115, 129
claims.retrieval_note: The plain _djvu.txt URL 404s for this item; I read archive.org/metadata to get the real filename ('Fernandez Duro La Armada invencible v 1_djvu.txt') and fetched that. Proof of identity: the title page reads 'LA ARMADA INVENCIBLE ... POR EL CAPITAN DE NAVÍO CESÁREO FERNANDEZ DURO, DE LA REAL ACADEMIA DE LA HISTORIA. TOMO I. MADRID'. I then proved the passage is the Santa Ana (not another prize) from its own heading two pages earlier - 'Declaracion que hizo Tomas de Alzola, maestre de la nao nombrada "Santa Ana", que robaron los ingleses en el cabo de San Lucas de la California' - and from the internal detail: left Cavite 2 July 1587, raised Cabo San Lucas 14 November, and Cavendish is named by name in the next paragraph. Running heads bracket it as p. 153.
claims.game_impact: Keep the red cross; add white-and-red colours at the mastheads. You can now cite the Spanish eyewitness for the visual, which is better than citing a flag chart.

claims.claim: ships.js draws St George's cross as the colours of Woodes Rogers's Duke, a Bristol privateer, 1709.
claims.finding: Wrong for 1709 by a specific, dated royal proclamation. A privateer's three flags were fixed by the Proclamation of July 1694, which ordered vessels holding letters of marque to wear, as Perrin summarises it (p. 125), 'in addition to the St George's flag at the masthead and the red ensign with canton of St George at the stern, "a Red Jack with the Union Jack described in a Canton of the upper corner thereof next the staff"'; Perrin adds that this distinguishing jack 'remained the distinguishing flag of a privateer until privateering was abolished in 1856.' The 1707 union then replaced St George in the canton of the red ensign: the Lord High Admiral's order to the Navy Board was 'to order St George's Cross to be taken out of all the ensigns and a Union Jack Flagg put into them in the roome thereof' (Perrin, pp. 118-119). So in 1709 the Duke should wear: the red ensign with the 1707 union canton aft, a RED jack with union canton at the bowsprit, St George at the masthead, and a pendant - Perrin cites Rogers himself being ordered to strike his pendant by the Arundel in August 1708. A plain St George's cross as her ensign is a flag about 35 years out of date. Separately, index.html's title-screen version gets the red ensign right but puts a plain UNION JACK at the bow; the Union jack was expressly forbidden to private commissioned ships without an Admiralty warrant (instructions of December 1681 and May 1693, quoted by Perrin pp. 124-125), though Perrin notes privateers wore it anyway and the 1704 privateer instructions muddled the point.
claims.quote: "That the merchants, captains, and others who shall have such letters of marque or commissions as aforesaid shall not weare in their said ships our Union flagg or jack (which is intended to distinguish our owne ships of warr from all others) at no time nor upon no pretence whatsoever"
claims.source: W. G. Perrin, British Flags (Cambridge, 1922), ch. V (ii) Private Men-of-War, pp. 124-126 (quoting the privateer instructions of December 1681 and the Proclamation of 12 July 1694), and ch. V (i), pp. 118-119 (the Order in Council of 21 July 1707)
claims.retrieval_note: Same verified Perrin file as F-1a. I located ch. V (ii) by its section head '(ii) PRIVATE MEN-OF-WAR' in the body and confirmed the page by the running head 'V] PRIVATE MEN-OF-WAR 125' immediately following the 1681 quotation. Independent cross-check that this is really the right section and not a summary: it cites Marsden, Law and Custom of the Sea (Navy Records Society), ii, 412 for the 1681 instructions, and it quotes Woodes Rogers's own Cruising Voyage on the pendant - which I then confirmed exists in my separately downloaded 1712 Rogers text.
claims.game_impact: Change: red ensign with pre-1801 union canton aft (index.html already draws this correctly - reuse texRedEnsign for the in-game Duke), a red jack with union canton at the bow, and drop the St George's cross from the ensign staff. On the title screen, swap the bow Union jack for the privateer's red jack.

claims.claim: ships.js draws St George's cross as the colours of Anson's Centurion, 1743.
claims.finding: Wrong on two counts. (1) The Centurion was one of His Majesty's ships in 1743, 36 years after the union was put into all ensigns; St George's cross had been taken out of English naval ensigns in 1707, and Perrin notes it had already fallen out of use by men-of-war outside home waters before 1707, to avoid confusion with Genoese ships. (2) The game draws no pendant, and the single most characteristic flag of this ship on this day was a broad pendant. Anson's own chaplain, who was aboard, records the moment the Centurion closed the galleon on 20 June 1743: she 'hoisted her broad pendant and colours' - two distinct things. Perrin (p. 105) records that officers given a squadron abroad wore the UNION broad pendant (the 'Budgee Pendant'), 'in analogy with the practice by which Admirals sent abroad were ordered to wear the Union flag when out of the Channel, instead of their squadronal flag', the first instance being Captain Aylmer in December 1690 ordered a pendant 'made with ye Union Crosses in place where other Distinction Pendants have only St Georges Crosse'. Anson was a commodore commanding a squadron abroad, so that is the flag the player should see at the main.
claims.quote: "Towards one o'clock, the Centurion hoisted her broad pendant and colours, she being then within gun-shot of the enemy"
claims.source: Richard Walter, A Voyage Round the World, in the Years MDCCXL, I, II, III, IV. By George Anson, Esq. (London: printed for the author, 1748), p. [378] (the engagement of 20 June O.S. 1743); with Perrin, British Flags, pp. 105, 118-119
claims.retrieval_note: Proof this is the 1748 first edition and not a later abridgement: the title page names 'RICHARD WALTER, M.A. Chaplain of his Majesty's Ship the Centurion, in that Expedition', the imprint 'Printed for the AUTHOR; By John and Paul Knapton, in Ludgate-Street. Mocexlviii', and 'Illustrated with Forty-Two COPPER-PLATES'. I then proved I had the right PASSAGE, not a paraphrase, by reading it continuously from the sighting at sunrise on '20th of June, O. S.' through the broad-pendant line to the printed signature '( 379)' on the following leaf. Long-s OCR ('ſ' read as 'f') is silently normalised in the quotation; the sentence is otherwise verbatim.
claims.game_impact: Change: union-canton ensign (the red ensign is the safe default - it was the legal ensign of Great Britain and Howe in 1782 still ordered 'In action, all the ships in the fleet are to wear red ensigns'), a Union flag as jack, and above all a UNION BROAD PENDANT at the main. Adding the pendant is the single cheapest way to make the Centurion read as a king's ship rather than a privateer.

claims.claim: ships.js: the Cross of Burgundy is 'what Spanish ships wore at sea' in 1579 and 1587.
claims.finding: I could not establish this, and the two period traces I did find point elsewhere - to the ROYAL ARMS. (1) The chief flag of a Habsburg fleet was the royal standard bearing the arms: Fernandez Duro describes the blessing and delivery of the Armada's royal standard in Lisbon cathedral in 1588, 'la régia insignia en que se ostentaban las figuras de Jesucristo y de la Vírgen María sobre las armas' - Christ and the Virgin over the arms - carried in procession to the flagship under salute. (2) For ordinary Spanish merchantmen at sea, Perrin's account of the taking of two Spanish ships by the Amity of London in 1592 records that 'The Spaniards were displaying a flag with the arms of the King of Spain, which caused the English to "judge them rather ships of warre then laden with marchandise."' Neither source mentions a saltire. I am NOT asserting the Cross of Burgundy was absent - Habsburg ships carried banners, flámulas and streamers in profusion and it may well have been among them - but the game's code comment states a fact I cannot support for these two dates, and the flag that the sources do name is a different one.
claims.quote: "were displaying a flag with the arms of the King of Spain, which caused the English to 'judge them rather ships of warre then laden with marchandise'"
claims.source: W. G. Perrin, British Flags (Cambridge, 1922), pp. 189-190, citing Hakluyt, Voyages, vii, 103; and Cesáreo Fernández Duro, La Armada Invencible, t. I (Madrid, 1884), pp. 45-46
claims.retrieval_note: Both files identity-proved as above. I searched the whole Perrin text for every occurrence of 'Spain', 'Spanish', 'Spaniard' and 'Burgundy' (21 hits total): the only Burgundy hit is the Duke of Burgundy campaigning with the French, and Perrin - writing on British flags - nowhere treats the Spanish ensign. That is a genuine null in the best English-language flag authority, not an omission in my search. In Fernandez Duro I searched for 'Borgo', 'aspa de', 'estandarte' and 'banderas' across the whole volume; 'Borgoña' occurs once, in a royal style ('Duque de Borgoña, de Bravante y Milan'), never as a flag.
claims.game_impact: Rewrite the ships.js comment: do not claim the Cross of Burgundy for 1579/1587. For those two levels the defensible flag is a white or coloured banner bearing the royal arms of Spain, plus devotional banners. If you want one device for all four eras for art reasons, say so as a deliberate simplification rather than a historical claim.

claims.claim: ships.js: the Cross of Burgundy is what Spanish ships wore at sea in 1743.
claims.finding: This is the find of the cluster, and it is better than the game's claim because it is more precise. The Ordenanzas of 1748 - five years after Anson took the Covadonga, same reign, Spain's own naval regulations - have a whole Titulo on flags, and it divides them: Art. I, ships of the ARMADA wear 'la Vandera ordinaria nacional blanca, con el Escudo de mis Armas' (the ordinary national flag, white, with the royal arms). Art. II, that flag is forbidden to PRIVATE ships, 'no podrán usar los de Particulares, sino de la blanca con Cruz de Borgoña' - private ships wear the white flag with the Cross of Burgundy - 'Pero los Navíos, que fueren armados en Guerra, y Mercancía, ó solamente en Guerra, podrán añadir, en medio de la Cruz, el Escudo de mis Armas' (ships armed for war-and-trade, or for war alone, may add the royal arms in the middle of the cross). So the Cross of Burgundy WAS worn at sea at this date, on a white field - but by non-Armada ships, and an armed trader added the arms in the centre. Walter calls the Covadonga 'a vessel fitted out principally for traffic' while noting she mounted 36 guns and 28 pedreroes and was commanded by a 'General': that is precisely Art. II's armed-for-war-and-trade category, i.e. white, Cross of Burgundy, royal arms in the middle of the cross. Walter's own eyewitness line is consistent and usefully two-part: she was 'hoisting Spanish colours, and having the standard of Spain flying at the top-gallant mast-head' - an ensign plus a royal standard. The game's flag is therefore right in kind for 1743 and wrong in detail: it is missing the royal arms, and the field is drawn cream (#efe6d2) where the regulation says white.
claims.quote: "De esta Vandera, que es distintiva de los Navíos de la Armada, no podrán usar los de Particulares, sino de la blanca con Cruz de Borgoña: Pero los Navíos, que fueren armados en Guerra, y Mercancía, ó solamente en Guerra, podrán añadir, en medio de la Cruz, el Escudo de mis Armas."
claims.source: Ordenanzas de su Magestad para su Real Armada (Madrid: Imprenta de Juan de Zuñiga, 1748), parte primera, Título Tercero, 'De las Vanderas, y Insignias, de que han de usar los Navíos de la Armada', arts. I-II, pp. 128-129; with Richard Walter, A Voyage Round the World (London, 1748), pp. [377], [390]
claims.retrieval_note: Found by searching Internet Archive for title:(ordenanzas) AND title:(armada), which returned only three candidates (1748, 1791, 1793); the 1748 is the only pre-1785 one. Identity proved from the title page - 'ORDENANZAS DE SU MAGESTAD PARA SU REAL ARMADA ... En Madrid: En la Imprenta de Juan de Zuñiga. Año de M DCC XLVIII' - and from the royal style opening 'DON FERNANDO, POR LA GRACIA DE DIOS, Rey de Castilla, de León, de Aragón...', which fixes the reign as Ferdinand VI. CRITICAL retrieval detail: a search for 'bandera/pabellón' returned nothing and I nearly recorded a false null; the 1748 orthography is 'Vandera', and searching that turned up 50 hits including the section head at p. 128. I then read the Título continuously through arts. I-VII to be sure art. II is a rule about ships and not, say, about boat flags, and to catch art. III. OCR here confuses long-s and f ('ufaran' for 'usarán'); I have normalised that and the 'b' for 'ó' in the quotation and nothing else.
claims.game_impact: Keep the Cross of Burgundy for 1743 but fix it: pure white field, and add the royal arms in the centre of the saltire, because the galleon is an armed trader not a ship of the Armada. Add a second flag at the main topgallant masthead for the royal standard - Walter saw one. And rewrite the comment: the Cross of Burgundy was the PRIVATE/merchant flag; a Spanish warship wore white with the royal arms.

claims.claim: ships.js: the Cross of Burgundy is what Spanish ships wore at sea in 1709.
claims.finding: Probable but not proved. The 1748 Ordenanzas open art. I with 'POR ahora usarán' - 'for now they shall use' - which implies a pre-existing practice it is confirming rather than inventing, but it gives no date and I found no earlier Spanish naval flag ordinance. The one eyewitness I have for 1709 names a flag but not a device: Rogers, on the bigger Manila ship (the Begoña) that beat him off, 'She kept a Spanish Flag at her Main-top-mast Head all the time she fought us.' That tells you position (main topmast head) and nothing about the pattern. Web searching for a Felipe V naval flag decree returned only Wikipedia, blogs and a flag retailer; the one decree those name, 28 February 1707, is an ARMY colours decree (bandera coronela, 'según estilo de sus tropas'), not naval, so I am not willing to use it.
claims.quote: "She kept a Spanish Flag at her Main-top-mast Head all the time she fought us"
claims.source: Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London: printed for A. Bell and B. Lintot, 1712), p. 302 (engaging the bigger Manila ship, 26 December 1709)
claims.retrieval_note: Identity proved from the title page: 'A CRUISING VOYAGE ROUND THE WORLD: First to the South-Seas, thence to the East-Indies ... Begun in 1708, and finish'd in 1712 ... By Captain WOODES ROGERS, Commander in Chief on this Expedition, with the Ships Duke and Dutchess of Bristol.' Proof I had the right ENGAGEMENT and not the earlier one: the chapter head reads 'Engaging the bigger Manila Ship', the marginal note 'Take her' belongs to the other action, and this passage sits between the Begoña's particulars ('she was call'd the Bigonia, of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns') and the committee minute of 'December 2[6]' signed by Rogers, Courtney and Dampier. Searching for 'Begoña' alone would have missed it: Rogers spells it 'Bigonia'.
claims.game_impact: Do not claim the Cross of Burgundy as established for 1709. Either use it and say in the comment that it is extrapolated back from the 1748 Ordenanzas, or flag the level as uncertain. What you CAN state from the record is the position: a Spanish flag at the main topmast head.

claims.claim: index.html: 'the Spaniard wears the CROSS OF BURGUNDY, used at sea until 1785' - i.e. the modern red-yellow-red ensign is 1785 and therefore out for all four eras.
claims.finding: The conclusion is safe; the stated date is not something I proved from a source I am willing to cite. What is solidly established is the premise: in 1748 Spain's own naval regulations prescribe a WHITE flag (with royal arms for the Armada, with the Cross of Burgundy for private ships). Red-yellow-red is therefore certainly wrong for 1579, 1587, 1709 and 1743, which is all the game needs. The 1785 date itself I could not confirm from a primary or scholarly text: every search result was tertiary (Wikipedia, blog posts, a flag shop, a Facebook post by the Armada), the BNE and datos.bne.es record pages returned 403 to WebFetch and a Cloudflare block page to curl, and the one institutional PDF I could reach (catedranaval.com) would not yield text. The decree's reported preamble - that the old national flag was being mistaken 'a largas distancias o con vientos calmosos' - is exactly the kind of detail I should not repeat on blog authority.
claims.quote: "POR ahora usarán todos los Navíos de la Armada de la Vandera ordinaria nacional blanca, con el Escudo de mis Armas, hasta que Yo tenga a bien disponer otra cosa"
claims.source: Ordenanzas de su Magestad para su Real Armada (Madrid, 1748), Título Tercero, art. I, p. 128
claims.retrieval_note: Same identity-proved 1748 Ordenanzas as F-2b. The negative half of this finding is a recorded null, not a gap: I tried datos.bne.es/buscar (403), bdh.bne.es/bnesearch/detalle (403 to WebFetch; a 1.3 MB Cloudflare block page headed 'SE HA BLOQUEADO EL ACCESO POR PARTE DE LOS SISTEMAS DE SEGURIDAD DE BIBLIOTECA NACIONAL DE ESPAÑA' to curl with a browser user-agent), europeana.eu item page (403), and the catedranaval.com PDF (fetched, 182 KB, no extractable text).
claims.game_impact: Keep the conclusion, drop or hedge the bare '1785'. Safer comment wording: 'Spain's 1748 naval ordinances prescribe a white flag, so the modern red-yellow-red is out for every era in this game.' That is a claim you can hand a referee.

claims.claim: play.html on screen and ships.js in comment: 'A square rig will not lie within about five points of the wind' (about 56 degrees) for the English ships; 'a Manila galleon not closer than about six and a half' (73 degrees). Code polars: irons 55/56/58/60 degrees for Golden Hind/Desire/Duke/Centurion, 70 degrees for the galleon.
claims.finding: Five points is not the square-rig figure. It is the figure for SLOOPS AND SMALL CRAFT, and Falconer says so in the same sentence. The standard period definition: 'In this manner of sailing the keel commonly makes an angle of six points with the line of the wind; but sloops, and some other small vessels, are said to sail almost a point nearer.' Six points is 67.5 degrees. Worse for the game, that is the HEADING, not the track: 'All vessels, however, are supposed to make nearly a point of lee-way, when close-hauled, even when they have the advantage of a good sailing-breeze and smooth water.' Falconer works the arithmetic out explicitly under TACKING - a ship heading WNW on a northerly wind, with leeway 'only one point, (and indeed it is seldom less in the smoothest water)', makes good W by N - so the course made good close-hauled is about SEVEN points, 79 degrees. The game therefore has its English square-riggers a full point more weatherly than the period authority, and it has borrowed the small-craft number; the irony is that five points is roughly right for doghole's schooner, from which this physics was ported. The galleon's 70 degrees is, by accident, about right for a generic square-rigger's heading. I found no period figure for a laden galleon specifically (see nulls).
claims.quote: "In this manner of sailing the keel commonly makes an angle of six points with the line of the wind; but sloops, and some other small vessels, are said to sail almost a point nearer. All vessels, however, are supposed to make nearly a point of lee-way, when close-hauled, even when they have the advantage of a good sailing-breeze and smooth water."
claims.source: William Falconer, An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (London: T. Cadell, 1769), s.v. CLOSE-HAULED; and s.v. TACKING (the leeway arithmetic); and s.v. SAILING ('a ship in that situation will sail nearly within six points of the wind')
claims.retrieval_note: Identity proved from the title-page block 'AN UNIVERSAL DICTIONARY OF THE MARINE' plus a bound-in bookseller's note on the front leaf, 'FALCONER (William). An Universal Dictionary of the Marine ... London, 1769. First edition.' Falconer is unpaginated and alphabetical, so a page citation would be false precision; I cite by headword and verified each headword sits in correct alphabetical position (CLOSE-HAULED between CLINCHER-WORK and CLOSE-QUARTERS; SAILING between SAIL and 'Order of Sailing'; TACKING before 'beating or turning to windward'). I also checked that the six-points statement is not a one-off: it appears independently under CLOSE-HAULED, under SAILING, and is worked arithmetically under TACKING. OCR long-s is normalised in the quotation ('fix points' -> 'six points', 'Hoops' -> 'sloops').
claims.game_impact: Change the numbers and the on-screen line. Defensible values: English square-riggers irons ~67-68 degrees (six points), galleon ~73-79 degrees (seven to seven and a half points, worse because deep-laden and foul). Keep the relative ranking - it was always the point of the table. If you want to be really good, model the extra point of leeway separately so the player's TRACK is a point worse than her heading: Falconer says so twice and no game does it. The on-screen text should read 'about six points' - and you can now put Falconer's sentence in the sources table.

claims.claim: vessel.js and play.html: she 'is fastest with the wind on the quarter' - i.e. a square-rigger is faster on a broad reach than on a dead run. Code bestA = 135-140 degrees for the English ships.
claims.finding: Confirmed verbatim by the period authority, with the mechanism given, and the game's 135 degrees is exactly the angle Falconer means. Under SAILING he walks a diagram of the 32 points: close-hauled is six points off the wind, and 'six points large' from there - twelve points, 135 degrees - is the quarter. His words: 'The ships h and q, steering S. E. and S. W. have the wind six points large, or more properly on the quarter, which is considered as the most favourable manner of sailing, because all the sails co-operate to increase the ship's velocity; whereas, when the wind is right aft, as in the ship m, it is evident, that the wind, in its passage to the foremost sails, will be intercepted by those which are farther aft.' He adds the detail that on a dead run the fore topsail and fore topgallant are 'entirely becalmed' and might be furled but for their value in preventing broaching-to. One small refinement: the galleon's bestA of 150 degrees is three points on the quarter, which Falconer treats as a distinct and less favourable trim than the quarter proper; 135-140 is the authority's figure.
claims.quote: "have the wind six points large, or more properly on the quarter, which is considered as the most favourable manner of sailing, because all the sails co-operate to increase the ship's velocity; whereas, when the wind is right aft, as in the ship m, it is evident, that the wind, in its passage to the foremost sails, will be intercepted by those which are farther aft"
claims.source: William Falconer, An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (London, 1769), s.v. SAILING (describing fig. 3, plate IX)
claims.retrieval_note: Same identity-proved Falconer. I read the SAILING entry straight through from its definition to the four-fold summary ('close hauled, large, quartering, and afore the wind') so that the quoted sentence is read in sequence with the ship-by-ship walk of the compass that gives 'six points large' its meaning - without that context the phrase could be misread as six points off the wind rather than six points from close-hauled. Long-s normalised.
claims.game_impact: Keep it exactly as is, and quote Falconer in the sources table - 'the most favourable manner of sailing' is a better line than any paraphrase. Consider pulling the galleon's bestA back from 150 to ~140.

claims.claim: ships.js: the galleon is 'slower than any of you' - a notably poor sailer, slower than an English private ship of the period - and the chase premise that 'the galleon runs in her best point of sail, and you must be faster'.
claims.finding: The ponderousness is defensible; 'slower than any of you' is not established, and the RUNNING is contradicted by both best-documented cases. What the record supports: she was huge and massively built. Rogers: 'These large Ships are built at Manila with excellent Timber, that will not splinter; they have very thick Sides, much stronger than we build.' The Begoña was 'of about 900 Tuns, and could carry 60 Guns', with 'above 450' men; the Covadonga, per Walter, 'was much larger than the Centurion, and had five hundred and fifty men, and thirty-six guns mounted for action, besides twenty-eight pedreroes', and was 'a vessel fitted out principally for traffic'. What the record does NOT support: (a) that she was uniformly slow - Rogers's prisoners said of the two Manila ships that the bigger one had parted company three months earlier and was reckoned already at Acapulco, 'she sailing better than this Ship', so one galleon outsailed the other; and Rogers's own Marquiss 'did not sail well enough to come up to their Assistance', so an English private ship could be the slow one. (b) That she ran. Both famous galleons stood and fought. Walter: 'The Commodore was surprized to find, that during all this interval the galeon did not change her course, but continued to bear down upon him; for he hardly believed, what afterwards appeared to be the case, that she knew his ship to be the Centurion, and resolved to fight him'; she then 'brought to under top-sails'. The Begoña 'lay driving' while Rogers lay alongside, and his committee signed a minute resolving 'to forbear any further Attempts upon her, having no Probability of taking her'. As for chase times, both are hours, not minutes: Cavendish 'gave them chase some 3 or 4 houres, standing with our best advantage and working for the winde' before getting up with the Santa Ana, and Drake sighted the Cacafuego 'about three of the clocke' and boarded 'about sixe of the clocke'. Recorded speeds in knots: I found none for a galleon. Walter's only knot figures are the Centurion going 'at the rate of six or seven knots' with a prize in tow, and a Spanish squadron ship running before a storm under foresail alone at 'ten knots an hour'.
claims.quote: "The Commodore was surprized to find, that during all this interval the galeon did not change her course, but continued to bear down upon him; for he hardly believed, what afterwards appeared to be the case, that she knew his ship to be the Centurion, and resolved to fight him"
claims.source: Richard Walter, A Voyage Round the World (London, 1748), pp. [377-380], [390]; Woodes Rogers, A Cruising Voyage Round the World (London, 1712), pp. 294, 299, 302-303; Francis Pretty's narrative of Cavendish, in Hakluyt, The Principal Navigations (Glasgow: James MacLehose, 1903-05), xi. 323-324; Drake's famous voyage, ibid., xi. 116
claims.retrieval_note: THIS IS WHERE A RETRIEVAL WENT WRONG AND I CAUGHT IT. My first Hakluyt download, identifier 'principalnavigat011hakl', is catalogued as volume 11 and returned HTTP 200 with 1.16 MB of plausible-looking text - but grepping 'Candish' found hits only in a contents list and in index lines, and reading the body at line 5000 turned up Marlowe's verse and 60,000 lines of general index. It was the Glasgow edition's index volume wearing a v.11 label. I discarded it and probed three further candidates by downloading each and counting body occurrences of 'Candish' before reading any of them. The one I used, 'principalnaviga07unkngoog' (catalogued volume 11), passes: 23 body hits, Francis Pretty's narrative present and continuous, the Santa Ana fight bracketed by the printed running heads 'CANDISHS CIRCUMNAVIGATION a.d. 1587' and the marginal note 'The fight betweene the S. Anna and us', and the printed folio reference '[III. 817.]' to Hakluyt's 1600 edition. Also note a spelling trap: searching 'Santa Anna' found only Brazilian place-names; the narrative spells it 'S. Anna'. Rogers and Walter identity-proved as in F-1c and F-1d.
claims.game_impact: Keep her ponderous, keep her thick-sided, drop 'slower than any of you' as a stated fact. Better still, change the premise: the historical galleon does not run, she shortens sail and waits for you, and you lose by being unable to hurt her. Rogers's committee minute is the real failure state, and it is more interesting than a stern chase. If you keep the chase for playability, say so in the sources table as a gameplay departure.

claims.claim: PLAN.md: 'Rule, Britannia!' (Arne, 1740), used as the title theme across all four levels.
claims.finding: Date, place and text confirmed from the 1740 first imprint; Arne's authorship confirmed from a later print of the same work. The 1740 quarto's title page reads 'Represented before Their Royal Highnesses The Prince and Princess of Wales, At CLIFFDEN, On the First of August, 1740. LONDON: Printed for A. Millar, over-against St. Clement's Church in the Strand, M DCC XL', and the Ode at the close of the masque begins 'When Britain first, at heaven's command, / Arose from out the azure main' with the refrain '"Rule Britannia, rule the waves; / Britons never will be slaves."' One honest caveat: the 1740 libretto names no composer. Arne's authorship I take from the 1773 print of the music, whose title page reads 'By Dr. ARNE, and other Masters' and whose advertisement recounts that Alfred was written by 'Mr. Thompson, in conjunction with Mr. Mallet, at the request of his Royal Highness Frederick Prince of Wales, and was performed at Cliffden-House, before their Royal Highnesses, on the first of August, 1740.' ANACHRONISM, which PLAN.md does not flag: 1740 postdates Drake 1579 by 161 years, Cavendish 1587 by 153, and Rogers 1709 by 31. It is in period only for Anson.
claims.quote: "When Britain first, at heaven's command, / Arose from out the azure main; / This was the charter of the land, / And guardian Angels sung this strain: / \"Rule Britannia, rule the waves; / Britons never will be slaves.\""
claims.source: [James Thomson and David Mallet], Alfred: a Masque. Represented before Their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales, at Cliffden, on the First of August, 1740 (London: A. Millar, 1740), the Ode, p. 40; and The Songs, Chorusses, &c. in The Masque of Alfred, as it is now revived at the Theatre-Royal, Drury-Lane ... By Dr. Arne, and other Masters (London: T. Becket, 1773), title page and advertisement
claims.retrieval_note: The 1740 item is one of eleven Alfred editions on Internet Archive spanning 1740-1781, several of them Mallet's heavily rewritten 1751+ versions; I deliberately took the 1740 imprint rather than a later one, because the whole point of the claim is the date. Identity proved from the title page and the imprint 'M DCC XL', and from the printed page number '40' in the running head 'ALFRED:' immediately above the Ode. I then fetched the 1773 songbook SEPARATELY to source the Arne attribution, rather than assume it, precisely because the 1740 text is silent on the composer - a 'summary is not the thing' trap: the famous date and the famous attribution come from two different documents. OCR of this item is poor (fraktur-style long-s garbling); the Ode's wording is legible and I have normalised long-s only.
claims.game_impact: Keep the attribution and date, which are solid. But add to PLAN.md's anachronism note: Rule, Britannia is also anachronistic for Rogers 1709, not just for Drake and Cavendish. Only the Anson level is clean.

claims.claim: PLAN.md: 'The British Grenadiers' (traditional), used as the victory cue in all four levels. What is its actual earliest datable form?
claims.finding: 'Traditional' is fair, but the tune has no secure early date and the standard authority says so outright. Chappell: 'The correct date of this fine old melody appears altogether uncertain, as it is to be found in different forms at different periods; but it is here placed in juxta-position to Sir Edward Noel's Delight, and All you that love good fellows, or The London Prentice, because evidently derived from the same source.' His own copy is late: 'The words are from a copy about a hundred years old, with the music' - i.e. roughly 1759, writing in 1859 - and the version he prints is 'as played by the band of the Grenadier Guards.' For the WORDS he gives a bracket in his appendix: they 'cannot be older than 1678, when the "Grenadier Company" was first formed, or later than the reign of Queen Anne, when grenadiers ceased to carry hand-grenades.' So: words c. 1678-c. 1714; no datable tune before the mid-eighteenth century. ANACHRONISM: flatly wrong for Drake 1579 and Cavendish 1587 (the word grenadier did not exist in English military use). For Rogers 1709 the words could just exist, but no contemporary tune is attested. Only Anson 1743 is comfortable, and even there the earliest surviving music is later.
claims.quote: "The correct date of this fine old melody appears altogether uncertain, as it is to be found in different forms at different periods"
claims.source: William Chappell, Popular Music of the Olden Time (London: Cramer, Beale & Chappell, 1859), vol. I, p. 152 (main entry, THE BRITISH GRENADIERS); and vol. II, p. 772 (Appendix note to p. 153)
claims.retrieval_note: Chappell's two volumes paginate separately but his index runs across both, and the index entry reads 'British grenadiers (The), 152, 772.' I nearly recorded the main entry as missing: I downloaded volume II first, found only the appendix note and an incidental Old King Cole comparison, and had to download volume I to reach p. 152. Identity and page proved by the running head 'ENGLISH SONG AND BALLAD MUSIC' with the printed folio '152' sitting immediately above the headword 'THE BRITISH GRENADIERS', and the appendix note in volume II is keyed 'p. 153' with the running head 'APPENDIX. 772'. I used Chappell rather than a web source because the song's tune-origin claims online (a 1588 Dutch march, and so on) are exactly the kind of thing Chappell himself declines to assert.
claims.game_impact: Keep the cue; change 'traditional' in PLAN.md to something checkable: 'words datable c. 1678-1714, tune of uncertain date, earliest copy with music c. 1750s (Chappell, 1859).' Add it to the anachronism note for the 1579 and 1587 levels.

claims.claim: PLAN.md: 'Marcha Real / Marcha Granadera' (anonymous, in print by 1761), rising when the galleon is sighted.
claims.finding: The 1761 date holds. 'Anonymous' and 'in print' do not. The Biblioteca Nacional de España holds the source, and its own catalogue record gives: title 'Libro de la ordenanza de los toques de pifanos y tambores que se tocan nuevamente en la ynfanta. española', year 1761, type 'Partituras', alternative title '[... (Manuscrito original)]' - a MANUSCRIPT, not a printed book. Creator: 'Espinosa de los Monteros, Manuel'. And the contents note names the piece and its composer in the same breath: 'La generala ; La samblea para marchar ; La marcha granadera ; El alto ; La retreta ; El bando ; La llamada ; La fagina ; La bandera o tropa ; La marcha de fusileros / Manuel Espinosa.' So the march is attributed in the source itself to Manuel Espinosa (de los Monteros), and the period title is 'La marcha granadera'; 'Marcha Real' is the later name. ANACHRONISM, and PLAN.md's flag is too narrow: it notes that the march 'postdates Drake and Cavendish by nearly two centuries', but 1761 also postdates Rogers 1709 by 52 years and Anson 1743 by 18. It is out of period for ALL FOUR levels.
claims.quote: "La generala ; La samblea para marchar ; La marcha granadera ; El alto ; La retreta ; El bando ; La llamada ; La fagina ; La bandera o tropa ; La marcha de fusileros / Manuel Espinosa."
claims.source: Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid, shelfmark reported as M/2791: Manuel Espinosa de los Monteros, Libro de la ordenanza de los toques de pifanos y tambores que se tocan nuevamente en la ynfanta. española, 1761 (manuscript score), BDH record bdh0000113427; catalogue metadata read via the Europeana Record API (data provider: National Library of Spain)
claims.retrieval_note: The BNE's own pages were unreachable (403 to WebFetch, Cloudflare block page to curl), so I did NOT take this from the blog and Wikipedia results that a search returned. Instead I queried the Europeana Record API, which serves the National Library of Spain's own catalogue metadata, and read the full record JSON. Proof the retrieval is the right item and not a near neighbour: dataProvider is 'National Library of Spain'; year is '1761'; the creator URI resolves inside the same record to an agent prefLabel 'Espinosa de los Monteros, Manuel'; the item's edmIsShownAt points at bdh-rd.bne.es viewer id 0000113427; and the contents field actually contains the string 'La marcha granadera', which is the specific thing I needed to verify rather than infer. The same query also returned a distinct 1769 item by the same composer ('Toques de guerra que deberán observar uniformemente los pifanos, clarinetes y tambores de S.M.'), which is a useful check that I am not looking at a later edition misdated to 1761. I have NOT seen the manuscript leaves themselves, so I am not vouching for the shelfmark M/2791, which came from a search snippet.
claims.game_impact: Fix PLAN.md: not anonymous - attributed to Manuel Espinosa de los Monteros in the source; not in print - a manuscript in the BNE; period title 'La marcha granadera'. And widen the anachronism note: 1761 is late for every one of the four levels, including Anson. Keep using it, say plainly that it is game music.

nulls: WHAT SPANISH SHIPS WORE AT SEA IN 1579 AND 1587 AS A MATTER OF REGULATION. Not established. Looked in: Perrin, British Flags (1922) - searched the whole text for 'Spain', 'Spanish', 'Spaniard', 'Burgundy' (21 hits); he is writing on British flags and never treats the Spanish ensign, and his single relevant aside is the 1592 Amity encounter. Fernandez Duro, La Armada Invencible, t. I - searched 'Borgo', 'aspa de', 'estandarte', 'banderas' across the volume; 'Borgoña' appears once and only as a royal style. Internet Archive searches for title:(ordenanzas) AND title:(armada) returned nothing earlier than 1748. No sixteenth-century Spanish naval flag ordinance located.

WHAT SPANISH SHIPS WORE AT SEA IN 1709. Not established. The 1748 Ordenanzas' 'POR ahora usarán' implies earlier practice but dates nothing. Web searches for a Felipe V naval flag decree returned only Wikipedia, blogs and a flag retailer; the one decree they name (28 February 1707) is an army colours decree, not naval, so I will not use it. The only period eyewitness I have is Rogers naming a 'Spanish Flag at her Main-top-mast Head' without a device.

THE TEXT OF THE 1785 REAL DECRETO. Could not read it. datos.bne.es/buscar: 403. bdh.bne.es record page: 403 to WebFetch; curl with a browser user-agent returned a 1.3 MB Cloudflare block page headed 'SE HA BLOQUEADO EL ACCESO POR PARTE DE LOS SISTEMAS DE SEGURIDAD DE BIBLIOTECA NACIONAL DE ESPAÑA'. europeana.eu item page: 403. catedranaval.com PDF: fetched (182 KB) but no extractable text. The decree's preamble is widely quoted on blogs; I have not repeated it.

WHICH SQUADRONAL ENSIGN HMS CENTURION WORE IN 1743 (red, white or blue). Not established. Walter 1748 says only 'her broad pendant and colours'. Perrin establishes the system and that the red was the principal and legal ensign of Great Britain, and quotes Howe's 1782 instruction that in action all ships wear red ensigns, but says nothing about Anson's squadron. No ship's log consulted.

ANY PERIOD FIGURE FOR HOW CLOSE A MANILA GALLEON WOULD LIE TO THE WIND. None found. Falconer 1769 has no galleon entry and gives one generic square-rig figure (six points of heading, about one point of leeway). Searched Walter 1748 and Rogers 1712 for 'points', 'close-hauled', 'weatherly' - neither gives a pointing figure for any ship. The game's 'six and a half points' for the galleon is an invention, though a plausible one.

ANY RECORDED SPEED IN KNOTS FOR A MANILA GALLEON. None found. Searched Walter 1748 for 'knots' (4 hits, none a galleon: the Centurion at 'six or seven knots' with a prize in tow; the Spanish Asia at 'ten knots an hour' running before a storm under foresail) and Rogers 1712 for 'knots' (3 hits, all the word 'knotty' or a rope knot). No log-line figures for either side's galleon.

ARNE'S AUTHORSHIP OF RULE, BRITANNIA FROM A 1740 IMPRINT. Not available: the 1740 Millar quarto of Alfred names no composer. I sourced the attribution from the 1773 printing of the music instead, and have said so rather than letting the 1740 citation appear to cover both facts.
surprises: THE SANTA ANA WAS UNARMED, AND THE SPANISH SIDE SAYS SO UNDER OATH. Fernandez Duro, La Armada Invencible, t. I, p. 153, extracting the sworn declarations of Tomas de Alzola (her own master) and Antonio de Sierra: 'La nao no llevaba artillería ni otras armas' - the ship carried no artillery nor any other arms. The merchant passengers mustered 'como docena y media de espadas y rodelas', the captain had 'dos arcabuces y un frasco de pólvora', and the sailors fought with 'los hierros de las bombas y piedras del lastre' - the pump irons and the ballast stones. Against that, 'la nave inglesa ... sosteniendo el fuego de artillería con 29 piezas y dos lombardas pedreras que tenía'. The English narrative corroborates by omission: Pretty says the Spaniards repelled the first boarding with 'lances, javelings, rapiers, & targets, & an innumerable sort of great stones'. A 1587 level in which the galleon fires a broadside is wrong in kind, not in degree. The game's own real drama for that level is an unarmed 700-ton ship with high close fights holding off 50 or 60 boarders for five or six hours.

THE DATE CROSS-CHECK IS PERFECT AND IS FREE AUTHENTICITY. Pretty dates the Santa Ana capture 4 November 1587 (Old Style); the Spanish declarations say they raised Cabo San Lucas on 14 November. That is exactly the ten-day Julian/Gregorian gap. Two independent archives, two calendars, same day. Worth a line in the sources table.

ROGERS TOOK HIS GALLEON BY DECOY, AND THE RIGHT FALSE FLAG FOR 1709 IS FRENCH. PLAN.md already wants a false-colours mechanic; the record names the flag. Rogers, p. 292: 'We then hoisted a French Ensign, and fired a Gun, (which the Stranger answer'd).' France and Spain were allies in that war, so a French ensign is what a Spaniard would answer. The game draws only St George, Burgundy and a white flag.

SPAIN'S OWN REGULATIONS MAKE FALSE COLOURS A COURT-MARTIAL OFFENCE, WHICH IS A FREE ASYMMETRY. Ordenanzas de su Magestad para su Real Armada (1748), Título Tercero, art. III: a ship of the Armada shall neither give nor receive a salute without her own flag, 'ni combatirá con Vandera falsa, pena de privación de Empleo a el Oficial que le mande' - nor fight under a false flag, on pain of the commanding officer's dismissal. The English privateer decoys; the Spaniard legally cannot. That is a better mechanic than giving both sides the same trick.

NEITHER FAMOUS GALLEON RAN, AND THE REAL FAILURE STATE IS A SIGNED MINUTE. The Covadonga bore down on the Centurion and brought to under topsails to fight. The Begoña 'lay driving' and beat Rogers off; his committee then signed, on board the Duke, a written resolution 'to forbear any further Attempts upon her, having no Probability of taking her, but to do our endeavours to secure the Prize we have already took' - undersigned Woodes Rogers, Stephen Courtney, William Dampier and five others. A level that ends with the player's own officers voting to give her up would be more faithful, and far more memorable, than a stern chase.

ANSON NEVER LAY AT CABO SAN LUCAS. play.html's briefing says the player lies 'in the bay under the lee of the cape, where the English lay for her twice in life'. Walter 1748 puts the Centurion's station off 'Cape Espiritu Santo, on the Island of Samal' in the Philippines - the galleons' first landfall from Acapulco - and the capture seven leagues off a port there. Drake's prize, the Cacafuego, was taken at 'Cape de San Francisco, about 150 leagues from Panama', and was a Peru silver ship, not a Manila galleon at all. The two who actually lay off Cabo San Lucas are Cavendish 1587 and Rogers 1709. 'Twice in life' is right; two of the four captains are in the wrong ocean.

FALCONER HANDS YOU THE EXACT LEEWAY MECHANIC NO GAME MODELS. Twice he says a close-hauled ship makes nearly a point of leeway 'even when they have the advantage of a good sailing-breeze and smooth water', and that 'the angle of lee-way, however, enlarges in proportion to the increase of the wind and sea'. So the player's TRACK should be about a point worse than her heading, and should get worse as the breeze freshens. Since doghole's vessel.js already has a leeway term, this is cheap and it is the single most period-correct thing you could add.

THE 1748 ORDENANZAS GIVE THE GALLEON A FLAG NO ONE DRAWS. Art. II: an armed trader may put the royal arms in the middle of the Cross of Burgundy. Walter independently saw the Covadonga with 'Spanish colours' AND 'the standard of Spain flying at the top-gallant mast-head', and records that a Spanish officer was risking his life to re-nail the standard to the main topgallant masthead during the fight, until Anson ordered his marksmen to stop firing at him. A white flag with a red raguly saltire charged with the royal arms, plus a royal standard aloft that the enemy deliberately spares - that is a better galleon than the plain cream saltire now in ships.js.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding holds on all four tests.

(1) QUOTE IS GENUINELY VERBATIM. I downloaded their URL (archive.org/download/universaldiction00will) and proved identity before trusting it: the title page reads "AN UNIVERSAL DICTIONARY OF THE MARINE ... By WILLIAM FALCONER, Author of The Shipwreck. LONDON: Printed for T. Cadell ... MDCCLXIX." The passage sits at line 16619 under SAILING, after the text sets the scene: "the plan of a number of ships proceeding on various courses are represented by fig. 3. plate IX. which exhibits the thirty-two points of the compass, of which C is the center: the direction of the wind, which is northerly, being expressed by the arrow." The sentence reads (long-s normalised, OCR noise marked): "The [s]hips h and q, [s]teering S. E. and S. W. have the wind [s]ix points large, [or] more properly on the quarter, which is con[s]idered as the mo[s]t favourable manner of [s]ailing, becau[s]e all the [s]ails co-operate to increa[s]e the [s]hip's velocity; whereas, when the wind is right aft, as in the [s]hip m, it is evident, that the wind, in its pa[ss]age to the foremo[s]t [s]ails, will be intercepted by tho[s]e which are farther aft." Their rendering matches word for word. The supplementary detail they report is also real: of ship m, "these latter are by consequence entirely becalmed, and might therefore be furled, to prevent their being fretted by flapping against the mast, but that their effort contributes greatly to prevent the ship from broaching-to."

CORROBORATED IN A SECOND PHYSICAL COPY. To rule out a one-scan artifact I pulled an independent edition, archive.org/download/universaldiction00falc (1780, UCLA copy, identity proved by its Admiralty dedication and the "Fifth Edition" Shipwreck advertisement). Same sentence, line 16150, trivial accidentals only ("its"/"it's", semicolon for comma, "further" for "farther").

(2) NOT OUT OF CONTEXT. The SAILING entry is a systematic walk of the 32 points answering exactly the question at issue, and Falconer builds an explicit speed gradient toward the quarter: at the beam "the effort of the wind being applied nearer to the line of the ship's course, her velocity is greatly augmented"; at three points large "the course accelerated in proportion"; at the quarter, "the most favourable manner of sailing"; then the run as the falling-off case. The entry closes with the four-fold division "close hauled, large, quartering, and afore the wind," so quartering and running are distinct trims he is deliberately comparing.

(3) GEOMETRY VERIFIED TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS, so "six points large" cannot be misread as six points off the wind. CLOSE-HAULED (line 6033) fixes the baseline: "In this manner of sailing the keel commonly makes an angle of six points with the line of the wind" = 67.5 degrees, hence six points large = 135 degrees. And the diagram settles it without the arithmetic: wind northerly, ships h and q steering S.E./S.W. = 135/225 degrees true wind angle. The game's 135 degrees IS Falconer's ships h and q. The close-hauled ships B and y steer E.N.E./W.N.W. = 67.5 degrees, which checks the baseline a third time.

(4) NO CONTRARY AUTHORITY FOUND. I searched the volume for any statement that a ship makes best speed afore the wind and found none; LARGE (line 11555) instead reinforces the quarter ("when it crosses the line of a ship's course in a favourable direction, particularly on the beam or quarter"). I checked for a later revision that might have corrected the passage; the 1780 reprint is unchanged. Note this is a null result properly bounded: I did not obtain full text of Lever 1819 or Burney's 1815 revision (no IA full view available), so "no period authority contradicts" is established for Falconer and his reprints, not for the whole period literature.

(5) SUPPORTS THE CLAIM ITSELF, NOT SOMETHING ADJACENT. Same rig class (full-rigged ships of the 1760s Royal Navy), same comparison (quarter vs dead run), same quantity (velocity), and the mechanism is the correct one (blanketing of the fore topsail and fore topgallant by the main).

THREE SOFT SPOTS, none fatal and none in the claim as coded:
- Their refinement that the galleon's 150 degrees "is three points on the quarter" is loose. Falconer's three-points-on-the-quarter ships i and p steer "S. E. b S." (the 1780 copy prints this plainly, resolving the 1769 scan's garbled "S. E.J- S."), i.e. 146.25 degrees, not 150. His scale here counts points off dead-aft: one point on the quarter = S by E = 168.75, two = S.S.E. = 157.5, three = S.E. by S = 146.25, and the quarter proper = S.E. = 135.
- Falconer does not actually SAY 146.25 degrees is "less favourable." That is inference from "most favourable" attaching to the quarter alone. Sound inference, but it is not text, and the finding presents it as something Falconer "treats."
- 140 degrees is not a compass point in his scheme. The authority's figure is 135 degrees exactly; 140 falls between S.E. and S.E. by S. "135-140 is the authority's figure" slightly overstates: 135 is, 140 is merely within one point of it.

None of these touch the proposition under test. Verdict stands at CONFIRMED, with the caveat that the exact authority figure is 135 degrees and the "less favourable at 150" gloss is inferential.
verdicts.counter_evidence: No counter-evidence to the claim. The only corrections are to the finding's own refinement, from Falconer's text: ships i and p steer "S. E. b S." (= 146.25 degrees), not 150 degrees, so the galleon's 150 is not precisely "three points on the quarter"; and Falconer nowhere calls that trim "less favourable" in words, he only reserves "most favourable" for the quarter proper (S.E., 135 degrees). Also, 140 degrees is not a point of the compass in his 32-point scheme, so the authority's figure is 135 degrees alone rather than "135-140." Boundary on my search: I confirmed no contrary statement in Falconer 1769 and in the independent 1780 reprint, but I could not obtain full text of Burney's 1815 revision or Lever 1819, so the absence of a contrary period authority is unestablished beyond Falconer.

TEST 1 (quote verbatim?) PASSES, but I did not settle it from their OCR. Their file (bim_eighteenth-century_alfred-a-masque-repres_thomson-james_1740_djvu.txt) is heavily garbled, so I pulled the page image itself via the IA BookReader (ia800801, leaf n41, scale=2) and read it. The printed page reads, in italic: "When Britain first, at heaven's command, / Arose from out the azure main; / This was the charter of the land, / And guardian Angels sung this strain: / " Rule Britannia, rule the waves; / " Britons never will be slaves."" Their transcription is word-for-word correct, including the unelided "heaven's" (the 1773 Drury Lane songbook prints "heav'n's" at the same line, so this was worth checking) and the comma-less "Rule Britannia" of stanza 1, which becomes "Rule, Britannia" at stanza 6 of the same print.

CITATION ERROR, must be fixed before publication. They cite "the Ode, p. 40" and say they proved the retrieval partly "from the printed page number '40' in the running head." The page image shows the running head is "42 ALFRED" — the Ode is on p. 42, not p. 40. The OCR string "3 40 ALFRED:" they relied on is a misread of "42 ALFRED". The heading is also "An ODE.", not "ODE." Their stated retrieval proof is therefore partly built on an OCR artefact, even though the conclusion is right. The title-page half of their proof does hold: the file's opening leaf reads "Represented before Their Royal Highnesses The Prince and Princess of Wales, At CLIFFDEN, On the First of August, 1740. LONDON: Printed for A. Millar, over-against St. Clement's Church in the Strand, M DCC XL".

TEST 2 (context) PASSES. The Ode is not wrenched from context: on p. 42 the Hermit cues it ("Yet ere you go, in our lov'd country's praise, / That noblest theme, hear what his rapture breathes."), and it runs six stanzas to the close of the masque.

TEST 3 (contrary source) — I went looking and found their Arne evidence is ADJACENT, not support. The 1773 songbook they lean on is weaker than they represent. Its title page does read "By Dr. ARNE, and other Masters," but its advertisement says the piece "is now revived with some few alterations, and with some New Music; the favourite airs of Dr. Arne, as they stood in the Masque altered by Mallet, are reserved" — i.e. it credits Arne's airs as they stood in Mallet's 1751 rewrite, in a 1773 revival that admits new music by unnamed hands, and it never singles out the Ode. That document cannot by itself carry Arne's authorship of the 1740 music. The claim survives only because I found a real authority: W. Chappell, Popular Music of the Olden Time (London, 1859), vol. 2, pp. 686-87, which states that the music of this "ode in honour of Great Britain" "was composed by Dr. Arne for his masque of Alfred, and first performed at Cliefden House, near Maidenhead, on August 1, 1740." Two caveats Chappell raises that the finding does not: (a) the MUSIC was first printed not with Alfred but "at the end of the masque of The Judgment of Paris, which appeared before Alfred, — Arne having composed the music to both," so 1740 is a composition/first-performance date, not a publication date; (b) an attribution challenge once existed — Schoelcher's charge that Arne copied from Handel — which Chappell reports as refuted in Notes and Queries, 2nd ser. Separately, Chappell pp. 686-87 documents a live dispute over the WORDS (Thomson vs Mallet, turning on Mallet's own 1751 advertisement, which I also found reprinted verbatim in the 1773 songbook). That does not touch the claim, which names only Arne, but it should not be glossed over if the sources table ever credits the lyricist.

TEST 4 (does it support the claim?) PASSES for date, place, text and title; and now, on Chappell rather than on their 1773 inference, for Arne. Their unprompted anachronism flag is correct and is a point in their favour: 1740 postdates Drake 1579, Cavendish 1587 and Rogers 1709, and is in period only for Anson.
verdicts.reasoning: I tried to break this four ways and it did not break, but two repairs are needed before it is published. The verbatim quote is genuinely verbatim — I verified it against the scanned page, not the OCR, because the OCR is unusable. The locator is wrong: the Ode is on p. 42 of the 1740 quarto, not p. 40, and their claimed retrieval proof ("the printed page number '40' in the running head") rests on an OCR misread of "42". The composer attribution, the one joint they themselves flagged as weak, is weaker than they allowed: the 1773 songbook credits "the favourite airs of Dr. Arne, as they stood in the Masque altered by Mallet" in a revival that announces "some New Music," so it attests Arne's music in the 1751/1773 stage versions and never names him as composer of the 1740 Ode. That is an adjacent document doing a job it cannot do. I replaced it with Chappell 1859, which states outright that Arne composed the music for Alfred, first performed at Cliveden on 1 August 1740. With that substitution the claim "'Rule, Britannia!' (Arne, 1740)" stands as CONFIRMED. I am not downgrading, because the defects are in the apparatus rather than the claim: fix the page to 42 and swap the Arne citation to Chappell. Chappell also adds a nuance worth carrying into the table — the music was first printed with The Judgment of Paris, not with Alfred, so 1740 dates composition and first performance only.
